With the commentary titled *Jyotsnā* by Brahmānanda;

They were established under their own control;

Śrīḥ.
The Haṭhayogapradīpikā (The Illuminating Lamp of Haṭha Yoga)
Accompanied by both the commentary and the vernacular explanation.
The First Instruction. Root Text.
Salutations be to that Śrī Ādinātha, by whom the science of Haṭhayoga was taught.
It shines like a staircase for one desiring to ascend to the lofty state of union with the King (the Supreme). || 1 ||
Commentary:
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Having bowed to the Guru, who is Śiva himself, this is being composed by Brahmānanda.
The Moonlight on the Haṭhapradīpikā, which illuminates the path of yoga. || 1 ||
Now, for the easy understanding of contemporary people,
having thoroughly grasped the heart of the Gorakṣasiddhānta,
I shall clearly explain even that which is extremely profound at the request of Meru Śāstrī and others.
The state of being. || 2 ||

The supremely compassionate Lord of Yogins, Svātmārāma, desiring to compose the *Haṭhapradīpikā*— which has liberation as its fruit by means of Rājayoga— for the benefit of those seeking emancipation, [proceeds] for the removal of obstacles thereto.

He first performs the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) characterized by salutation to the venerable Ādinātha, the founder of Haṭhayoga, beginning with the words "To the venerable Ādinātha... The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Salutation be to that venerable Ādinātha. He is both the "Ādi" (the primordial) and the "Nātha" (the Lord).
The meaning is that Ādinātha is Śiva, the Lord of All. "To the venerable Ādinātha" means: he whose beginning is the word *śrī* is *śrī-ādi*;
and he who is both *śrī-ādi* and *nātha* is *śrī-ādinātha*, to him.
"To Śrī-Ādinātha" means "to Śrīnātha Viṣṇu.
Regarding the absence of *yaṇ*-sandhi in the term "Śrī-ādināthāya," those learned in prosody maintain: "One may even commit a month's worth of sin, but one should avoid breaking the meter of speech."
It should be understood that [this is] due to tradition and the excellence of the pronunciation. In reality, however,

rather than accepting the non-composed reading (*asaṃhitapāṭha*), when the reading *śrī-ādināthāya* is accepted, it is not subsumed under the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the objective of the obligatory rule (*nityavidhi*).
Thus (p. 2) || Root Text ||
Having prostrated before the venerable Guru, the Lord, the yogi Svātmārāma teaches the science of Haṭha solely for the sake of Rājayoga. (2)
|| Commentary ||
Because of the possibility of its being fully established,
even for the two examples cited here, there is the defect arising from the destruction of the eternal nature of light due to such a disparity in the objects of comparison.

Furthermore, although literary critics have stated that the defect known as *asaṃmṛṣṭavidheyāṃśatā* (the failure to clearly distinguish the predicate element) arises because it is not accepted by grammarians, they themselves have occasionally admitted it—
as when the grammatical masters accept a *karmadhāraya* compound in cases such as *ekāj*.

Let the wise discern that because he is disregarded in every way, there is an extreme degree of contempt; let there be a state of prostration. The verb is in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood used for a request.
In response to the expectation "to whom?", he says: "By whom. That is, by whom—namely, Ādinātha—it was taught.
To Girijā belongs the science of Haṭhayoga. *Ha* and *ṭha* are "haṭhau," referring to the sun and the moon;

their union is *haṭhayoga*. By this, it is meant that *prāṇāyāma* is characterized by the unification of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths, which are denoted by the term *haṭha* as the sun and the moon.

Thus, the definition of Haṭhayoga is established. Accordingly, it has been stated by Gorakṣanātha in the *Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati*: "The letter 'Ha' is proclaimed as the Sun, and the letter 'Ṭha' is said to be the Moon."

"From the union of the sun and the moon, Haṭhayoga is proclaimed. The science that expounds this is Haṭhayogavidyā, which is to say, the Haṭhayogaśāstra. The instruction on the science of Haṭha given by Ādinātha to Girijā is found in the Mahākālayogaśāstra and other such works.
It is well-known. "Pronnata" means pre-eminently elevated;

because Rājayoga constitutes the higher stages (*uttarabhūmi*) relative to the lower stages (*adharabhūmi*) such as Mantra-yoga, Haṭha-yoga, and so forth, it possesses this quality of being pre-eminently elevated. And what is Rājayoga?
Asamprajñāta-yoga is characterized by the cessation of all mental modifications.

For the seeker of liberation who desires that state, it shines forth like a ladder; for it is a "ladder" (adhirohiṇī) in the sense that one ascends by means of it, and it shines forth—that is, it is especially radiant and beautiful—just as a staircase does. Just so:
Just as a staircase enables one who wishes to ascend a lofty palace to reach that palace without effort,
so too does the *haṭhadīpikā* enable one who wishes to ascend the lofty *rājayoga* to attain *rājayoga* without effort.
Thus it is said. This is the figure of speech known as *upamā* (simile). The meter is called *indravajrā*. || 1 ||

Having thus performed the auspicious rite characterized by salutation to the Supreme Guru, and because a multiplicity of auspicious rites is required when obstacles are numerous, [he performs] that which consists of salutation to his own guru.
Root Text
For those who do not know the royal yoga, due to the great darkness of delusion.
Commentary:
Performing an auspicious invocation, he demonstrates the subject matter, purpose, and other elements of this work:
having bowed down—that is, having prostrated with great devotion—to his own Guru, Śrīmad Guru, Śrīguru, Nātha, and Śrīgurunātha; by Svātmārāma.

The construction is as follows: "by that [yogi] who possesses yoga" (yoginā yogo 'syāsti tena); "only for the sake of Rājayoga" (kevalaṃ rājayogāya) means "solely for the purpose of Rājayoga," and thus the Haṭha-vidyā is taught. The intention of the word "only" (kevala-) is that the primary fruit of the science of Haṭha is indeed Rājayoga itself, and not the supernatural powers (siddhis).

The supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are merely incidental. Thus, the subject matter of this treatise is Haṭhayoga together with the fruit of Rājayoga; its result is liberation (*kaivalya*) through the gateway of Rājayoga; and the qualified seeker is one who desires that [liberation]. This constitutes the relationship between the treatise and its subject matter.

The relationship between the treatise and its subject matter is that of the expounder and the expounded (*pratipādyapratipādakabhāva*). The relationship between the treatise and liberation (*kaivalya*) is that of the means and the end (*prayojyaprayojakabhāva*). The relationship between the subject matter of the treatise—which is yoga accompanied by its fruit—and liberation is that of the means and the goal (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*).
Thus it has been said. || 2 ||
Now, one might object: "If Rājayoga is accomplished through mantra-yoga, saguṇa-dhyāna, nirguṇa-dhyāna, mudrās, and so forth alone, what is the purpose of the instruction on Haṭha-vidyā?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author states that] for those whose minds are distracted (vyutthita-citta), Rājayoga is not achieved through mantra-yoga and the like, but only through Haṭha-yoga.
Declaring the accomplishment of Rājayoga, he makes a formal promise regarding the treatise with the words: "By means of delusion... and so forth.

In the dense darkness consisting of the manifold forms of mantra-yoga and other such practices, there arises a delusion or error; because one who has set out for the sake of Rāja-yoga does not find it in each of those various means. And he will say later: "Without Rāja-yoga," and so forth.

Likewise, for those who do not know *rājayoga*—the word "ajānatām" meaning "of those who do not know"—for such ignorant persons, [it is] the knowledge of *rājayoga*; this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). He is a "doer" (*karaḥ*) because he acts;
thus, he is a "doer of mercy" (*kṛpākaraḥ*), or rather, a "mine of mercy" (*kṛpāyā ākaraḥ*). Such is he.
By this, it is stated that compassion for the ignorant alone was the motive for composing the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.

One who delights in one's own self (*svātmārāma*) undertakes [this work]. Because it is like a lamp (*pradīpikā*) that illuminates *haṭha*—that is, *haṭhayoga*—it is called the *Haṭhapradīpikā*. Alternatively, *haṭha*...
It is indeed a lamp because it illuminates the Royal Yoga (rājayoga); "he bears," "he maintains," or "he performs" it—meaning he brings it about.
By the phrase "one who delights in his own Self" (svātmārāma), it is indicated that he has attained the seventh stage of knowledge.
p. 4) || Root Text ||
Svātmārāma, the compassionate one, holds forth this Haṭhapradīpikā. || 3 ||
|| Commentary ||

It has been stated that he is "the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman. And so says the Śruti: "He who sports in the Self, who delights in the Self, and who is active—such a one is the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman. Furthermore, the seven stages have been described in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*: the stage of knowledge called "Pure Desire" (*śubhecchā*).
The first is proclaimed; the second is *vicāraṇā*; the third is *tanumānasā*; the fourth would be *satvāpatti*; then the one named *asaṃsakti*;
the sixth is *parārthābhāvinī*; and the seventh is remembered as *turyagā*. This is its meaning.
That which has the name "desire for the auspicious" (śubhecchā) is called śubhecchā.

Endowed with discrimination and dispassion, preceded by tranquility (śama) and the other [eight limbs], and characterized by an intense longing for liberation—this is declared by the yogis to be the first stage (bhūmikā) of knowledge; this is the remainder [of the sense].
The second stage of knowledge (*jñānabhūmi*) would be *vicāraṇā*, consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*).
When the mind, which grasps many objects, abandons those various objects and becomes like a continuous flow of activity directed toward a single object, that [stage] is *tanumānasī*.
The third stage of knowledge is that which consists of *tanumānasā*, characterized by *nididhyāsana* (contemplative meditation); this is the implied meaning. || 3 ||
These are the three stages of practice (*sādhanabhūmikā*). In these stages, one is called a "practitioner" (*sādhaka*).

Through these three stages, within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of a pure being (*śuddhasattva*), there arises a direct cognitive modification (*aparokṣavṛtti*) characterized by the realization "I am Brahman," which is termed the attainment of being (*sattvāpatti*).

The fourth is the stage of knowledge (*jñānabhūmi*). This is the fourth stage of fruition (*phalabhūmi*). In this stage, the yogi is called a "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*). This is the stage of *samprajñāta-yoga*. (4)

The three stages of asamprajñāta-yoga to be described hereafter follow immediately after the attainment of sattva; when the perfections known as "attainment of sattva" have been reached, there is the fifth stage of knowledge called "non-attachment," which belongs to one who is unattached to those perfections.
It may be so. In this state, the yogi emerges by himself. Having attained this stage, he is called the best among the knowers of Brahman. || 5 ||

That sixth stage of knowledge (*jñānabhūmi*) is "that which does not conceive of any object other than the Supreme Brahman" (*parārthābhāvinī*); in this stage, the yogi arises from meditation only when awakened by another. Having attained this—
He is called the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman. || 6 ||

The seventh stage is known as Turyagā. In this stage, the yogin does not undergo emergence from samādhi, whether by himself or through another. One who has attained this is called the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman. The scriptural authority for this has been stated right here; previously, this very [stage] was also mentioned.
He alone is called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta) and is referred to here by the term "one who delights in his own Self" (svātmārāma); enough with further elaboration. || 3 ||
p. 5) || Root Text ||
Indeed, Matsyendra, Gorakṣa, and others understand the science of Haṭha.
Or else, the yogi who delights in his own self knows it through its grace. || 4 ||
|| Commentary ||
By praising the science of haṭha because it has been practiced by the great, he demonstrates his own honor derived from having obtained that very science of haṭha from a great master.
Regarding the phrase "the science of Haṭha (haṭhavidyāṃ) indeed (hi)": the word "hi" indicates what is well-known. Matsyendra and Gorakṣa are those who are the first among them;
thus they are called "Matsyendragorakṣādyaḥ. By the word "ādya" (and others), Jālandharanātha, Bhartṛhari, Gopīcandra, and so forth are to be included. They...

They "know the science of Haṭha"—meaning they specifically understand the science of Haṭhayoga through its methods, characteristics, divisions, and fruits. He is "Svātmārāma," meaning one whose name is Svātmārāma; or else, the word [svātmārāma] serves as a conjunction. He is a "Yogin," meaning one possessed of yoga.

The grammatical construction is: "Know [this] by His grace," that is, "by the grace of Gorakṣa. That this knowledge was practiced even by the Supreme Great One, Brahmā, is stated in the *Yogiyājñavalkyasmṛti*:
"Hiraṇyagarbha is the speaker of Yoga; there is no other ancient one. And as for the status of being a speaker..."
Since it is preceded by mental activity, "mental" refers to the activity [of the mind], which implies traditional scripture (*āgama*).

And so says the Śruti: "Whatever one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech. This knowledge was spoken by the Blessed One to the Bhāgavatas, such as Uddhava and others; however, Śiva—

The yogi is indeed well-known. And thus, this Vidyā is practiced by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, who are the most excellent of all. Nor should it be suspected that the yogi was rejected by Vyāsa, the author of the Brahmasūtras;
for [he rejected] only the aspect of duality [by those who know the independence of Prakṛti].
Because it is rejected; however, [it is not rejected] in the case of yoga in the form of a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā*), since such cultivation is accepted by everyone. (p.
Root Text
Śrī Ādinātha, Matsyeṃdra, Śābara, Ānandabhairava, Cauraṅgī, Mīna, Gorakṣa, Virūpākṣa, and Bileśaya. || 5 ||
Commentary:

For without it, even happiness is impossible. Thus it is said in the Bhagavad Gītā: "There is no discernment for one who is undisciplined, nor is there contemplation for one who is undisciplined; there is no peace for one who does not contemplate, and for one who lacks peace, whence can there be happiness? Nārāyaṇatīrtha has also stated:

Through his own composed Brahma-sūtras, Vyāsa refuted by means of scriptural statements the notion of the reality of independence in Pradhāna and the reality of the distinction between consciousness and matter; he likewise refuted the yoga known as Bhāvanā,
as well as that yoga which bestows the self.

The wise one himself gave the exposition; therefore, among the commentaries and other works, it is considered by the masters led by Ācārya [Śaṅkara] that Yoga is esteemed there. Yet, in the Gītā, Yoga was made superior to others by the Blessed One; for that reason, Śuka and others have treated it here.

"The virtuous are exceedingly respectful. For it is stated by the Blessed One: "Having realized this, the yogi transcends all that merit and fruit which is prescribed in the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities, and gifts, and attains the supreme, primordial abode. What more need be said?

By stating that "even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*)," the Blessed One has described the excellence of even the seeker of yoga, let alone the yogi himself;
[this is also supported] by Nārada and other foremost devotees, as well as Yājñavalkya and other preeminent knowers of truth.
Because it is not contradictory even for devotees and those possessing knowledge [to practice this], we shall now conclude. || 4 ||

In order to generate interest in Haṭhayoga, he speaks of the Siddhas who attained mastery through the science of Haṭha, beginning with "Śrī Ādinātha" and so forth. Ādinātha is Śiva, the first lord among all lords; from him originated the Nātha tradition.

The followers of the tradition of Nātha say that [the lineage] has been set in motion. And he known as Matsyendra was a disciple of Ādinātha. Regarding this, there is the following oral tradition: once, while Ādinātha was staying on a certain island, thinking it to be a secluded place, he [bestowed the teaching] upon Girijā.
He taught yoga. A certain fish, staying in the water near the shore, heard that instruction on yoga and remained with a one-pointed mind and an immovable body.
Seeing him in such a state, [the teacher] thought, "He has heard the yoga," and [approached him].
The compassionate Ādinātha (Root Text, p. 7).
Maṃthāna, Bhairava, Yogī, Siddhi, Buddha, and Kaṃthaḍi.
Koraṇṭaka, Surānanda, Siddhapāda, and Carpaṭi. || 6 ||
Kānerī, Pūjyapāda, Nityanātha, Nirañjana, Kapālī, Bindunātha, and the one named Kākacaṇḍīśvara. || 7 ||
Commentary:

He sprinkled [the fish] with water. By that mere sprinkling, the lord of fishes (Matsyendra) attained perfection as a divine body. It is he whom they call Matsyendranātha. There was a certain Siddha named Śabara, and another named Ānandabhairava.
These form a mutual dvandva compound. "Chinnahastapāda" (one whose hands and feet are severed) is called *cauraṅgī* in the Hindustani language.
Once, while wandering the earth after having obtained yoga from Ādinātha...
By the mere glance of Matsyendranātha’s compassion, a certain thief dwelling in a forest had his hands and feet sprout; and he,
having his hands and feet restored through that grace, thinking "I am [whole] again," prostrated at his feet.
He prayed, "Grant me your grace. Matsyendra also favored him, and by virtue of that favor, he became the renowned Siddha known as Caurāṅgī. Mīna is Mīnanātha; Gorakṣa is Gorakṣanātha.
Those named Virūpākṣa and Bileśaya; [the compound] "cauraṅgīprabhṛtīnām" is a dvandva-samāsa. || 5 ||
"Maṃthāna, Bhairava, and Yogin" are adjectives qualifying all [the deities] beginning with Maṃthāna.
He whose name is Kākacaṇḍīśvara is so called; the others are clear. (p. 8) [Root Text]
Allāma, Prabhudeva, Ghoḍā, Colī, Ṭiṃṭiṇi, Bhānukī, Nāradeva, Khaṇḍa, and likewise Kāpālika. || 8 ||
These and other great Siddhas, by the power of Haṭhayoga, having shattered the staff of Death, roam about within the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa). || 9 ||
The practice of Haṭha is a sheltered hut for those scorched by the heat of all sufferings without exception.
Haṭha is the tortoise that serves as the foundation for all those engaged in yoga without exception. || 10 ||
|| Commentary ||
The word "tathā" (likewise) is used in the sense of conjunction.

"Those whose [beginning] is as previously stated" means those for whom the aforementioned ones are the first; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), Tārānātha and others are to be included. "Great" (mahāntaḥ) and "perfected ones" (siddhāḥ) means those whose sovereignty is unimpeded.
"By the power and efficacy of Haṭhayoga" means *haṭhayogaprabhāvataḥ*.

The suffix *tasil* is used here in the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamī*). "Time" (*kāla*) means death; its "punishment" (*daṇḍana*) or "rod" (*daṇḍa*) is the activity conducive to the separation of the body and the vital breaths.
Having shattered—that is, having cut asunder—that [rod], meaning having conquered death, they wander within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
The meaning is that they move with a particularly unimpeded gait. As it is said in the *Bhāgavata*:
"They say the movement of the masters of yoga, whose inner selves are like the wind, extends both within and outside the three worlds. (9)
He describes how Haṭha destroys all torments and accomplishes all Yoga through the metaphor of the hut and the tortoise: "All" (aśeṣa) refers to those which are threefold,
distinguished as internal (ādhyātmika), external (ādhibhautika), and celestial (ādhidaivika).
Therein, internal suffering is of two kinds: physical and mental. Of these, physical suffering arises from disease, while mental suffering arises from desire and the like.
External suffering (ādhibhautika) is that produced by tigers, snakes, and so forth; celestial suffering (ādhidaivika) is that produced by planets and the like.

And those [austerities] and those [fevers], by means of them, for men who are heated—that is, thoroughly tormented—there is *haṭha*, which is *haṭhayoga*. "Perfectly resorted to" (*samāśraya*) means it is the resort (*āśraya*), the very abode (*maṭha*) that serves as a refuge; thus, *haṭha* is indeed the monastery itself. So too is *haṭha*.
Just as Kamaṭha is the foundation for those engaged in all forms of yoga— meaning those engaged in mantra-yoga, karma-yoga, and so forth—
so too is Haṭha the refuge for men tormented by the three kinds of suffering. And it is just like this:
The tortoise is the support of all; likewise, the meaning is that Haṭha is the support of all yogins. || 10 ||
p. 9) || Root Text ||
The science of Haṭha must be kept strictly secret by a yogi desiring success;
it becomes potent when guarded, but powerless when revealed. || 11 ||
|| Commentary ||
Now, he states the extreme secrecy of the science of Haṭha with respect to all other sciences.

Regarding the phrase "the science of Haṭha": for a yogi who desires success (*siddhi*) such as the powers of atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth, or who desires the ultimate success that is liberation (*kaivalya-siddhi*), the science of Haṭhayoga is "paramatyanta-gopyā"—meaning it must be strictly concealed, kept secret, and is worthy of being guarded. He states the reason for this:
For when the science of *haṭha* is guarded, it becomes endowed with vigor and capable of producing unimpeded sovereignty;
it becomes capable of producing liberation (*kaivalya*), or rather, capable of producing the attainment of liberation.
Now, the one qualified for yoga is he who has conquered the senses, who is peaceful, and who is intent on liberation.

It should be given to one who is free from defects, unattached, liberated, and not lacking in qualities other than those [defects], and who performs what has been prescribed; it should not be given by force to anyone else. Yājñavalkya says:
"One who is engaged in actions prescribed by the rules, who is free from desire and mental resolve, and [endowed] with restraints..."
Endowed with observances, free from all attachments, accomplished in learning, having conquered anger,
devoted to truth and righteousness, intent on serving his guru, dedicated to his father and mother, established in his own stage of life, and of virtuous conduct, he is esteemed by the wise.

Regarding the term "well-trained" (*suśikṣita*): it is stated in some places that [this teaching] should not be given to one who is devoted only to his genitals and belly, nor to one who merely wears the external garb. On this point, the authors of the *Yogacintāmaṇi* say: "Even though [it is said]: 'The woman of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras is purifying...'"

In Purāṇic statements such as, "There is no other means for the pacification of karmas than yoga; there is none for liberation," the eligibility for yoga is found to belong to every living being. Nevertheless, the fruit in the form of liberation accrues only to one who is dispassionate toward yoga; therefore, it belongs only to such a person.

The qualification for yoga is appropriate [only for such a person]. And so it is stated in the Vāyusaṃhitā: "He whose mind is detached from objects, both those seen and those heard of in scripture, has the qualification for this yoga, and no one else whatsoever."—Sureśvarācārya.

They say that eligibility for this yoga belongs only to someone who is detached from this world and the next, who desires to abandon cyclic existence (saṃsāra), and who truly seeks to know it. It has also been stated by the elders: "This should never be given to one who is ill-behaved."
p. 10) || Root Text ||
In a well-governed, righteous country, where food is abundant and free from calamities.
Within a distance of one bow-length, in a secluded place free from stones, fire, and water, the Haṭha-yogin should remain inside a small hut. || 12 ||
Commentary:
For that knowledge must be kept secret to yield its proper fruit; indeed, the Goddess of Speech, if placed in an unworthy person, will soon consume him with her wrath.
Now, with a half-verse, he describes the place suitable for the practice of Haṭha-yoga: "In a good kingdom," and so forth.

The state or activity of a king is "rājyam" (kingship); that in which this is excellent is a "surājya" (well-governed kingdom). According to the great saying, "As is the king, so are the subjects," the excellence of the king indicates the excellence of the subjects as well. [This occurs] in a righteous [kingdom].

*Dharmavatī*: by this, the obtainment of favorable food and so forth for the practitioner of *haṭha* is indicated. By the term *subhikṣa* (abounding in food), the obtainment of that [food] without effort is indicated. And *nirupadrave* (free from calamity) means devoid of calamities such as thieves, tigers, and the like; by this, [the quality] of the location [is indicated].

The suitability for dwelling for a long period of time is indicated. "Dhanuḥ-pramāṇam" (the measure of a bow) refers to a distance of four cubits; within that limit, one should choose a place free from stone, fire, and water—"stone" meaning a rock, "fire" meaning flame, and "water" meaning liquid.

"Devoid of those" means free from them; the meaning is that at the place where the seat is located, within a space of only four cubits, there should be no stones, fire, or water. By this, the absence of the disturbances of cold and heat is indicated. "In solitude" means in a secluded place. By this—
The absence of quarrels and the like is indicated by the absence of the gathering of people; [for] in a crowd of people...
(p. 11) || Root Text ||

It is said that [the chamber] should have few doors, no cracks, crevices, or holes; it should not be too high, low, or long; it should be perfectly smeared with thick cow-dung, stainless, cleared of all living beings, beautiful with a pavilion, altar, and well at the entrance, and surrounded by a wall.
This is the definition of a yoga-maṭha as established by the perfected ones who practice haṭha-yoga. || 13 ||
Commentary:

However, strife and the like would certainly arise. As it is said in the *Bhāgavata*: "Among many there will be quarrel; even between two there may be dispute. In such a small cell—*maṭhikā* being a small *maṭha*;
the suffix *-kan* is used for diminutives—in the midst of that, by a *haṭhayogin*.
A *haṭhayogī* is a yogi who practices *haṭha*; this is a compound (samāsa) similar to *śākapārthiva* ("vegetable-king").
"It should be stayed" means it is fit for staying. By the phrase "in the middle of the small hut" (*maṭhikāmadhya*), the absence of suffering caused by cold, heat, and so forth is indicated. Here...

"By means of proper diet and conduct for the sake of attaining success in Haṭhayoga"—this half-verse has not been commented upon by some because it was omitted; [therefore,] this is a commentary on the root verses alone. Likewise, as for those verses that I have not commented upon further on, [the same applies].
It should be understood that all those [faults] found in the *Haṭhapradīpikā* have been cast aside here.
Now he describes the characteristics of the hermitage (*maṭha*): "having few doors," etc. That which has few doors is such [a place]. A *randhra* is a window and so forth; a *garta* is a sunken area;
a *vivara* is a hole made by mice and the like—that which is devoid of these is such [a place]. It should not be excessively high.
And that which is low and that which is very high and low—that is "very-high-low"; and that which is long and that which is very high, low, and long—that is "very-high-low-long.
According to the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57), because of the inclusion of the word *bahulam* ("frequently"), there is a *karmadhāraya* compound of qualifiers.

Now, one might object: how can there be a *karmadhāraya* compound for words such as "high," "low," and "long," which have distinct meanings? If you argue that this is because the definition of a *karmadhāraya* is "a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a common substratum" (*samānādhikaraṇa*), we say no; for in the case of those [words], in a monastery...

Because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible. Nor is it the case that "not very high or very long" (*na-atyuccanīcāyatam*) results from a compound with the word *na* where there is no elision of *na*, or that *na* is a separate word; for [if it were so], there would be fatigue in climbing what is very high, and in descending what is very low.

There would be fatigue. To prevent the vision from reaching too far into the distance, it is said: "neither too high, nor too low, nor too long. It should be made compact with cow-dung—that is, with *go-purīṣa*—in a perfectly proper manner.

Likewise, it was smeared; it was stainless, pure, and entirely abandoned— that is, deserted and devoid of all creatures such as mosquitoes, bugs, and the like— in the exterior area outside the monastery, where there was a pavilion (maṇḍapa), a specific type of hall, and an altar (vedi) that had been consecrated.
The ground consists of wells and various reservoirs; it is beautiful and delightful, and is properly surrounded on all sides by a wall or enclosure.
Root Text
Staying in such a monastery, free from all anxieties,
one should practice yoga alone according to the path instructed by the guru.
|| Commentary ||
The meaning is "provided with walls. By the *siddhas* who practice *haṭha*, that is, those whose habit is the practice of *haṭhayoga*.
This previously mentioned characteristic and essential nature of the yoga-maṭha, beginning with the small door and so forth.

It has been declared and stated. In the Nandikeśvara Purāṇa, however, the characteristics of a monastery (maṭha) are described as follows: "The temple should have a beautiful layout, be pleasing to the mind, and be scented with fragrances."

The wise man should construct a beautiful yoga-hall, adorned with heaps of fragrant flowers such as incense and perfumes; graced by sages, sacred fords, rivers, trees, lotus-pools, and mountains; fashioned like a work of art, and variegated with diverse types of paintings.

By beholding peaceful sages depicted in a painting, the mind attains tranquility through the auspicious path; by seeing perfected ones (siddhas) depicted in a painting, the intellect becomes inclined toward spiritual exertion. Then, one should draw the maṇḍala of saṃsāra and a cremation ground in the center of the yoga-hall.

One should sometimes depict the most terrible hells; seeing those of terrifying form within this essence-less saṃsāra, the yogi who desires accomplishment becomes free from despondency, even while beholding those afflicted by disease.
Creatures that are elevated, intoxicated, or with moving sores. || 13 ||
Having described the characteristics of the monastery (maṭha), he states what ought to be done within it: "In such a manner," and so forth.

Thus, "of such a kind" (evaṃvidha) means one whose manner or mode is as previously described; that is to say, one possessing the characteristics mentioned before. Having remained—that is, having established his stay—in that state, he is "specifically devoid of all thoughts," meaning he is free from every single thought.

One should always, that is, constantly, practice yoga alone by means of that path taught by the Guru, which consists of the method of practicing *haṭha*. By the word "alone" (*eva*), it is indicated that other types of practice act as obstacles to yoga. As it is said in the *Yogabīja*:

One should always serve that Guru by whom mastery over the winds (marujjaya) has been accomplished; through the grace of the Guru’s mouth, the wise man should achieve mastery over the vital breaths (prāṇajaya). This is in the context of Rājayoga.
[This is not attained] through the utterances of Vedānta and Tarka, nor through various Āgamas and collections of diverse scriptures.

The Wish-Fulfilling Gem (Cintāmaṇi) cannot be attained through honors such as meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the like, except by relying on the sole Guru. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "Having obtained the essence of Yoga from the Teacher, one of steady intellect personally attains that which has been described."
p. 13) || Root Text ||
Excessive eating, overexertion, idle chatter, adherence to restrictive vows, attachment to people, and fickleness—by these six, yoga is destroyed. (15)
Through enthusiasm, daring, fortitude, knowledge of reality, and firm resolve.
Through the renunciation of association with people, yoga is perfected by means of the six [qualities]. || 16 ||
Commentary:
By that, one also attains liberation—so says Sureśvarācārya:
"Through the grace of the Guru, one obtains yoga endowed with its eight limbs;
through the grace of Śiva, one obtains the eternal perfection of yoga."
And there is also the Śruti: "To that high-souled one who has supreme devotion for the Lord, and for the Guru as for the Lord, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth."
And also: "A person who has a teacher knows [it]. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.13)
Now, he states the obstacles to the practice of yoga: "Excessive eating," and so forth.

Excessive eating (*atyāhāra*) is eating more than is required by one's hunger. Exertion (*prayāsa*) is activity conducive to producing fatigue. Idle chatter (*prajalpa*) is excessive talking. [Bathing] with cold water...

The undertaking of observances (niyama) consists of the adoption of rules such as bathing at dawn, eating only at night, or subsisting on fruit and the like. Association with people (janasaṅga) refers to socializing with others, because such contact gives rise to desire and other passions. Fickleness (laulya) is the state of being restless or unsteady.
Yoga is destroyed by the six [obstacles], beginning with overeating; through the obstruction of practice, it perishes, and specifically, it is utterly ruined. 15.

Now he speaks of those things that bring about the perfection of yoga: "From enthusiasm," and so forth. Enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is the exertion [thinking], "I shall indeed restrain the mind which is inclined toward sense objects. Rashness (*sāhasa*) is engaging suddenly after having considered whether a goal is achievable or unachievable. Lack of weariness (*akheda*) is the thought, "It will certainly be accomplished as long as I live."
Fortitude: Sense objects are unreal, like the water of a mirage; Brahman alone is the truth—this is the reality.

Now, the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas): non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, forbearance, fortitude, compassion, straightforwardness, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten restraints. || 1 ||
Austerity, contentment, faith in the scriptures, charity, and worship of the Lord.
Hearing the words of the established doctrine, as well as wisdom, austerity, and sacrifice; || 2 ||

The experts in the science of Yoga have declared ten essential observances (niyamas). Because it is the primary limb of Haṭha, posture (āsana) is described first. One should practice that posture [for the sake of] stability, health, and lightness of the limbs. (17)
|| Commentary ||
Knowledge (*jñāna*) means the knowledge of reality, or the authentic knowledge of practitioners;
conviction (*niścaya*) in the words of the scriptures and the teacher is what is meant by faith (*śraddhā*).
It is through the renunciation of association with people who are adverse to the practice of yoga.
The meaning is that through these six, yoga is accomplished pre-eminently and without delay. || 16 ||
At the outset, in the statement regarding the seat (āsana), he has described the general connection and its fruit.

Regarding the phrase "of Haṭha": the four limbs of Haṭha to be described hereafter— namely, posture (*āsana*), breath control (*kumbhaka*), the various gestures (*mudrā*) as a practice (*karaṇa*), and the contemplation of sound (*nādānusaṃdhāna*)— are [the limbs] beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and ending with meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
The inclusion [of posture] occurs within the contemplation of the *nāda*.
The connection is that, because posture (*āsana*) is the first limb among those [eight], posture is mentioned first;
it is the steadiness of the body in that posture.
One should establish steadiness by means of destroying the quality of *rajas*, which is characterized by the flickering of the mind;

for there is the statement: "By means of the posture (*āsana*), one destroys *rajas*. Health (*ārogya*) is the absence of diseases that cause distraction of the mind. It has been stated that disease causes distraction of the mind.
In the *Pātañjala-sūtra*:
illness, mental agitation, doubt, negligence, laziness, lack of renunciation, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage [of practice],
and instability [are the obstacles].
p. 15) || Root Text ||
And by sages such as Vasiṣṭha, and by yogins such as Matsyendra.
I shall now describe some of the accepted postures (āsanas).
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs, sitting with the body straight—this they call Svastika. || 19 ||
|| Commentary ||

"These distractions of the mind are obstacles. By this, it is also stated that the lightness of the limbs—their buoyancy—is the destruction of the quality of darkness (tamas) characterized by heaviness.
Furthermore, by the word "and" (ca), hunger, its increase, and so forth are also to be understood. || 17 ||
He says: "Among the seats approved by Vasiṣṭha and others, I shall declare the most excellent ones."

"By Vasiṣṭha and others" means by those sages, such as Yājñavalkya and the rest, who are characterized by reflection (*mananaśīla*); the word "and" (*ca*) implies those devoted to mantras and so forth. "By Matsyendra and others" means by those such as Jālandharanātha and the rest; [the word] "by yogis."

By those practicing *haṭha*—the word "and" (*ca*) implying those devoted to *mudrā* and so forth—the eighty-four postures (*āsana*) have been accepted. Among them, I shall describe some of the most excellent ones.
Although both [systems] possess the practice of mental reflection (*manana*) and *haṭha*, nevertheless...

The mention of Vasiṣṭha and others separately is because their primary practice was *manana* (contemplation), while that of Matsyendra and others was primarily *haṭha-abhyāsa* (the practice of physical and yogic disciplines). || 18 ||

In this regard, because it is easy to perform, he first describes the *svastika* posture: "Between the knees and thighs," and so forth. "Knees" (*jānu*) and "thighs" (*ūru*). Here, by the word "knee," the part of the shank adjacent to the knee is to be understood; the reading "shanks and thighs" (*jaṅghorvoḥ*) would be more appropriate. "Between those two" means in the middle of them.
Having placed both soles of the feet against the regions of the thighs, with the body straight and the torso even—wherever one sits in this manner, that posture is called *svastika*;
"the yogins say" is the ellipsis. This was stated by Śrīdhara.
Placing the thighs and calves between them, with the forefeet positioned between the knees— the wise know that posture of the yogin to be Svastika.
p. 16) || Root Text ||
One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back; likewise, one should place the left [ankle] on the right side.
This cow-faced posture (gomukha) has the shape of a cow's face.
One should place one foot upon one thigh while the other remains on the ground; likewise, the other thigh [is placed] upon the other foot—this is declared to be the Vīrāsana posture. || 21 ||
Having blocked the anus with the two ankles in reverse order, one should remain composed.
Those who know yoga understand that this is the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana). || 22 ||
Commentary:

He describes the cow-faced posture (gomukhāsana): "On the left," etc. On the left side of the back—that is, on the left side below the waist according to tradition—one should firmly place the right ankle.
That which has the form of a cow's face is the posture known as gomukha.

He describes the *vīrāsana*: "One," etc. One, namely the right foot—*tathā* being used here for metrical completion—one should place it upon the left thigh. Upon the other, the left foot, one should place the right thigh. That is declared and described as the *vīrāsana*.

He describes the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana): "The anus," etc. Having restrained and fixed the anus with the two heels, when one is properly placed and situated in reverse order, this becomes the tortoise posture; such is the connection [of the verse] as understood by those who know yoga. || 22 ||
p. 17) || Root Text ||
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) by placing the hands between the knees and the thighs and resting them on the ground,
one establishes the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana), which is situated in the void.
Seated in the cock-posture (kukkuṭāsana), he should bind his neck with both arms.
It should be flat like a tortoise; this is the "tortoise-flat" [type]. || 24 ||
Having grasped the two big toes with both hands up to the ears,
One should perform the drawing of the bow; this is called the bow posture (dhanurāsana). || 25 ||
Commentary:
He describes the cock posture (*kukkuṭāsana*). Regarding "the lotus posture" (*padmāsana*): having properly placed the lotus posture, which consists of placing the soles of the feet upon the thighs;
the term "knee-region" (*jānupada*) refers to the part of the shank situated near the knee; and that [shank] together with the thigh is the "thigh-knee" (*jānūrū*).
Having placed the two hands between them, in the middle, and having set them upon the ground—
the word "hands" is understood to apply here as well— that which is situated in the void, in the sky,
and resembles the lotus posture is the kukkuṭāsana. || 23 ||

He describes the Uttānakūrma posture: "In the cock-posture," etc. Remaining in that binding of the cock-posture mentioned in the previous verse, one should join the neck with both arms (bāhu) and lie face upwards like a tortoise.
In which case this posture is known as the "upward-facing tortoise" (uttānakūrmaka). || 24 ||

He describes the bow posture (*dhanurāsana*): "The two big toes," and so forth. Having grasped the two big toes of the feet with both hands, one should act in such a way that there is a drawing of the bow as far as the ears—that is, up to the level of the ears.
The meaning is that one should extend one hand with the thumb grasped, and bend the other hand with the thumb grasped up to the ear; this is called the bow posture (dhanurāsana). || 25 ||
p. 18) || Root Text ||
With the right foot placed at the root of the left thigh and the left foot wrapped around the outside of the knee.
Standing with the limbs turned back while holding [the hands], this shall be the posture declared by the illustrious Matsyanātha. || 26 ||

The Matsyendrapīṭha bestows upon men, through practice, the blazing of the belly-fire, the weapon that shatters the circle of fierce diseases, the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī, and the stabilization of the moon. || 27 ||
Commentary:
He describes the Matsyendrāsana: having placed the right foot at the root of the left thigh and secured it from behind with the left hand according to tradition by grasping it above the ankle;
Having grasped the big toe of the left foot with the right hand— which itself encircles the outer part of the right knee—
and having turned the body so that the face is directed toward the back by means of the left side; thus.

He by whom a limb has been turned or rotated is "one who is thus"; that posture (*āsana*) in which he may stand or maintain his position is what was spoken—that is, declared—by Matsyendranātha. Because it was spoken by him, they call it by that very name. Thus...
Having placed the left foot upon the root of the right thigh, and having grasped it with the right hand reaching behind, while the right foot is wrapped around the outside of the left knee,
and the left hand is grasped by wrapping it around the outside of the right knee.
One should practice with the body turned such that the face is directed toward the back on the right side. || 26 ||

He describes the fruit of the Matsyendra-āsana: "Matsyendra... [The text states: the Matsyendra-pīṭha is like a weapon for the purpose of shattering—that is, cutting asunder—the fierce and unbearable circle (maṇḍala), which is the multitude of diseases (ruj).
Matsyendrāsana. From daily practice, that is, from the practice consisting of repetition every day. Root [text]. (p. 19)
Extending both legs on the ground like staffs and grasping the tips of both feet with the two arms, one should rest the forehead upon the knees;
this they call *paścimatāna* (the backward bend). || 28 ||
Thus, this foremost of backward-bending postures causes the vital breath to flow through the posterior channel.
It increases the digestive fire and brings about leanness of the abdomen and freedom from disease for men.
Commentary:
It bestows upon men an excellent radiance and increase of the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) within the stomach; likewise, it awakens the *kuṇḍalinī*— the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*)—
from its state of sleep, as well as [awakens] the moon situated above the palate.
The meaning is that it bestows stability upon that which flows and the absence of flowing [upon that which is stable]. || 27 ||

He describes the final posture: "Having extended," etc. Having extended—that is, having made them straight—on the ground (bhūmi), the two feet which have the form of a staff (daṇḍākāra) with the ankles joined; [and] with the two arms (dorbhyām), that is, the two hands, whose index fingers are bent.

Having firmly grasped both the foreparts of the two feet— that is, the pair of big-toe regions— by means of a forceful pull, in such a way that the lower part of the knees does not rise from the ground.
That posture in which one dwells with the forehead placed above the knees is called the *paścimatāna* (backward-bending) posture. || 28 ||

Now, regarding that fruit: "Thus" means as follows. Among the aforementioned postures, the foremost or primary one is the "backward-stretching" (paścimatāna). It is called "paścimatāna" because it stretches backward. Regarding "pavana": *pavana* refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). It is "flowing backward" (*paścimavāhī*) because it flows through the western path—that is, through the *suṣumnā* channel. One should practice that [posture].

It produces such [effects]: it brings about the rising—that is, the increase—of the fire within the stomach; it produces leanness, or thinness, in the belly, that is, in the middle region; and by the use of the word "ca" (and), it produces health and the equilibrium of the channels, the wind, and so forth. || 29 ||
p. 20) || Root Text ||
Supporting the earth with both hands, with his elbows placed at the sides of his navel.
If it stands upright like a staff on a high seat, they call this the Mayūra-pīṭha.
The illustrious Mayūra-āsana quickly removes all diseases, overcomes disorders such as abdominal tumors and enlargement, reduces all consumed unwholesome food to ashes,
generates digestive fire, and would even digest the Kālakūṭa poison. (31)
|| Commentary ||

Now he describes the peacock posture (*mayūrāsana*). Regarding the phrase "the earth" (*dharām*): with both hands—that is, with the pair of two hands—one should support and grasp the earth; that is to say, having placed the two hands close together, with the palms touching the ground and the fingers extended. Of that...

With both hands placed upon the joints in the middle of the arms at the elbows, and with the sides of the body held level with the sides of the navel, he is one whose seat is high— meaning his seat is elevated—
and who has risen like a staff in the void, as if in a vacuum.
Wherever one stands facing upwards, that is called "peacock-like" (māyūra); because it belongs to a peacock, yogis declare it by that name—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 30 ||
He states the qualities of the peacock posture (*mayūrāsana*): "It removes," and so forth. *Gulma* is a specific type of disease; *udara* is dropsy (ascites).

Those [diseases] beginning with *gulma* and *udara*, such as *plīha* (enlarged spleen) and others, are referred to thus. It quickly—that is, instantaneously—removes, meaning it destroys, all those diseases, that is, all diseases whatsoever.
The phrase "the glorious peacock-throne" (*śrīmayūramāsanam*) is to be connected with everything [that follows].

It overcomes—that is, it suppresses—the defects of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*), as well as those that cause lethargy. Furthermore, whatever poor food or bad meal has been eaten in great excess, all of that [is digested].

The meaning is that one should reduce everything to ashes, that is, cause it to be cooked. One generates—that is, brings forth—the digestive fire, the internal flame. One should digest—that is, cause to be consumed—Kālakūṭa poison, or food that is harmful like Kālakūṭa. One should cause it to be worn away, that is, digested.
"One should make" means "one should cook. || 31 ||
p. 21) || Root Text ||
Lying supine on the ground like a corpse is that "corpse-posture" (śavāsana). This corpse-posture removes fatigue and brings rest to the mind. || 32 ||
Eighty-four types of seats have been described by Śiva; taking from among them a quartet that constitutes the essence, I shall now speak of them.
The fourfold [postures] are the Siddha, the Padma, the Siṃha, and the Bhadra.
Moreover, among those, one should always remain in the most excellent posture for bliss, the Siddhāsana.
Commentary:

The corpse posture (*śavāsana*) is described as follows: "Supine" means that the back is pressed against the ground like a corpse—that is, like a dead body—so that the body lies flat on its back; this reclining position, which is like the posture one assumes when sleeping, is the corpse posture.

The seat called Śava. He states the purpose of the Śava-āsana in the second half [of the verse]: "Śava-āsana removes fatigue"; it removes fatigue—that is, the exhaustion resulting from the practice of Haṭha—and it is the resting place of the mind's repose.
The agent. || 32 ||
Stating the superiority of the four seats that are about to be described, he says:
"Eighty-four": eighty-four seats (*āsana*) have been taught by Śiva, the Lord; and by the word "and" (*ca*), eighty-four hundred thousand [seats] are also included. This was stated by Gorakṣanātha:
There are as many seats as there are species of living beings;
Maheśvara knows all their varieties. Each one consists of eighty-four lakhs, and from that, sixteen were excluded by Śiva.
"Having made a hundred [of them]. From among those eighty-four thousand seats spoken of by Śiva, having taken— that is, having grasped— the most excellent ones, which are the essence.
The grammatical connection is: "I declare that the group of four is the most excellent. || 33 ||
He indicates that very same tetrad by name: "Siddham" means the Siddhāsana; "Padmam" (p.
Root Text
Having firmly placed the soles of the feet joined at the root of the perineum,

and having fixed one foot upon the other, one should keep the chin steady against the heart. With the senses restrained, like a pillar, one should gaze with an unmoving vision at the space between the eyebrows.
This is declared to be Siddhāsana, which effects the breaking open of the door to liberation. || 35 ||
Commentary:

The lotus posture (padmāsana), the lion [posture] (siṃha) which is the lion throne (siṃhāsana), and the auspicious [posture] (bhadra) which is the auspicious throne (bhadrāsana)—these four are excellent and most highly praised. Among those four, one should always remain in the Siddhāsana, which is pleasant and brings about happiness. By this, [the superiority of] Siddhāsana [is established].
It is indicated that [this practice] is the most excellent among all four. || 34 ||
Since it is the most excellent among the four types of postures, he first describes Siddhāsana.

Regarding the term *yonisthānakam*: *yonisthānakam* is simply *yonisthānam*, with the suffix *ka* added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*). That which is the region between the anus and the genitals is the *yonisthāna*.
It is joined by the heel—the root of the left foot—that is, the rear part of the left leg.
Having joined [the feet] together, one should place one foot— the right foot— firmly upon the upper part of the *meḍhra* organ; then,
having made the jaw and chin perfectly steady near the heart, one should remain thus.

The secret is that one should act so that there is a distance of four finger-breadths between the chin and the heart. One who has restrained the senses—that is, turned them away from sense objects—is "one by whom the senses are controlled.
With an immovable gaze—that is, a steady vision—one should likewise [fix it] upon the space between the eyebrows, the middle.

One should observe this: for it is well known that it produces the breaking—that is, the destruction—of that which is the established door-panel acting as an obstruction to liberation; such is the posture named Siddhāsana, belonging to the perfected ones (siddhas), the yogins.
It is called *āsana* because one sits (*āste*) upon it, or because one is seated by means of it. This is the Siddhāsana.
The meaning is "it would be. || 35 ||
Root Text (Mūla) (p. 23)
According to another opinion: Having placed the left ankle above the genitals, and likewise having placed the other ankle upon that, this becomes Siddhāsana. (36)
They call this Siddhāsana; others know it as Vajrāsana. Some speak of it as Muktāsana, while others call it Guptāsana. (37)
Just as moderation in food is primary among the restraints (yamas) and non-violence among the observances (niyamas), the perfected ones know Siddhāsana to be the foremost among all postures. || 38 ||
Commentary:
Having described Siddhāsana as approved by Matsyendra, he speaks in order to describe that which is approved by others.
Regarding the phrase "but in another opinion": he demonstrates that very point with the words "from the penis," and so forth.

Having placed the left ankle upon the upper part—that is, the upper portion—of the genitals and the pubic region, and likewise having placed the other ankle—the right ankle—upon the principal foot (the right foot), as in the case of the left [in the previous step], but not upon the left ankle, one should remain; this is the remainder of the sense. This...
The meaning is that there is no difference, as Siddhāsana is held in common by other schools of thought. || 36 ||

In this regard, in order to clarify that this is the first [posture] approved by the Mahāsiddhas, he states the different names for it due to the differences in opinion: "This," etc. They say that "this"—referring to the aforementioned Siddhāsana, which is named Siddhāsana—"others" (the word *kecit* being understood) [say this, while] others [say something else].

The wise know *vajrāsana* as that which is designated *vajrāsana*. Some call it *muktāsana*, by the name *muktāsana*; others say it is *guptāsana*, known as *guptāsana*. Herein lies the knowledge of the postures (*āsana*): in this [posture], one places the heel of the left foot in the region of the *yoni*.
Having placed the heel of the right foot above the genitals,
that is *siddhāsana*. Alternatively, having placed the heel of the left foot in the region of the perineum (*yoni*) and the heel of the right foot above the genitals, that is *vajrāsana*.

When, however, the two heels— the right and the left— are joined with their upper and lower surfaces and then joined at the region of the perineum, that is the *muktāsana*. And when the two heels, joined as before, are placed above the genitals, [that is another posture].
That is the guptāsana (the secret posture). || 37 ||
Now, with seven verses, they praise Siddhāsana.
By means of [the verses] beginning with "yameṣu" and so forth; like one who has moderate food at the Yama [fasting days].
(p. 24) || Root Text ||
One should constantly practice that which is already perfected within the eighty-four sacred seats (pīṭhas).
The purification of the impurities of the seventy-two thousand channels. || 39 ||
Meditating on the Self and restricting his diet, the yogi shall attain perfection through the constant practice of the Siddhāsana for twelve years.

What is the use of many other seats when the Siddhāsana has been mastered? When the vital breath (prāṇānila) is restrained with attention in the pure kumbhaka [breath-retention], [all is accomplished]. || 41 ||
|| Commentary ||
"Moderate diet" is that which will be described by the words "food that is very unctuous and sweet," and so forth.

Just as non-violence is among the observances (niyamas), the connection is that among all postures (āsanas), those who are accomplished know one [specific posture] to be the principal Siddhāsana. || 38 ||

Regarding the phrase "eighty-four": among those eighty-four pīṭhas (sacred seats) that exceed eighty by four, one should always—meaning at all times—practice *siddhāsana* alone, which is indeed perfected. The qualifying description of *siddhāsana*, containing a reason for its constant practice, concerns the seventy-two thousand [nāḍīs].
It is the purifier that cleanses the impurities of the channels. || 39 ||
"Contemplating the self" (*ātmadhyāyī*): one who meditates upon the self is "one who contemplates the self.

"Moderate in food" (*mitāhārī*): one who possesses measured food. The compound *yāvaddvādaśavatsaram* is an avyayībhāva formed with the sense of limitation (*yāvad-avadhāraṇe*). This means for as many as twelve years, i.e., for the duration of twelve years.

This is a compound. The meaning is "up to twelve years. Always—that is, at all times—the yogin, the practitioner of yoga, through the practice of *siddhāsana*, shall attain completion, which is the perfection of yoga, even without the practice of other yogic methods.
The meaning is that one shall attain perfection merely by the practice of Siddhāsana. || 40 ||
"What is the use of others? means that once the *siddhāsana* has been mastered, there is no need for any other numerous seats or postures (*pīṭha*); the sense is that they serve no purpose at all.
Root Text
The state of Unmanī arises spontaneously and without effort; likewise, when the single, firm Siddhāsana is perfected, the three bandhas arise spontaneously and without effort.
There is no posture equal to Siddhāsana, no Kumbhaka equal to Kevala, and no [mudrā] equal to Khecarī.
There is no dissolution like that of sound. || 43 ||

Now, the lotus posture (*padmāsana*): having placed the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left foot upon the right thigh, one should hold them firmly with both hands according to the prescribed method.
|| Commentary ||
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is held in the state of pure kumbhaka with full attention,
that state of Unmanī arises— spontaneously and without effort, like a digit of the moon (candralekhā)— because it is inherently delightful. Thus it is said.
When one [bandha] has been thus established, made firm, and bound in this manner, then the three bandhas—
consisting of the mūlabandha, uḍḍīyānabandha, and jālandharabandha— will occur without effort by pressing [the heels] together along the path of the heels (pārṣṇi).

The meaning is that the exertion involved in the mūlabandha and other such practices—which will be described later, such as "one should contract the perineum" (yonim ākuñcayet)—arises spontaneously by itself, without that [effort], arising of its own accord. || 42 ||

Regarding "nāsanam" (there is no posture): the ellipsis is that there is no posture equal to Siddhāsana, which has been perfected. There is no *kumbha*—that is, no *kumbhaka* (breath-retention)—equal to the *kevala* (pure) *kumbhaka*. There is no *mudrā* equal to Khecarīmudrā.
Dissolution is like a reed; there is no cause for dissolution. || 43 ||
He begins to describe the postures with the words "Now" (atha). He describes the lotus posture (padmāsana).

"Upon the left thigh": upon that which is the left thigh, [he places] the right one. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of completing the meter. *Saṃsthāpya* means having placed it correctly, that is, having positioned it with the sole facing upward.
Root Text

Placing the thumbs upon the heart and the chin against the chest, one should gaze at the tip of the nose; this is called the lotus posture (padmāsana) for self-restrained practitioners, which brings about the destruction of disease.
Having carefully placed the two feet flat upon the thighs, and likewise having placed the two hands with palms upward between the thighs, one should then fix the gaze [between the eyebrows]. || 45 ||
One should place [the tongue] at the tip of the nose, at the root of the upper teeth with the tongue.
Commentary:

Having placed the left foot, which is like the right foot, upon the right thigh, with the back part—that is, the rear portion—[of the foot]; the word "vidhi" means the method, namely, by means of the two hands. Thus, by both hands...
Holding and grasping both big toes as firmly as possible,
having placed the right hand behind [the back],
and having grasped the big toe of the right foot which is positioned upon the left thigh with the left hand—

"Having placed behind" means having grasped the big toe of the left foot while it rests upon the right thigh. "In the heart" means near the heart; this is a locative case used in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpikādhāra*).
"Placing the chin on the chest at a distance of four finger-breadths" means placing the chin—the jaw—at a distance of four *aṅgulas* from the chest.

The secret [instruction]: one should look at, that is, gaze at, the tip of the nose; because this causes the destruction of disease for self-restrained yogis, it is called by the name "Lotus Posture" (Padmāsana), which brings about the destruction of disease—this is what remains to be understood as proclaimed by the perfected ones (siddhas). || 44 ||
He describes the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is favored by Matsyendranātha: "The two [feet] turned upward," etc.
The two feet—meaning the two soles—with their backs joined to the thighs, should be placed upon the thighs with great effort—that is, with excellent exertion—so that they rest properly on the thighs.

Having positioned them thus upon the thighs; "in the middle of the thighs" means between the thighs. Likewise, for the sake of clarity: having placed both hands palms upward, with the left [foot]—whose back is joined to the heels of both feet which are resting on the thighs and turned upward—[placed there].
The meaning is: having placed the left hand palm upwards, and then having placed the right hand palm upwards over it; "then" means immediately after that; "dṛśau" means the two eyes. || 45 ||
"One should place [the mind] on the tip of the nose"—that is to say, one should place it specifically with complete immobility. (p.
27) Regarding the "royal teeth" (*rājadaṃta*):
Root Text
Pressing the chin against the chest and slowly raising the breath, || 46 ||
This is declared to be the *padmāsana* (lotus posture). Having gradually restrained the breath (*pavana*), one should gaze at the upper teeth with the eyes; this destroys mental anguish (*ādhi*).
It is difficult for anyone to attain, yet it is obtained on earth by the wise. (45–47)
Having joined the palms together in the *saṃpuṭita* gesture, firmly assuming the *padmāsana* posture,
and placing the chin tightly against the chest, one should meditate upon that [object] within the mind.
Repeatedly exhaling the upward-moving breath from the abdomen and drawing it back in, a person attains incomparable awakening through the power of the *śakti*. (48)
Commentary:
Having propped up both root-locations at the bases of the fangs situated on the left and right sides with the tongue, one should hold it upward;
this "tongue-binding" (jihvābandha) is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru, [along with] the chin pressed against the chest.
The word "having placed" (*nidhāya*) is understood as the ellipsis. Having slowly, that is, very gently, raised the *pavana* or wind—by this, the *mūlabandha* (root-lock) is described.
The *mūlabandha* must also be understood solely from the mouth of the Guru; in reality, however, it is accomplished by the *jihvābandha* (tongue-lock) alone.
"He has accomplished his purpose," say those who know the secret of Haṭha-yoga. || 46 ||

Thus, that upon which one sits is called *padmāsana*, the name for the lotus posture—this being understood by those who know postures (*āsanajña*). Of what nature is it? It is the specific destroyer of all diseases, yet it is difficult to attain by anyone lacking merit, while for the wise it is easily obtained.
It is obtained or attained on earth, that is, upon the ground. || 47 ||

And in order to clarify that this is the position approved by the great yogins, he states another specific action to be performed in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*). [The verse begins with] "Having done... The two hands are joined together, meaning they are placed in a hollowed-out gesture (*saṃpuṭita*) while resting in the lap; [the adverbial phrase] "very firmly" means with extreme firmness.
The meaning is: having firmly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana); having placed the chin—the jaw—firmly and tightly against the chest, that is, near the breast;
at a distance of four finger-breadths.
This is to be understood from the tradition of the yogis; the meaning is that one should perform the Jālandhara-bandha.
That [Brahman] is either in the form of one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) or as Brahman itself. "Oṃ tat sat" is the designation.
Root Text
The yogi seated in the lotus posture who holds the vital air, filled through the gateway of the *nāḍīs*, is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (49)
Now, the lion throne.
And one should place [the two] ankles below the scrotum, on both sides of the suture.
One should place the right ankle upon the left [thigh], and the right [thigh] upon the left [ankle].
Commentary:

Because it is stated by the Blessed One that "the Brahman is remembered as being threefold," one meditates— that is, reflects— upon it within the *cetasa*, the mind. Driving the *apāna* wind— that is, the downward-moving vital air— upward by performing the *mūlabandha*, one [leads] the *prāṇa* upward through the path of the *suṣumṇā*.
Drawing in the breath filled by inhalation (*pūraka*) and internalizing the vital air (*prāṇa*),
causing it to descend— that is, leading it downward— the word *añcat* here implies a causative sense;
the meaning is that having brought about the union of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, the person (*naraḥ*, the man) attains incomparable awakening (*atulaṃ bodham*).

Through the power and influence of the incomparable knowledge, one attains—that is, reaches—the power known as the *ādhāra-śakti*, which is *kuṇḍalinī*. When the *prāṇa* and *apāna* are unified, the awakening of *kuṇḍalinī* occurs; upon the awakening of *kuṇḍalinī*, the *prāṇa* [ascends] by way of the *suṣumnā* path.
It goes to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra). When it has gone there, stability of the mind occurs.
The meaning is that through self-restraint (saṃyama) upon the stability of the mind, the direct realization of the Self (ātmasākṣātkāra) arises. || 48 ||

Regarding the term "padmāsana": the yogin, seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) and practicing yoga, having led the wind (māruta)—that is, the air brought inside by means of inhalation (pūraka)—to the head via the path of the Suṣumṇā (the remainder of the sentence), should hold it, meaning he should make it steady; such a person is liberated.
The logical connection here is that there is no doubt [regarding this]. || 49 ||

Regarding the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), he says: "And the two ankles. One should place, impel, or—so to speak—establish them below the testicles, on both sides of the perineum, that is, on both parts of the sīvanī. He explains the very manner of placing the ankles:
p. 29) || Root Text ||
Having placed both hands upon the knees and fully extended one's fingers, [one should remain thus].
With mouth open, he should gaze at the tip of his nose, being well-composed.
This lion-throne is worshipped by the foremost among the yogis.
And he performs the joining of the three bonds, which is the supreme posture (āsana). || 52 ||
Now, the auspicious posture (bhadrāsana).
And one should apply [the paste] to the two ankles, below the scrotum, and on both sides of the perineal seam.
Likewise, the left ankle on the left [side], and the right ankle on the right.
Commentary:
Regarding "on the right": one should place the left ankle on the right side of the suture (sīvanī).
On the left, one should place the right ankle on the left side of the suture. || 50 ||
"Regarding the hands": having placed the two hands properly above the knees so that their palms are firmly joined to the knees,
and having fully extended one's fingers— that is, the fingers of the hands.

With his mouth slightly open and his long tongue extended, he remains well-composed with a one-pointed mind, gazing at the tip of the nose—that is, the very end of the nose—upon which he fixes his sight. || 51 ||

This shall be the lion-throne (siṃhāsana). Of what nature is it? It is that which is honored by the best of yogis, the foremost among practitioners; it is the preeminent throne among all seats, consisting of the union of the triad of bandhas, such as the root-bandha (mūlabandha) and the others.
He makes a store. || 52 ||

He describes the *bhadrāsana*: "The two ankles," and so forth. Below the scrotum, on both sides of the perineal seam—that is, on either side of the seam—one should place the two ankles, which are the knots of the feet.
He explains the manner of placing them as follows: "the left ankle," meaning on the left side of the seam.
One should throw the left ankle [toward the right]; likewise for the completion of the movement. One should throw the right ankle toward the side of the right suture (sīvanī). || 53 ||
p. 30) || Root Text ||
Having firmly bound the sides and the feet with both hands, making [the body] perfectly motionless.
This shall be the auspicious posture (bhadrāsana), which destroys all diseases. || 54 ||
The accomplished yogis indeed call this the Gorakṣāsana. Thus, among the various postures, the lord of yogis becomes free from fatigue.

One should practice the purification of the channels, the yogic exercises for the vital breath such as the mudrās, as well as the postures (āsanas), the various breath-retentions (kumbhakas), and the techniques known as mudrās. || 56 ||
Commentary:
Having firmly bound the two feet, which are positioned near the sides, with the two hands— that is,
with the two arms— using those hands whose fingers are interlocked and whose palms are pressed against the abdomen.
The meaning is "having bound. This shall be the Bhadrāsana. Of what nature is it? It is the specific destroyer of all diseases. || 54 ||

Regarding "Gorakṣa": those who are both perfected ones (*siddha*) and yogis are *siddhayogins*. They call this auspicious posture (*bhadrāsana*) the "Gorakṣāsana. Because it was primarily practiced by Gorakṣa, they refer to it as the "Gorakṣāsana. Thus, the postures have been described.

He states what is to be done regarding them with the word "evam" (thus). "Evamukteṣu" means among those aforementioned methods of binding the posture (*āsana-bandha*). "Vigataśrama" means one whose fatigue has departed; that is, one who is free from exhaustion in the binding of the postures. "Yogīndraḥ" means the lord of yogis. || 55 ||

The purification of the channels (nāḍī) and the channels (nāḍikā); and the activity of the wind (pavana), that is, the vital breath (prāṇa), [performed] by drinking it through the iḍā in a regulated manner— referring to such mudrās as will be described hereafter, beginning with Sūryabheda and others.
And one should practice that which consists of breath control (prāṇāyāma). Now, he describes the sequence for practicing Haṭha Yoga.

Regarding "the posture": the posture has the characteristics already described; it is manifold, consisting of various types of *kumbhaka* (breath retention) such as *sūryabheda*, *ujjāyī*, and others to be mentioned hereafter. That which is called by the name "mudrā" is the practice of forms such as *mahāmudrā* for the attainment of *haṭha*.
It is that which provides the most excellent assistance; and so it is with respect to the object. 56.
Root Text (Mūla) (p. 31)
Now, the contemplation of the *nāda* and the sequence of practice in *haṭha* [yoga]:
one who is celibate, moderate in diet, renounced, and devoted to yoga shall become perfected after one year;
there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (57)
Food that is very smooth and sweet, consumed while omitting one-fourth part for the sake of pleasing Śiva—that is called "moderate diet" (mitāhāra). || 58 ||
Commentary:

Now, following the performance of these three, the contemplation— that is, the reflection— upon the *nāda*, the unstruck sound (*anāhatadhvani*), constitutes the practice (*abhyāsa*) in *haṭha*, which is *haṭhayoga*; its sequence refers to the order of priority and succession.

He states the limit for the attainment of *haṭha*: "A celibate" (*brahmacārī*), etc. One who possesses celibacy, one whose food is moderate—meaning he has that which is to be described as "moderate-eating"—one who is renunciant, meaning habitually giving or one who has abandoned sense objects, and one who is devoted to yoga, meaning intent upon the practice of yoga.

After one year from the beginning, one becomes perfected; that is, one attains the "perfection of the yogic posture" (siddhahaṭha). Regarding this matter stated here, no doubt should be entertained as to whether it is so or not;
the meaning is that this is indeed certain. || 57 ||

In the preceding verse, it was stated that one should be moderate in diet; in response to the inquiry as to what kind of moderate diet is appropriate for yogins, he says: "Very unctuous" (susnigdha), meaning exceedingly oily, and that which is sweet—such is [the diet].
Food [should be] with a fourth part omitted, meaning deprived of one-fourth. As it has been stated by the learned: "One should fill two parts with solid food and fill one part with water;
one should leave the fourth part remaining for the movement of the vital air (vāyu). Śiva is the individual soul (jīva).

Or [it may refer to] the Lord; for there is the scriptural statement: "The enjoyer is the god Maheśvara. For the sake of his complete satisfaction—that is, for the purpose of perfect gratification—he who is eaten is called "one of measured food" (mitāhāra). || 58 ||
p. 32) || Root Text ||
Bitter, sour, pungent, salty, and hot [tastes], green vegetables, *sauvīra* wine, oil, sesame seeds, mustard, liquor, and fish.
They say that the flesh of animals born from eggs and the like, curd, buttermilk, horse gram, jujube, oil-cake, asafoetida, garlic, and so forth, are unwholesome. (59)
One should know that food which has been reheated and made dry is harmful to him.
One should avoid food that is excessively salty, sour, or dominated by unwholesome meals and potherbs. || 60 ||
Commentary:
Now, he describes what is unwholesome for yogis in two verses, beginning with "Kaṭvī" (Pungent).
Pungent refers to *kāravella* and the like; sour refers to the fruit of the *ciñcā* tree and the like; sharp refers to black pepper (*marīca*) and the like;
salty is well known; hot refers to jaggery (*guḍa*) and the like; *harīta* refers to leafy vegetables; and *sauvīra* is fermented gruel.

Kāñjika is fermented gruel; oil refers to the fats of sesame, mustard, and so forth; sesame (tila) is well known; mustard (sarṣapa) refers to white mustard (siddhārtha); liquor (madya) is wine (surā); and fish (matsya) is a large fish (jhaṣa).
These form a mutual dvandva compound. These they call unwholesome. "Ajyam" means belonging to a goat (aja).
That which begins with that [goat] is "goat and so forth" (*ajādi*); that and its meat is "goat-meat and so forth" (*ajādimāṃsa*).
Curd (*dadhi*) is a specific transformation of milk; buttermilk (*takra*) is curd from which the essence has been extracted;
*kulattha* and the like are specific types of legumes (*dvidala*); *kola* is the fruit of the *kolyā* plant; and *badara* is the jujube fruit.

*Karkandhū*, *badarī*, and *koli*—thus says Amarasimha. *Piṇyāka* is a sesame cake; *hiṅgu* is *rāmaṭha*; and *laśuna* is garlic. These form a mutual *dvandva* compound. That which has these as its "firsts" (*ādya*) is so described. By the word "firsts" (*ādya*), [the following are included:]...

Onions, leeks, intoxicants, beans, cooked rice, and so forth are to be avoided; they are unwholesome and harmful. The phrase "for yogins" is to be supplied as the ellipsis, and the words "the yogins say" are to be understood as an implicit addition.
Regarding "food": it refers to that food which has been heated by contact with fire, such as soup, boiled rice, flatbread, and so forth;

which is dry and devoid of ghee and the like; and which is excessively salty—that is, *atilavaṇa*—meaning either that in which salt is present in excess, or that which has surpassed the limit of saltiness.
"Cākūvā" is well known in the world as a type of vegetable, along with barley-alkali and the like;
since salt must be avoided in every respect, this constitutes the latter position (p.
Root Text
At the outset, one should practice the avoidance of fire, women, travel on roads, and meat-eating;
for such is the word of Gorakṣa.
One should avoid the company of the wicked, as well as fire, women, and travel on roads.
Likewise, [he should avoid] the practice of bodily mortification, such as bathing at dawn, fasting, and so forth. || 61 ||
|| Commentary ||

Excellent! And so says Dattātreya: "Now I shall describe those things to be avoided which cause obstacles to yoga: salt, mustard, sourness, pungent, sharp, and dry food; excessive eating, as well as excessive sleep and excessive talking, must be abandoned."
In the *Skanda Purāṇa* as well: "One should abandon pungent, sour, and salty [foods], and should always subsist on milk.

"Combined with sour" (*amlayuktam*) means joined with a sour substance; if even that which is joined with a sour substance is to be abandoned, how much more so the sour itself? Here, the third word is *palalam* (meat/minced meat).
Some read "tilapiṇḍam" (sesame balls), which has this meaning: *palalam* is meat;

*tilapiṇḍam* is oil-cake; *kadaśanam* is bad food, such as *yava*, *nāla*, *kodrava*, and so forth; *śākam* refers to any vegetable other than those prescribed; and *utkaṭam* is *vidāhin* (burning) food, known in common parlance as *miraci*.
This is well known. "Miraca" is the term in the Hindustani language.
