"Kadaśanādi" is a collective dvandva compound [referring to bad food and so forth]. "Atilavaṇādikaṃ varjyam" means that which is excessively salty and the like is to be avoided—that is, worthy of being shunned. In the reading "duṣṭam," it refers to what is spoiled, such as putrid or stale food.
It should be construed as "unwholesome. || 60 ||
Having thus stated what should always be avoided by yogins, [the author] states with a half-verse what should be avoided at the time of practice:
"Fire," etc. Fire, women, and roads—their "service" (sevā) consists of such things as tending the fire, sexual union with women, and going on pilgrimages. Of these...
One should practice avoidance at the beginning and during the period of training; however, once mastery has been achieved, it may be done occasionally.

By the phrase "and so forth," it is indicated that for a householder, the use of fire in cold weather, approaching one's own wife during her fertile period, and traveling on a road during a pilgrimage or similar journey are not prohibited.
In this regard, he introduces the authority of Gorakṣa’s statement with the words: "For it is thus."

He recites that [verse]: "One should avoid," etc. "The proximity of the wicked" means dwelling near the wicked; in some places, the reading is "the friendship of the wicked. "Serving fire, women, and the path" has been explained previously. "Morning bath and fasting" refers to those practices such as subsisting on fruit and so forth, of which these are the beginning.

And that [term] is a collective *dvandva* compound of those two. For a beginner, a disturbance caused by cold arises during the morning bath; and through fasting and so forth, the production of *pitta* (bile) and other humors occurs. "The practice involving bodily affliction" refers to the rule or action that causes physical hardship.

[This refers to] the form consisting of many prostrations to the sun and so forth, and the form consisting of carrying heavy burdens and so forth. The word "tathā" (likewise) indicates a conjunction. Here, the connection with the verb is "one should avoid" at every step. || 61 ||
p. 34) || Root Text ||
Wondrous foods such as wheat, śāli rice, barley, and ṣāṣṭika rice;
milk, clarified butter, sugar-candy, fresh butter, white sugar, and honey.
The five vegetables beginning with ginger and patola fruit, along with divine water such as mung beans and the like, are the path of Yama and Indra.
The product of the cow is nourishing, very sweet, unctuous, and promotes the growth of the bodily constituents.
A yogi should partake of food that is wholesome and desired by the mind.
Commentary:
Now he states what is suitable for the practitioner (yogin), beginning with the words "wheat" (*godhūma*) and so forth:
wheat, rice, barley, and *ṣāṣṭika*— those specific varieties of grain that ripen in sixty days— these constitute excellent food, pure food, such as *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, and the like.
And this is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) of these items: milk (*kṣīra*), which is *dugdha*; clarified butter (*ājya*), which is *ghṛta*;

sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*), which is *śarkarā*; fresh butter (*navanīta*), which is the essence of churned curds; and white sugar (*sitā*), known in common parlance as *tīvrapadī* or *khaṇḍaśarkarā*, and popularly called *misarī* in the Hindustani language.
*Madhu* refers to honey; this is a mutual *dvandva* compound. *Śuṇṭhī* is well-known.
*Paṭolaphala* is the vegetable known in the vernacular as *paravara*; that which has *paṭolaphala* as its first member—such as *kośātakī* and others—is "that beginning with *paṭolaphala*."
The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. The collective aggregate of five vegetables is *pañcaśākam*. As it is stated in the medical treatises (*vaidyaka*):
"All vegetables are detrimental to the eyesight, except for the group of five vegetables (*śākapañcaka*), which is beneficial for the eyes."
Jīvantī, vāstukamūlya, akṣī, meghanāda, and punarnavā.
Mudga is a specific type of split pulse (dvidala), and that which has this as its beginning is "mudgādi. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), āḍhakī is to be included.
Divya means faultless water. Those who possess restraint (yama) are called "yaminaḥ."
Among them, Indra is the best of gods; he is the lord of yogis, and his path is beneficial and wholesome.
Now, he states the rule regarding the food of the yogin: "Nourishing," etc. "Nourishing" refers to rice and other foods that cause the nourishment of the body.
Root Text
Whether young, old, or very aged, or even diseased or weak;
Through practice, one who is untiring attains perfection in all yogas.
Success belongs to one who is engaged in practice; how could it belong to one who does not act? The perfection of yoga is not produced by the mere recitation of scriptures. (65)
|| Commentary ||

Very sweet food accompanied by sugar and the like, unctuous food with clarified butter, and products of the cow such as cow’s milk and ghee; in the absence of cow-products, buffalo milk and so forth should be taken.

For the nourishment of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), sweets such as *laḍḍukas* and cakes, as well as whatever is desired by the mind, should be consumed during the [periods of] nourishment and the like.

Whatever is pleasing to the mind, that alone should be consumed by the yogin. To the question of whether even what is desired by the mind may be consumed if it is not prescribed, he says: "proper" (*yogya*). This means "only that which is prescribed.
The meaning is that the yogin should perform his eating, characterized by the previously mentioned qualifications.
The intended meaning is that one should not, however, maintain oneself by means of parched grain, roasted grains, and so forth. || 63 ||
He states that for one who practices yoga, there is no dependence on factors such as age or health: "A youth," etc.
Whether one is young, a youth, old— having reached the state of old age— or very old— having entered extreme decrepitude—
one attains perfection through the practice of postures, breath-retentions (kumbhaka), and so forth.
One attains that which consists of the nature of concentration and its fruit. While describing the very method of practice, he specifies:
"in all yogas. This means being untiring and diligent in all yogas, that is, in the limbs of yoga;
the meaning is that one attains perfection through the practice of the limbs of yoga. [This pertains to] the means of sustaining life.

Just as the term "livelihood" (jīvana) is applied to agriculture, trade, and so forth, the term "yoga" is applied to the limbs of yoga (yogāṅgas), which are the means for achieving yoga, either directly or indirectly. || 64 ||
Confirming that accomplishment arises from practice alone, he says the following in two verses:

Regarding the phrase "of one engaged in action" (*kriyāmuktasya*): action consists of the performance of the limbs of yoga; for one joined with that, there shall be success, namely the success of yoga. For one who is inactive—that is, devoid of the performance of the limbs of yoga—how could it happen? The meaning is: not at all. [Objection: But surely, by the study of the Yoga-śāstra...
The Accomplishment of Yoga (Yogasiddhi),
page 36.
Root Text.
Neither the wearing of [ascetic] dress nor talk thereof is the cause of perfection; action alone is the cause of perfection—this is the truth, there is no doubt. (66)
The various seats (pīṭhas), the diverse breath-retentions (kuṃbhakas), and the divine methods (karaṇas)—all these, in the practice of Haṭha Yoga, culminate in the fruit of Rājayoga. || 67 ||

Thus ends the first instruction, titled "The Description of the Method of Postures," in the *Haṭhapradīpikā* composed by the lord of yogis, Svātmārāma, the wish-fulfilling gem of the lineage of Śrī Sahajānanda.
Commentary:

He says "it might not be so": "No. By the mere recitation—by the simple reading—of the scripture, that is, the Yoga-śāstra, the accomplishment of yoga is not produced; the meaning is that it certainly does not arise. "No.
The wearing of the dress, such as saffron-colored garments and the like, [is not sufficient for] success, that is, the accomplishment of yoga.
It is not the cause; nor is the discourse on that yoga the cause. What, then, is the cause of accomplishment? To this he says: "It is action alone. (66)
He states the limit for the practice of the limbs of yoga: "The seats," etc.
The various seats (*pīṭha*) are the diverse postures; the *kuṃbhakas* are the breath-retentions such as *sūryabheda* and others;

the divine and excellent causes are the *mahāmudrā* and so forth. In the attainment of *haṭha*, all these possess the quality of being causes by virtue of their excellence as aids in the practice of *haṭha*.
The postures (pīṭha), breath-retentions (kumbhaka), and practices (karaṇas) are to be performed until the fruit of Rājayoga;
that is, up to and including that limit, they must be practiced—this is the remainder of the sense. || 67 ||
Thus ends the first instruction in the *Śrī Haṭhapradīpikā*, titled *Jyotsnā*, composed by Brahmānanda. || 1 ||
The Second Instruction.
Root Text.
Then, on a firm seat, the self-controlled yogi, eating wholesome and moderate food, [should practice].
One should practice the breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) according to the path taught by the guru. || 1 ||
When the breath moves, the mind moves; when it is still, the mind becomes still. The yogi attains the state of a pillar (immobility); therefore, he should restrain the vital air. || 2 ||
As long as the vital air remains in the body, so long is it said to be life; death is its departure from there, therefore one should restrain the vital air.
Commentary:
Now, immediately after the instruction on the postures, he begins to describe the breath controls (*prāṇāyāma*). [He says] "Now" (*atha*).

The word "atha" (now/then) is for the purpose of auspiciousness. When a firm seat is available, one who is self-controlled—that is, one who has conquered the senses—and who eats that which is wholesome (*hita*), beneficial (*pathya*), and moderate (*mita*) according to the characteristics described in the previous instruction, such a person is one whose food is wholesome and moderate (*hitamitāśana*). This refers to the path taught by the Guru.

Regarding the method of practicing *prāṇāyāma*: by means of that [method], one should practice the *prāṇāyāmas* to be described hereafter correctly, with enthusiasm, courage, fortitude, and so forth. Alternatively, the construction may be understood as: "in a firm and stable posture, such as *siddhāsana*, which is free from [distractions like] the cock [posture] and others. || 1 ||

As it is said by the Great One (Mahat), "Even a fool does not act without a purpose," there is an absence of activity due to the absence of a purpose; therefore, he states the purpose of breath control (prāṇāyāma):
"When the wind is moving... When the wind is moving, the mind becomes moving; when the wind is still...

The phrase "the mind shall become motionless" is also connected here. When both the breath and the mind are motionless, the yogi attains the state of a pillar—that is, stability and long life—or else he attains lordship. Therefore, for that reason, one should restrain the wind, the vital breath, by means of kumbhaka (retention). || 2 ||
"As long as" means: for as long as the vital air (vāyu), namely the life-force (prāṇa), remains within the body (deha), for that duration of time, it is called "living" by people. (p.
Root Text

When the channels are congested with impurities, the vital breath does not move through the central channel; how then could the state of *unmanī* arise, and how could the perfection of the goal be attained? (4)
When the entire network of channels, which was previously clouded by impurities, becomes pure, at that very moment the yogi becomes capable of mastering the vital breath.
Then, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) daily with a mind characterized by sattva.
Commentary:

Since the very conjunction of the body and the vital breath constitutes the state of being alive, the departure of that breath from the body upon their separation is called death; therefore, one should restrain that wind. || 3 ||
He states, by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), that the purification of impurities (*mala-śuddhi*) produces the accomplishments of *haṭha*:

"In the channels (*nāḍīṣu*) crowded with impurities... While the channels are crowded with—that is, pervaded by—impurities, the vital breath (*māruta*), the *prāṇa*, would not be "moving in the middle," flowing through the path of the *suṣumṇā*; rather, it occurs only when they are purified of impurities.
The meaning is that he becomes situated in the middle. "The state of Unmanī" means the becoming or existence of Unmanī;

how could it occur? It could not occur in any way whatsoever—this is the meaning. "The accomplishment of the effect," which is the nature of Kaivalya (isolation), its completion; how could it happen? It could not happen by any means whatsoever—this is the meaning. || 4 ||
He states that even through the positive method (*anvaya*), the purification of impurities is the cause for the attainment of *haṭha*: "It attains purity."
When, at whatever time, the entire wheel— the whole collection— of the channels (nāḍīs) becomes pure, that is, free from impurities,
at that very moment the yogin, the practitioner of yoga, [is capable] in the seizing of the vital breath (prāṇa).
He becomes patient and capable. || 5 ||

In response to the inquiry as to how the purification of impurity (*mala-śuddhi*) occurs, he states *prāṇāyāma* as its purifier: "Prāṇāyāma. For without the purification of impurity, one is not capable of restraining the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, from that [arise] devotion to the Lord, enthusiasm, audacity, and so forth.
(p. 39) || Root Text ||
Just as the impurities residing in the suṣumnā channel attain purification.
The yogin, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), should fill [the body] with breath through the moon (the left nostril);
having retained it according to his capacity, he should again exhale through the sun (the right nostril). || 7 ||
Having drawn in the breath through the sun (the right nostril), one should slowly fill the abdomen.
Having performed the breath-retention (kumbhaka) according to the prescribed rule, one should again exhale through the moon (the left nostril).
|| Commentary ||

One should constantly perform *prāṇāyāma* with a sattvic intellect (*dhī*)— characterized by clarity and serenity— which has overcome the rajasic and tamasic qualities such as distraction and laziness through diligent effort;
in such a manner that the impurities situated within the *suṣumnā* channel are [removed].
They attain purity and disappearance; the meaning is that they perish. || 6 ||

He describes the method of breath control (prāṇāyāma) for purifying the impurities with two verses, beginning with "having assumed the lotus posture" (baddhapadmāsana). A yogi who has assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) should fill the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the vital air, with the moon— that is, through the lunar channel (nāḍī), the iḍā.

Having restrained [the breath] according to one's capacity— that is, without exceeding one's power— and having performed *kumbhaka* (retention), one should again exhale through the sun, namely the *piṅgalā*, which is the solar channel. The inhalation (*pūraka*) is the taking in of external air through a specific effort.
Kumbhaka is the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa) preceded by the Jālandhara-bandha and other locks.
Recaka is the movement of the restrained air through a specific effort.
These two definitions apply specifically to recaka and pūraka, which are limbs of prāṇāyāma.
The bellows of a blacksmith involve exhalation and inhalation performed with haste;
thus, there is no over-extension of the definition to these secondary (gauṇa) exhalation and inhalation, because they do not possess the status of being the primary objects of definition. || 7 ||
"Prāṇam" means: having drawn in and grasped the vital breath (prāṇa) through the sun, that is, through the solar channel (piṅgalā), one should slowly and very gradually fill the belly, the stomach.
Having performed the retention (kuṃbhaka) according to the rule, preceded by the [three] locks (bandhas).
Furthermore, one should exhale through the left [nostril] by means of the moon. || 8 ||
p. 40) || Root Text ||
Having drunk with that [tube], one should retain it without obstruction; then, one should expel it with another [tube], very slowly and not with force. || 9 ||

If one drinks the breath through the iḍā, having restrained it, one should exhale it again through the other; then, having drunk the air through the piṅgalā, one should bind it and release it through the left (iḍā).
For those self-controlled practitioners who constantly perform this practice regarding the sun and the moon according to this method, the collection of channels becomes purified after three months.
|| Commentary ||

Having explained *prāṇāyāma*, he states the specific detail [of its practice] with the words "by which": by means of either the moon (*caṃdra*) or the sun (*sūrya*), one should exhale (*atyajet*); having inhaled by that same [nostril], one should fill [the body] by that very same [nostril].
This is done through "intense restraint" (*atirodhataḥ*), meaning by a restraint that is excessive, reaching the point of producing perspiration, trembling, and so forth.

The suffix *tasil* is used in the sense of all case endings. One should exhale slowly through the [nostril] other than that through which inhalation was performed, but not with force; for by exhaling with force, there would be a loss of strength. Inhalation should not be performed through the same [nostril] through which exhalation was performed; rather, inhalation should be performed through the very same [nostril] through which exhalation was performed.
Such is the intended meaning. || 9 ||

Summarizing and restating the meaning already expressed in the verse beginning with "baddhapadmāsana," he states the intermediate result of *prāṇāyāma*: "The vital breath... If one should drink—that is, fill—the *prāṇa* through the *iḍā*, the left channel, then [the breath] is restrained and held in *kuṃbhaka*.

One should exhale the breath again through the other [channel], the Piṅgalā. Having inhaled the wind—air—through the Piṅgalā, the right channel, and having filled it, then after filling it, having bound it—that is, having performed kumbhaka—one should release it through the left [channel]; one should exhale.

"Sūrya" and "Candramā" [form] "Sūryācandramasau"; in this dual compound of deities, the suffix *ānaṅ* is applied. By this stated rule and method, one should always—constantly—practice [prāṇāyāma], filling with the moon and retaining [the breath] with the sun.

For those self-controlled practitioners who expand [the practice] by exhaling through the sun, filling [the vessel], and retaining it, and then exhaling through the moon— their groups of channels (nāḍīgaṇa),
that is, the collections of channels, [become purified] after three months, meaning beyond a period of three months.
They become pure, free from impurity. || 10 ||
The Vernacular Text.
p. 41) || Root Text ||
At dawn, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight, one should perform the kumbhaka breath-retentions.
One should practice slowly up to eighty times, four times [a day].
In the lowest degree there is perspiration; in the middle degree, trembling occurs.
Commentary:
Now he states the time for the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and its duration, beginning with the words "In the morning."
Morning (prātaḥ) is the period beginning from the dawn of the first light until three ghaṭikās after sunrise;
midday (madhyandina) is the middle portion of the day divided into five parts; and evening twilight (sāyaṃsaṃdhyā) occurs at that time.
At the time of twilight (saṃdhyākāla), characterized as being three nāḍīs before sunset and likewise three nāḍīs after [sunset], "midnight" (ardharātra) refers to the middle of the night;
it consists of two muhūrtas at that midnight.
"Gradually," up to eighty—that is, reaching the number eighty—four times;
the accusative case is used here according to the rule "in the sense of continuous connection with time or distance.
During four periods of time, one should perform eighty breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) during each individual period.
If one is unable to perform it at midnight, the traditional teaching is that it should be performed during the three junctions of the day.
If performed four times every day, there are three hundred and twenty breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) in total.
If performed three times, they amount to two hundred and forty (240). || 11 ||

He states the specific characteristics of the minor, middling, and superior breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) in their respective order: "In the minor," and so forth. In the minor—that is, the lowest—breath-restraint, perspiration (*sveda*) arises; it is to be inferred by the presence of sweat.
The lowest [stage]. In the middling breath-control (prāṇāyāma), trembling occurs; the middling stage is to be inferred from trembling. In the highest breath-control, steadiness [occurs].
Root Text
One attains the highest state; thereafter, one should bind the breath.
Commentary:

One reaches the *brahmaraṃdhra*. The highest [attainment] is to be inferred from the acquisition of that station. Thereafter, one should firmly bind—that is, thoroughly restrain—the wind, which is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The characteristics of the *kaniṣṭha* and other [levels] of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) have been stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*.

Māna is said to consist of twelve mātrās; the low (nīca) breath is declared to be a single udghāta of twelve mātrās, while the medium (madhyama) consists of two udghātas and twenty-four mātrās. The primary (mukhya), however, consists of three udghātas.
The thirty-six measures (*mātrā*) are described as follows: perspiration, trembling, and rising [from the seat] occur respectively; bliss (*ānanda*) arises here, as do sleep and smoke;
horripilation, the perception of sound, the bending of limbs, and shaking.

When one overcomes the fainting of consciousness caused by hearing, sweating, talking, and so forth, then that most excellent and beautiful *prāṇāyāma* is said to have been achieved. "Smoke" refers to the oscillation of the mind. Gorakṣa also says: "In the inferior [stage], twelve [counts] are prescribed; in the middling, they are remembered as being double."

In the best [type of] breath control (prāṇāyāma), the measures are threefold for the most excellent twice-born. Now, the characteristic of the *udghāta*: when the *apāna* is compressed by the *prāṇa* as it is being exhaled, and having gone upward, it turns back—this is the characteristic of the *udghāta*.

Yājñavalkya states the measure (*mātrā*): "The wise declare that the measure (*mātrā*) consists of the snapping of the thumb and fingers, the wiping around the knees three times each, and also the clapping of hands three times. In the Skanda Purāṇa: "It consists of a single breath."
The measure (*mātrā*) of *prāṇāyāma* is thus declared. This has been explained in the *Yogacintāmaṇi*:
"The measure of *prāṇāyāma* is said to be that duration of time in which a single breath goes out and comes back for a person who has fallen under the influence of sleep."

The duration of a *prāṇāyāma* is a period delimited by twelve breaths plus half a breath. Six breaths constitute one *pala*. Thus, it is established that the duration of a *prāṇāyāma* consists of two and a half *pala*s of breaths.

That prāṇāyāma which measures twelve and a half mātrās is indeed called the "superior" (uttama) prāṇāyāma. Nor is there any contradiction with the previously cited statements from the Liṅga Purāṇa and Gorakṣa; for therein—

It should not be suspected that [this contradicts other texts] because of the statement that a breath-control (prāṇāyāma) consisting of only twelve [counts] is inferior; for the Skanda Purāṇa states: "One should circumambulate the knee neither too quickly nor too slowly;
as long as it takes to snap the fingers once, that duration is declared to be one 'count' (mātrā)."

And from the Skanda Purāṇa: "The release of the thumb and fingers, as well as the rubbing of the knees, and the snapping of the fingers—up to that point it is called a *mātrā*. Thus, the thumb is counted as a *mātrā*.

And because of the words of Dattātreya; for in the statements of the *Liṅgapurāṇa*, Gorakṣa, and others, a period of time delimited by a single snap of the fingers (*ekacchoṭikā*) is intended to be the measure (*mātrā*). This is also the case in the statements of Yājñavalkya and others.
[This refers to] that which is delimited by three snaps of the fingers.
(p. 43) || Root Text ||
One should perform a massage of the limbs with water produced from physical exertion; by that, firmness and lightness of the body are produced. || 13 ||
|| Commentary ||

Because time is intended here as a measure, there is no contradiction in the statement that even the lowest, which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), may become supreme; this has also been stated therein. Among all the means for accomplishing yoga, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is primary, because when it is perfected, withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other practices are accomplished, whereas in its absence they are not.

Furthermore, because withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs] are not established [independently]; in reality, however, it is *prāṇāyāma* alone that is designated by the terms "withdrawal" and so forth. Thus it is said in the *Yogacintāmaṇi*:
"Prāṇāyāma itself, increasing through the sequence of practice..."
It is expressed by the terms *pratyāhāra*, *dhyāna*, *dhāraṇā*, and *samādhi*. As it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) is declared to consist of twelve *prāṇāyāmas*."
Dhāraṇā is proclaimed to consist of twelve pratyāhāras;
for the sake of union with the Lord, dhyāna consists of twelve dhāraṇās;
by twelve dhyānas alone, samādhi is defined. That which is supreme in samādhi—

The light is infinite and self-luminous; when that is seen, the coming and going of the ritualistic path ceases. Likewise: "Meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) lasts for five *nāḍīs*, meditation (*dhyāna*) for sixty *nāḍīs*, and [the final state] is attained in twelve days."
And it is said: "Samādhi may arise from the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma). Gorakṣa and others have also stated this very same thing.

Herein is the established rule: the duration of the shortest prāṇāyāma consists of thirty-eight *vipalas* less a small fraction; this same duration is that which is delimited by a single snap of the fingers (*ekacchoṭikā*).

With the intention of defining time in terms of *mātrās*, twelve *mātrās* constitute the duration of a moderate breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). This consists of slightly less than eighty-four *vipalas*.
This is intended as the measure (*mātrā*) for a period of time delimited by a single snap of the fingers.

The duration of twenty-four *mātrās* consists of one hundred and twenty-five *vipalas*. This is the supreme duration for a *prāṇāyāma*. When this is intended as a measure (*mātrā*) of time delimited by a single finger-snap (*cchoṭikā*), it constitutes a duration of thirty-six *mātrās*.
However, with the intention of defining the measure of time as delimited by three snaps of the fingers,
it consists of exactly twelve measures. When, preceded by the binding [of the breath],
it lasts for up to one hundred and twenty-five *vipalas*, then...
When steadiness in *prāṇāyāma* is attained, then the vital breath (*prāṇa*) enters the aperture of Brahma (*brahmaraṃdhra*).
When the vital breath, having entered the aperture of Brahma, remains there for as long as twenty-five *palas*, then it is *pratyāhāra*. When [it remains] for as long as five *ghaṭikās*...

When it remains [steady] for that long, it is *dhāraṇā*. When it remains for as long as sixty *ghaṭikās*, then it is *dhyāna*. When it remains for as long as twelve days, then it becomes *samādhi*; thus everything is delightful. || 12 ||
Regarding the specific [result] that occurs when perspiration arises for one practicing *prāṇāyāma*, he says: "With water," etc.
Born from fatigue—that is, from the fatigue resulting from the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). (p. 44) || Root Text ||
At the initial stage of practice, a diet of milk and clarified butter is recommended; once the practice has become firm, such strict adherence to rules is no longer required.
Just as a lion, an elephant, or a tiger may be gradually brought under control, so too is the vital air (vāyu) when practiced properly; otherwise, it destroys the practitioner. || 15 ||
Through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other techniques, the destruction of all diseases occurs; through improper practice of yoga, the arising of all diseases occurs. || 16 ||
Commentary:

One should perform a rubbing of the limbs—that is, of the body—with that water and perspiration, as if applying an oil massage. By that rubbing, firmness, lightness, and the absence of heaviness arise and manifest in the limbs. || 13 ||

Now, he states the dietary rules consisting of milk and so forth for the first and subsequent practices: "At the time of practice. "Milk" (*kṣīra*) means cow's milk; "ghee" (*ājya*) means clarified butter; "eating that" refers to a meal joined with milk and ghee.
This is a compound similar to *śākapārthiva* ("the vegetable-loving king") and others. [This applies] when the practice is *kevala-kumbhaka*.
Once [the goal] is accomplished, the practice becomes firm; the rest is clear. || 14 ||
He says that one should bring the vital breath (*prāṇa*) under control gradually, like a lion and other [wild animals], and not all at once; thus he says, "Just as... (*yathā*).
Just as a lion, the king of beasts, an elephant, a wild tusker, a tiger,
or a leopard becomes submissive and under control only gradually and not all at once,
in that very same manner, the vital air (prāṇa) becomes submissive when practiced or cultivated.
Otherwise, if seized too hastily, it kills the practitioner who is still in training, just like a lion or other such beasts. || 15 ||
He states the result of what is appropriate and inappropriate: "By means of breath control," and so forth.

Prāṇāyāma preceded by the proper application of diet and so forth, and distinguished by the application of the Jālandhara-bandha and other bandhas, is called "properly practiced" (yukta). By that, there is the destruction of all diseases— of all diseases whatsoever.
p. 45) || Root Text ||
Hiccups, labored breathing, coughing, and pains in the head, ears, and eyes—various diseases such as these arise from the provocation of the wind (vāta). || 17 ||
One should exhale the breath properly, fill it properly, and bind it properly;
in this way, one shall attain perfection. || 18 ||
But when the purification of the channels occurs, then external signs will certainly arise; the body becomes slender and radiant. (19)
Commentary:

There would be decay and destruction. Through breath control (prāṇāyāma) joined with that practice which is "excessive"—meaning a practice devoid of the proper method—there occurs the "arising of all diseases," that is, the complete emergence and production of every kind of ailment. || 16 ||
In response to the inquiry as to what diseases arise from improperly performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), he says:

"Hikketi" means: hiccups, dyspnea, and cough are specific types of diseases; "head, ears, and eyes" (śiraḥkarṇākṣi) refers to pains in the head, ears, and eyes; and "various" (vividhā) means manifold diseases such as fever and so forth.
They arise from the provocation of pavana, the wind. || 17 ||
Since various diseases arise from the provocation of the wind (vāyu), therefore—

"Yuktaṃ yuktaṃ" means: one should exhale the wind, which is the vital breath (prāṇa), bit by bit. The meaning is that at the time of exhalation (recaka), one should exhale very slowly indeed, and not with force. One should fill [the breath] bit by bit, neither too little nor too much; and bit by bit...
One should bind [the breath] with the Jālandhara-bandha and other techniques and perform kumbhaka;
if one practices in this manner, one shall attain perfection—the perfection of Haṭha Yoga. || 18 ||
He states the signs of the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*) arising for one practicing breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) through two verses, beginning with "But when": *yadā tu* etc.
When, at whatever time, the purification of the channels—that is, their freedom from impurity—occurs, then from the outside...
The external [factors].
Root text, page 46.
The retention of breath at will and the kindling of the internal fire.
From the purification of the channels, the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda) and health arise.
One whose fat and phlegm are predominant should first perform the six purificatory acts (ṣaṭkarma); however, another should not perform them due to the equilibrium of the humors (doṣas). || 21 ||
Dhauti, basti, as well as neti, trāṭaka, and likewise naulika.
And these six acts, including the shining of the skull, are proclaimed [as the duties]. || 22 ||
This sixfold ritual action, which effects the purification of the jar, must be kept secret.
Commentary:
The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). "Marks" (*cihnāni*) means characteristics (*lakṣaṇāni*);

by the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the meaning is that there are also internal marks. He states those very marks [in the verse beginning] with "of the body" (*kāyasya*). "Of the body" (*kāyasya*) means of the physical frame; "emaciation" (*kārśya*) is thinness, and "radiance" (*kāntiḥ*) is luster.
A beautiful dawn will surely arise. || 19 ||
The voluntary retention of the vital breath (prāṇa) for many cycles during the kumbhaka stages;
the kindling of the internal fire (analasya), that is, the intense radiance of the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni);
the manifestation and clarity of the sound (nāda); and health, which is the state of being free from disease.
From the purification of the channels—due to their cleansing and freedom from impurities—it arises. || 20 ||

He states another method for one in whom fat and phlegm predominate: "One in whom fat and phlegm are excessive. This refers to a person for whom both fat (*medas*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*)—that is, *meda-śleṣmaṇau*—are excessive. This applies prior to the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), but not after it.

At the time of practicing *prāṇāyāma*, one should properly perform the six actions (*ṣaṭkarmāṇi*) that will be described hereafter. However, another person who is free from an excess of fat and phlegm need not perform those six actions. He states the reason for this: [regarding] the humors (*doṣāṇām*).
The state of being equal among wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) is "samabhāva," meaning equanimity; the meaning is: from that equanimity of the humors (doṣas). || 21 ||
He teaches the six practices. Regarding "dhauti": this is clear. 22.
The Vernacular Text.
p. 47) || Root Text ||
Possessing a collection of diverse virtues, it is honored by the foremost among yogis. || 23 ||
Among those, there is *dhauti*.
One should slowly swallow the cloth, which is four finger-breadths wide and fifteen cubits long, having moistened it according to the path instructed by the Guru.
One should draw this back again; that which has been described is the practice of *dhauti*.
Commentary:

He says, "This is the secret. Regarding the phrase "the hexad of rites": this is designated as the "performer of the purification of the jar," because it effects the purification—that is, the removal of impurities—of the jar, which is the body.
This is the hexad of rites.
The practices such as *dhauti* and so forth are to be kept secret and concealed; for it is said: "One who effects various qualities.
This means one whose nature (*śīla*) is to effect—that is, to perform—the various (*vicitra*), distinct (*vilakṣaṇa*) qualities consisting of the six-fold action (*ṣaṭkarma*).

It is worshipped and honored by the best of yogis, the preeminent among practitioners. The underlying sense is that if there were no concealment, even others might perform these six rites, which would lead to the undesirable consequence that the state of being worshipful belongs to the yogi alone. By this, it is shown that this [concealment] is indeed the primary fruit of the sixfold rite.
This has been indicated, because the destruction of fat, phlegm, and so forth is possible even through *prāṇāyāma*s.
As it has been said: "One who is intent on the practice of breath-control attains the yoga of the six acts.
This is also because the natural sense of the preceding and following passages is exactly the same. || 23 ||
He speaks of the practice of *dhauti*: "Four fingers" means a collection of four fingers is *caturaṅgula*;
that which has such a width of four fingers, and is fifteen cubits in length—that is, long—and moistened with water.
One should take a slightly warm cloth or garment— specifically a fine piece from a new turban or similar item—
and swallow it very slowly, bit by bit, using the method of swallowing the cloth as instructed by the Guru.
On the second day he should swallow two cubits, on the third day three cubits; thus, increasing by one day, he should swallow an additional cubit each day.
Having forcefully fixed its tip between the two front teeth and properly moved the cloth situated within the abdomen by means of the *naulī* practice, one should then slowly withdraw that cloth,
vomit it up, and expel it; this is declared to be the *dhauti* practice.
Thus it was told by the Siddhas. Root [text], p. 48.
It cures cough, asthma, splenic disorders, leprosy, and twenty types of phlegm-related diseases. || 25 ||

By the power of the practice of *dhauti*, they certainly proceed [to the desired goal], there is no doubt. Standing in water reaching up to the navel, with the anus placed upon the mouth of a tube while seated in the *utkaṭāsana* posture; || 26 ||
|| Commentary ||

He states the fruit of the practice of *dhautika*: "Cough, asthma," and so forth. "Cough" (*kāsa*), "asthma" (*śvāsa*), "splenic enlargement" (*plīha*), and "leprosy" (*kuṣṭha*) form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).
Cough and the others are specific diseases numbering twenty, as well as the twenty-five diseases of phlegm (*kapha*).
"By the power of the practice of *dhautika*, they certainly proceed;
there is no doubt"—this is the meaning of "this is indeed certain. Now, he describes the practice of *basti*: "Reaching to the navel," and so forth.

"Nābhiparimāṇam" means reaching the navel; the suffix "daghna" is used here in the sense of measure. In that water reaching the navel—that is, in the water of a river or similar body—the anus (pāyu) is placed, and into that [anus] a tube (nāla) made of bamboo is inserted.

Taking a bamboo tube six finger-breadths in length, provided with a hole suitable for inserting the little finger, one should insert four finger-breadths into the anus and leave two finger-breadths outside. He who is in the *utkaṭa* posture—

The Utkṭāsana (the squatting posture): Placing the buttocks upon the two heels while standing on the toes of the feet is the utkṭāsana. One should perform a contraction of the base [the perineum] such that water may enter within; the water that has entered within—
Having stirred [the contents] by means of the *nauli* practice, one should expel them; this cleansing is called the *basti* practice.
Both the *dhauti* and *basti* practices should be performed before eating; thereafter, one should not delay even for a moment in eating. However, some say that first, by means of the *mūlādhāra*...

Standing in water where they have practiced, they perform enema therapy (*basti-karma*) by drawing in air through the anus without even inserting a tube; when performed in this manner, not all of the water comes out. Therefore—
Furthermore, because various diseases, the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and so forth may arise, the enema procedure (*bastikarma*) should not be performed at all;
otherwise, why would he say that one who delights in his own self has placed a stalk into his anus? (26)
p. 49) || Root Text ||
One should perform contraction of the base; that is the cleansing enema procedure (bastikarma).
As well as abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement, and dropsy (udara), arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha.
By the power of the enema treatment (basti-karma), all diseases are destroyed. || 27 ||
The practice of the water enema (jalabasti) bestows clarity upon the elements, the sense organs, and the internal faculties,
as well as luster and a fiery radiance; it destroys the accumulation of all defects when practiced regularly.
Commentary:
He describes the benefits of the enema therapy (basti) with two verses: "Gulma, splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy...
Gulma and *plīha* (enlarged spleen) are specific diseases; *udara* refers to ascites (*jalodara*).
This is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). [The term *vātaja* refers to] those arising from *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*.

All diseases whatsoever— whether arising from a single cause, from two causes, or from all causes combined— are diminished and destroyed by the power and efficacy of the enema therapy (bastikarma). || 27 ||

Regarding the term *dhātu*: the water enema (*jalabasti*), when practiced—that is, being performed—bestows [benefits] upon the practitioner; this is the ellipsis. The *dhātus* are said to be the bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*) consisting of chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen, as well as the sense organs.
The five organs of action are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals;
the five organs of cognition are hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell;
and the internal organs consist of mind, intellect, consciousness, and ego. Of these—

*Prasāda* is the manifestation of *sāttvika* qualities— such as happiness, clarity, and lightness— through the cessation of *rājasa* and *tāmasa* qualities such as distress, distraction, grief, delusion, heaviness, obscuration,
and dejection; it is that grace, splendor, and luster, as well as the radiance of the fire of digestion (*jaṭharāgni*).

And [it bestows] excellent luster. Likewise, it thoroughly destroys the accumulation—and by extension, the depletion—of all [three] defects (doṣas), namely wind, bile, and phlegm. Health, which consists in the equilibrium of the defects, is what it utterly destroys.
The meaning is that one should perform [it]. || 28 ||
p. 50) || Root Text ||
Now follows the negation.
One should insert a very smooth thread, one span in length, into the nasal passage.
And this thread should be drawn out from the mouth; thus it is declared by the Siddhas. || 29 ||
She is the purifier of the skull-cup and the bestower of divine vision.
And this neti quickly destroys the multitude of diseases arising above the collarbone.
|| Commentary ||

Now he describes the practice of *neti*: "The thread," and so forth. "A span" (*vitasti*)—measured as one span—is an indicative term that includes more than that as well; one should take whatever length of thread is necessary for the *neti* practice to be performed correctly. It should be very smooth (*susnigdha*), meaning exceedingly glossy.

The thread, free from knots and the like, should be taken as very firm, multiplied ninefold, tenfold, or fifteenfold. One should insert it into that "stalk"—the nose being the nose itself—because it possesses a cavity; one should cause it to emerge from the mouth, meaning one should draw it out.
The procedure for that is as follows:

one should insert the end of the thread into the nasal duct, close the other nostril with a finger, and perform inhalation (*pūraka*). Then, one should exhale through the mouth. By doing this repeatedly, the end of the thread will emerge from the mouth.
Having grasped both the end of that thread and the end of the thread situated outside the nose,
one should move it slowly; by the word "and" (ca), it is stated that one should cause it to enter through one nostril and exit through the other, and that method is as follows regarding one nostril:

One should insert the tip of the thread into the other nostril while blocking it with a finger and perform inhalation (*pūraka*); afterwards, one should exhale (*recaka*) through the other nostril. By doing this repeatedly, the tip of the thread reaches the other nostril, and its movement is performed as before.
"One should perform [it]"—this method occurs only occasionally for one who practices it many times.
This has been taught by the *siddhas*, those endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest. As it has been said:
"The *siddhas* are defined by the wise as those who have attained the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya*)."
It is called "Neti," it is described as "Not this. || 29 ||

He states the qualities of the Neti [practice]: "The purifier of the skull" (kapālaśodhinī). It is called the purifier of the skull because it purifies the skull—that is, it makes it clean and free from impurities.
By the word "and" (ca), [it is implied] that it also [purifies] the nasal passages and so forth. The word "only" (eva) is used for emphasis. [It leads to] the divine...
p. 51) || Root Text ||
With a concentrated mind, one should gaze with a steady eye at a subtle object.
The masters have declared that *trāṭaka* is practiced until tears begin to fall.
It is the release from eye diseases and the bolt against drowsiness and other ailments.
The Trāṭaka should be guarded with great effort, just like a casket of gold.
Commentary:
The practice of *netikriyā* is called "bestowing divine vision" because it intensely bestows a vision that perceives subtle objects;
it is that which is "born above the collarbones," meaning born in the upper portion, above the junctions of the shoulders (*jatrūnām skandhasaṃdhīnām*). And that is it.
And it swiftly and instantly destroys the flood of diseases. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
According to Amara, "skandha" refers to the shoulder—the head of the arm—and its two joints are the *jatru*s.
[The author] now describes *trāṭaka*: "He should gaze," etc. "Samāhitaḥ" means with a one-pointed mind; "niścalā" [means motionless].

And that [vision] is sight; by means of that, the "subtle object" (sūkṣmalakṣya) is that which is both subtle and the object of focus. The "falling" (pāta) is the complete descent of tears; up to that point—by this, the limit of the gazing is stated. One should gaze, meaning one should look.
This *trāṭaka*, this practice of *trāṭaka*, has been remembered—that is, taught—by the teachers, such as Matsyendra and others. || 31 ||
He states the qualities of *trāṭaka*: "Liberation" (*mocanam*). This refers to the liberation—that is, the destruction—of eye diseases (*netraroga*).

It is the "door-bolt" (*kapāṭaka*) for those things of which lethargy (*taṃdrā*) is the first, such as indolence and the like; that is to say, it is that which, like a door-bolt, conceals them or overcomes them.
Lassitude (*taṃdrā*) is a specific modification of the mind characterized by *tamas*. Regarding *trāṭaka*, the practice known as *trāṭaka*:
it must be kept secret with great effort—that is, it is to be concealed. He provides an illustration for this concealment: "Just as... [the example is] a casket of *hāṭaka*, which is gold.
Just as that which is known in the world as a "box" (peṭī) is concealed in such a manner, so it is here.
(32, p. 52) || Root Text ||
Now, the nauli.
Bending the torso, one should whirl it from side to side with the force of a non-gentle vortex;
this is declared by the perfected ones (siddhas) to be *nauli*.
It is always the kindler of a weak digestive fire, the promoter of digestion, the restorer of health, and the bestower of bliss.
This *cauṇḍālī* is the crest-jewel of all haṭha practices, drying up the diseases of all defects without exception;
it consists of the forceful inhalation (*pūra*) and exhalation (*recaka*), like the bellows of a blacksmith. (34)
Commentary:
He describes the practice of *nauli*: "With slow... and so forth. A man whose shoulders (*aṃsau*) or scapulae are bent—that is, brought low—is called *natāṃsa*.

With a speed (*vega*) or impetus like that of a whirlpool (*āvarta*), such as a circular motion of water, he [agitates] his *tuṇḍa*, which is the belly (*udara*); *picaṇḍa* and *kukṣi* are synonyms for the belly.

"Jaṭhara," "udara," and "tuṇḍa" mean the belly; "stana" and "kuca" mean the breasts—thus says Amara. "Savya" and "apasavya" mean the left and right sides; from these two, "savyāpasavyataḥ" [is formed].
The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the locative case. One should cause it to whirl, that is, impel it as it revolves. This [method] is perfected by the Siddhas.
Nauli is now being proclaimed; it is being described. || 33 ||
He states the nine qualities of nīlī: "Mandāgni," etc.

That which is slow is this fire—the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni). Its kindling is "proper kindling" (samyaṅ-dīpana), and its digestion is the "digestion of consumed food" (bhuktānna-paripāka). That which has "the kindling and digestion of slow fire" as its primary functions is called "mandāgni-saṃdīpana-pācanādi"; it is the restorer of that [fire].

The ordainer; by the word "etcetera," [it includes] the purification of impurities and so forth. She is always, at all times, the bringer of bliss and happiness. She is the dryer-up of all—that is, the entirety of—those defects such as wind (vāta) and the like, as well as diseases (āmaya).

This is called *nauli*, which is the sovereign—like a crown (*mauli*) among the practices of *haṭha* such as *dhauti* and the rest, because it is the foremost due to its dependence upon both *dhauti* and *basti*. It is the agent of drying. || 34 ||
He describes that quality of the skull-illumination with the words "like a bellows" (bhastrāvat). It is like the fire of a blacksmith's bellows, which serves as the means for blowing [the flame].
Root Text
The Kapālabhāti has been proclaimed as the dryer of the disorder of phlegm (kapha). || 35 ||
Once the grossness, phlegm, defects, impurities, and so forth have been removed by the sixfold action (ṣaṭkarma), one should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
thus it is accomplished without effort. || 36 ||
"All impurities are dried up by breath-control (prāṇāyāma) alone"; thus, for certain teachers, no other ritual action is approved. || 37 ||
|| Commentary ||

Like leather, those two which exist together with agitation—namely, the exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), known as *kapālabhāti*—are characterized by intense agitation. Of what nature is it? It is that which dries up the defects of phlegm (*kapha*); for the defects of phlegm are divided into twenty varieties.
As it is stated in the Nidāna: "There are twenty diseases of phlegm; [this remedy] is their desiccant and destroyer. (35)
He states that the sixfold action (ṣaṭkarman) is conducive to the state of breath control (prāṇāyāma): "The sixfold action," etc.

[The channels] have emerged [from the body] by means of the six practices beginning with *dhauti*. "Coarseness" (*sthauilyam*) is the state of being coarse (*sthūlasya bhāvaḥ*), that is, coarseness itself. He is one for whom there are twenty types of phlegm disorders (*kapha-doṣa*) and impurities (*mala*) and so forth;
thus he is described as such. The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...
[The humors] such as bile (pitta) and so forth. One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).

From that, following the sixfold ritual (ṣaṭkarman), yoga is accomplished without effort or hardship; this is the remainder [of the sense]. However, if the sixfold ritual is not performed during breath control...
The sense is that there would be an excess of fatigue. || 36 ||
He states the lack of utility for the six rites according to a different opinion: "By means of breath-restraints," etc.

"By means of *prāṇāyāmas* alone. The word "alone" (*eva*) serves to exclude the six ritual actions (*ṣaṭkarman*). "All impurities" (*sarve malāḥ*) dry up. The term "impurities" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for [the removal of] grossness, phlegm, bile, and so forth; this is the view of certain teachers.

For Yājñavalkya and others, the other [set of] six duties (*ṣaṭkarma*) is neither approved nor intended. The definition of a teacher (*ācārya*) is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "He gathers the meaning of the scriptures, he establishes [others] in right conduct (*ācāra*), and he practices it himself."
Because he is the teacher, for that reason he is called "Ācārya. || 37 ||
p. 54) || Root Text ||
Having forced the downward-moving wind (apāna) up through the throat-passage, they vomit up the substance that has entered their stomachs.
The practice of gradually mastering the network of channels is called *haṭhakaraṇī* by those who know *haṭha*;
even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were devoted to the practice of breath control.
Since there was no fear of death [from such causes], one should therefore practice breath control (pavana). || 39 ||
As long as the wind is bound within the body, and as long as the mind remains undisturbed.
As long as one's vision remains fixed between the eyebrows, how can there be any fear of time? || 40 ||
Commentary:

He speaks of the *gajakaraṇī*: "Having gone into the belly," etc. The *apāna* wind—that is, the *apāna-vāyu*—having been raised up (*udīrya*) and cast upward (*utkṣipya*) into the throat-tube—the throat being like a tube is the "throat-tube"—and having reached (*gataḥ*) and arrived at the belly (*udaragataḥ*), that very [wind]...

The "object" (padārtha) refers to the food and water that have been consumed and drunk; those yogins by whom [that object] is vomited up or ejected by another—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Through gradual familiarity and practice, the wheel of the channels (nāḍī-cakra) necessarily comes under one's own control.
That [practice] is "tathā" (such). That action is called or described as "gajakaraṇī" by those who know haṭha—that is, by those proficient in haṭhayoga and the like.
Regarding the reading found in some places, "kramaparicayavaśyanāḍīmārga," its meaning is as follows: [the path of the channels is brought under control through gradual practice].
Through gradual practice, the path of the śaṅkhinī channel becomes subject [to control] as far as the throat; she in whom this occurs is thus described. || 38 ||
Indicating that prāṇāyāma must necessarily be practiced because it has been practiced by the most excellent of beings and because it yields great fruit, he says in four [verses]:
"Brahmā and the others": those of whom Brahmā is the first are "Brahmā and the others";

the meaning is, "what then of others? "Tridaśāḥ" means the gods. He who brings them to an end is "Antaka," that is, Time (Kāla). Fear of him is "Antakabhaya. From that [fear], the practice of *pavana*—the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*)—[is recommended].
They became devoted to and attentive toward that practice of prāṇāyāma, which is distinguished by its divisions of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka).
Therefore, one should practice the wind; one should practice the vital breath (prāṇa). || 39 ||

"As long as" means: for as long as a period of time, the vital breath (*marut*), the life-force wind, remains bound within the body—the physical frame—and is devoid of the activity of inhalation and exhalation. (p.
Root Text
When the network of channels has been purified through the proper performance of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), the vital air enters easily, piercing the opening of the Suṣumnā. || 41 ||
When the vital breath (māruta) moves with moderate flow, steadiness of mind arises; that state in which the mind becomes perfectly steady is itself the state of *manonmanī*. 42.
To achieve that, those who know the ritual procedures perform various types of breath-retentions (kumbhakas).
|| Commentary ||
As long as the mind—the internal organ—is undisturbed, undistracted, and concentrated;

as long as the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows and the activity of the internal organ [remains there]; "dṛśi" here having the general sense of knowledge—so long, for that duration of time, one perceives.

Time is the ender; therefore, whence can there be existence? The meaning is: from nowhere at all. And so he will say later: "The yogi who is joined with samādhi is not devoured by time, nor is he afflicted by karma; he is not overcome by anyone, for he has become self-dependent."
This is the meaning. || 40 ||
"According to rule" means:

When the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*)— the collection of channels within that [body]— has been purified by means of the prescribed breath-restraints (*prāṇasaṃyāma*) and the practices of *āsana*, *jālandharabandha*, and so forth, the vital air (*māruta*), which resides between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* in the center of the *suṣumnā*, [enters it].
Having pierced the mouth—the opening—of that nāḍī, it enters the interior of the Suṣumṇā easily and without effort; this is the implied meaning. || 41 ||

Regarding the term *māruta*: when there is "movement through the center"—that is, a thorough progression or movement [of the breath] within the *suṣumnā* reaching as far as the crown of the head—steadfastness of the mind arises; that is, a continuous flow of mental modifications in the form of the object of meditation becomes manifest.
That which is the state of the mind becoming well-stabilized, its thorough stabilization, is precisely the state of *manonmanī*. The word *manonmanī* is a synonym for *unmanī*.
As he will state further on: "Rājayoga, samādhi," and so forth. (42)
In order to generate engagement with the various types of *kumbhaka*, he states their primary and intermediate results: "For the sake of attaining those [perfections]."
p. 56) || Root Text ||
Through the practice of various types of breath-retentions (kumbhaka), one shall attain manifold accomplishments (siddhi). || 43 ||
Now, the varieties of *kumbhaka* (breath-retention).
Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, Sītkārī, Sītalī, Bhastrikā, Bhrāmarī, Mūrcchā, and Plāvinī—these are the eight types of kumbhaka. || 44 ||

At the end of inhalation (pūraka), the bandha called Jālandhara should be performed; at the end of retention (kuṃbhaka) and at the beginning of exhalation (recaka), Uḍḍiyānaka should be performed. || 45 ||
Commentary:
Those who know the procedure— that is, those who know the method of practicing *kumbhaka*—
are "knowers of the procedure" (*vidhānajña*). For the sake of attaining that perfection, namely the state of *unmanī*,
they perform various types of *kumbhakas* of diverse kinds, such as *sūryabheda* and others.
And those breath-retentions (kumbhakas) are diverse;

through the practice and performance of those diverse kumbhakas, there arises— through the various distinctions such as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and so forth— a manifold or distinct [attainment] born of birth, herbs, mantras, or austerity.

As it is said in the *Bhāgavata*: "Whatever perfections are attained here through birth, herbs, austerity, or mantras—all those one attains through yoga; by no other means does one reach the goal of yoga.
The sense is that one would attain them through the successive stages beginning with sensory withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). || 43 ||
Now, he points out the eight types of breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*) by their names: "Sūryabheda" and so forth.
This is clear. || 44 ||

Now, with three verses beginning with "At the end of the inhalation" (pūrakānte), he explains the method common to all *kumbhakas*, which is the *pāramahaṃsī* [state] perfected through *haṭha-yoga* and not achieved by any other means.
That which has the designation "Jālandhara" is called Jālandharābhidha;

it is a "bandha" (lock) because it binds the vital breath (prāṇavāyu). The Jālandhara-bandha consists of placing the chin upon the heart preceded by the contraction of the throat, at the end of the inhalation (pūraka).

At the end of *pūraka*—that is, immediately after *pūraka*—it should be performed instantaneously. By the word "but" (*tu*), it is implied that *uḍḍiyānabandha* is also to be applied at the beginning of *kumbhaka*. Furthermore, at the end of *kumbhaka*—meaning toward the conclusion of *kumbhaka*, when a small portion of *kumbhaka* remains—at the beginning of *recaka*, that is, prior to *recaka*.
It should be performed with special effort. (p.
57) Root Text.
By quickly contracting the lower part and constricting the throat, and by applying a backward tension in the middle, the vital breath (prāṇa) shall enter the Brahma-nāḍī. || 46 ||
Commentary:
The drawing upward of the region of the navel toward the back is the uḍḍiyāna-bandha. || 45 ||

"Below" means: *kaṇṭhasaṃkocana* is the contraction of the throat; when that is performed—that is, when the *jālandhara-bandha* has been performed—immediately thereafter, by means of contraction from the lower region, [one performs] the contraction of the *ādhāra*.
"By the *mūlabandha*" means by the binding of the base. "In the middle," that is, in the region of the navel;

"from behind," meaning from the back; "stretching," meaning the act of stretching or drawing [the breath upward]—by this is meant the *uḍḍiyānabandha*. By the three bindings performed according to the method described:

The meaning is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the wind (*vāyu*), goes to the *brahmanāḍī*, the *suṣumnā*; thus, one should be a "goer of the *brahmanāḍī*," meaning one who travels through the *suṣumnā* channel. Herein lies the secret:
if the binding of the tongue (*jihvābandha*) has been correctly understood from the mouth of the venerable Guru, then...

Prāṇāyāma is accomplished solely through the Jālandhara-bandha preceded by the tongue-bind (jihvābandha). By this, all the signs arise, such as the absence of agitation of the vital air (vāyu), the non-thinning of the bodily constituents (dhātu), and serenity of the face.
The *mūlabandha* and *uḍḍiyānabandha* are not required,
because they are accomplished otherwise by means of the *jālandharabandha*, which is preceded by the *jihvābandha*.
If the *jihvābandha* is not known, it should be performed according to the method stated in the verse beginning with "by contraction below" (*adhastāt kuñcanena*).

Prāṇāyāmas should be performed. All three bandhas must be learned from the mouth of a guru. If the mūlabandha is not properly understood, it gives rise to various diseases; for instance, if dhātu-kṣaya (depletion of the bodily constituents) occurs when the mūlabandha is performed.
If there is suppression of the digestive fire, dullness of voice,

and feces that take on the form of a mass of pills like those of a goat, then it should be understood that the *mūlabandha* has not been properly mastered. However, if there is proper nourishment of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), [it is successful].
When there is purification of impurities, kindling of the fire, and the perfect manifestation of the *nāda*, then it should be known that the *mūlabandha* has been correctly accomplished. || 46 ||
p. 58) || Root Text ||
Having raised the apāna upward and led the prāṇa down from the throat, the yogi, being freed from old age, becomes sixteen years of age. || 47 ||
Then, having assumed a comfortable posture, the yogi should perform the binding of the seat (āsana).
Commentary:

Regarding "apānam": having raised the *apāna*—the *apāna-vāyu*—upward by contracting the *ādhāra*, one should lead and bring the *prāṇa*—the *prāṇa-vāyu*—down from the throat to the lower part; he who does so is a *yogī*, meaning one who possesses yoga as a practice, a practitioner of yoga, [who is not overcome] by old age.
Being liberated from old age, he is especially liberated; he should be one whose age is a collection of sixteen years— that is, sixteen years of age—
even though [the practice] is to be performed at the end of the *pūraka* and so forth for all three.

Although the meaning of the verses culminates in a single point, nevertheless, by the phrase "it must be performed at the end of the *pūraka*," the timing of the *bandhas* is stated; by the phrase "by contracting below," the nature of the *bandhas* is stated; and by the phrase "having raised the *apāna* upward,"...

The fruit of the *bandhas* has thus been stated; this is the distinction. When the *jālandhara-bandha* and the *mūla-bandha* have been performed, the *bandha* called *ākarṣaṇa* (drawing upward) below the navel necessarily becomes the *uḍḍiyāna-bandha*; therefore, it was not mentioned separately in this verse. And so it has been said:

In Jñāneśvara’s commentary on the sixth chapter of the Gītā, it is stated that when the *mūlabandha* and *jālandharabandha* have been performed, the *bandha* known as *ākarṣaṇa* (drawing upward) occurs spontaneously in the region below the navel. || 47 ||
I shall describe the sequence for the practice of yoga for the sake of the yogis' attainment of yoga. Having risen at dawn or at daybreak, the wise one— || 1 ||
Having recollected the Guru at the crown of his head and his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in his heart, and having performed purification,
he should carry out the cleansing of the teeth and the application of sacred ash.
In a pure place, having established a soft seat in a delightful monastery, one should sit there and,
with the mind, call to mind the Guru and the Lord.
Having proclaimed the place and time and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the prescribed rule:

"Today, etc., preceded by the grace of the venerable Supreme Lord, for the sake of attaining the fruit of meditative absorption, I shall perform the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other rites, beginning with the postures (āsana)."
One should prostrate to the infinite god, the Lord of Nāgas, for the sake of attaining perfection in the sacred seat (pīṭha).
Salutations to Ananta, the king of serpents, who supports the circle of the earth with a thousand hoods shining with jewels.
Then, one should practice the postures (āsanas); when fatigue arises, the breath-control (śvāsana). At the end, one should practice that [posture] thoroughly.
But in the absence of fatigue, one should not practice. || 5 ||
p. 59) || Root Text ||
Having slowly drawn in the external air through the right channel (nāḍī), || 48 ||
Commentary:
One should practice the technique called Viparītakaraṇī prior to the kumbhaka,
as a means to facilitate Jālandhara-bandha through its application before the retention.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and the breath control (prāṇāyāma) as an ancillary part of the rite,
and having paid homage to the lords of yogis and others, according to the words of Śiva from the Kūrma Purāṇa.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa, the words of Śiva are as follows:
"Having paid homage to the lords of yogis along with their disciples, to Vināyaka, and to my own guru, the yogi, being well-composed, should then engage in yoga. (8)

Having bound [the breath] at the seat of accomplishment (siddhapīṭha) preceded by the lock of the pot (kumbhakabandha), ten [repetitions] should be performed on the first day, increasing by five each subsequent day.
The lord of yogis, being well-composed, should first perform the practice of the moon and the sun, practicing eighty *kuṃbhakas* at a time.
The wise call this "in accordance with and against the grain" (anuloma-viloma); having practiced Sūryabheda, one of single-minded intellect should perform it preceded by bandha. 11.
Then one should perform Ujjāyinī, then Sītkārī, and then Śītalī;
having practiced Bhastrikā as well, one should perform the other nine [prāṇāyāmas]. 12.
Having learned the mudrās from the mouth of the guru, one should practice them in their proper sequence;
thereafter, having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should perform the contemplation of the inner sound (nāda).
One should diligently perform every practice as an offering to the Lord;
having arisen from one's practice, one should bathe with warm water.
Having bathed, the wise man should daily perform his obligatory rites in brief;
likewise at midday, having practiced them and rested for a short while, he should take his meal.
A practitioner of yoga should always avoid what is unwholesome; he may, however, consume cardamom or cloves at the conclusion of his meal.
Some desire camphor as well as excellent betel-leaf; however, that which is devoid of lime powder is recommended for yogins who practice the breath-control of *pavana*.
Thus, the statement of the Cintāmaṇi does not possess inherent consistency, because by the word "some" (kecit),
those two [the sun and moon] are the causes of cold and heat respectively.
After the meal, one should engage in the study of the scriptures on liberation, or listen to the Purāṇas, or chant the names of the All-pervading Lord. (19)
Having performed the evening twilight ritual (saṃdhyā), one should practice yoga as before;
one should perform the practice when three ghaṭikās remain of the day.
Immediately after the practice, the wise should always perform the evening twilight ritual (sāyaṃsaṃdhyā).
At midnight, the self-controlled practitioner should perform the practice of Haṭha as previously described.
However, one should not practice the inverted posture (viparītākaraṇī) in the evening or at midnight, nor after eating, because it is not recommended for those times. || 22 ||
Now, desiring to explain the sequence of the instructions regarding the *kumbhaka* breath-retentions, [the author] first states the root verse (mūla) on page 60.
One should perform kumbhaka (retention) from the hair to the tips of the nails until cessation; then, one should slowly exhale the breath through the left nostril. 49.
Commentary:

He describes the piercing of the solar orb (sūryabhedana) and its qualities in three [verses], beginning with "In a seat" (āsane): "Having established a firm seat for oneself in a pure place—one that is pleasant, neither too high nor too low. (Yoga Sūtra 2.46) "In a pleasant" means that which bestows comfort; in such a comfortable [place]. "In a pure place," having firmly established one's own seat, neither excessively elevated nor excessively low.

In a secluded place characterized by the previously described features—namely, "with cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass as the upper layers"—the practitioner, being pure and seated comfortably with neck, head, and body held erect according to the Vedic injunction, sits upon that seat (āsana). It is called *āsana* because one sits upon it (*āste 'smin*) or because one is seated by means of it (*āsyate 'nena*); therein the yogi remains.
The practitioner of yoga, having assumed— meaning having accomplished and performed— one of the postures such as Svastika, Vīra, Siddha, Padma, or others,
or indeed the primary Siddhāsana itself; then, immediately after the binding of the posture, the right...

The meaning is: having slowly, very gently drawn in through the *piṅgalā*—the channel situated on the right side—the external wind or air existing outside the body, one performs a slow *pūraka* (inhalation) by means of the *piṅgalā*. || 48 ||
"Up to the hair (*ākeśāt*)" means having made the hair the limit, [it is] "up to the hair" (*ākeśam*);

from that, having made the tips of the nails the limit, it is "up to the tips of the nails" (*ānakhāgram*). One should perform the *kumbhaka* (retention) in such a way that the boundary or limit of the cessation—that is, the obstruction—of the breath (*vāyu*) occurs within that action.
The meaning is that one should perform *kumbhaka* with extreme effort in such a way that the restraint of the breath extends from the hair to the tips of the nails. Now, it may be objected:
"If this breath is restrained by force, it might escape through the pores of the skin and leave the body."

This [prāṇa] tears [the body] apart and even produces diseases such as leprosy; therefore, it must be brought under control gradually, like a wild elephant. A wild elephant or a lion becomes gentle through gradual training;
it then carries out the commands of its trainer and does not transgress them. So too is the prāṇa.
Residing in the heart of yogis, when grasped through the gradual yoga and practiced, it attains a state of confidence.
Root Text
It purifies the skull, destroys disorders of wind (vāta), and removes defects caused by worms. This supreme Sūryabheda [prāṇāyāma] should be performed again and again. 50.
Now follows the ujjāyī [breathing technique].
Having restrained the mouth, one should slowly draw the breath through the two channels so that it resonates with sound as it moves from the throat down to the heart.
Commentary:
If it is asked, "How can it be said that one should perform *kuṃbhaka* with effort, since that contradicts the statement [of the scriptures]?"—
the answer is no; for the undertaking is made with the thought, "By the power of the statement 'this *prāṇa* is restrained by force (*haṭha*'), I shall achieve mastery over the *prāṇa* before long."

And thus, because of the priority of being intent on extensive practice, and because of the natural aptness of the analogy "like a wild elephant in the forest," it is said: "Having held [the mind] in practice upon the sun and the moon,
one should hold it firmly according to one's capacity," and "by means of restraint."
It is consistent [with reason]. Therefore, the *kumbhaka* (retention of breath) must be performed with extreme effort.
To the extent that the *kumbhaka* is performed with greater effort, to that same extent there will be an increase in its qualities (*guṇa*). And to the extent that the *kumbhaka* is lax...

It may be so; there would be a deficiency of qualities. In this matter, the experience of yogis is also an authority. The inhalation (*pūraka*), however, should be performed very slowly, or it may be performed with force;
for even when the inhalation is performed with force, there is no fault. The exhalation (*recaka*), however, must be performed only very slowly.

It should be performed slowly, for if exhalation (*recaka*) is performed with force, there is the danger of loss of strength; "therefore, one should exhale very gradually and not with force," as stated by the author in various places in his works. Thus, following the limit of retention (*nirodha*), after the *kumbhaka*, [the exhalation should be performed].

The left channel (savyanāḍī) is the channel situated on the left side; through that left channel, namely the iḍā, one should exhale—that is, expel—the breath or air slowly. The repetition of the word "slowly" indicates that it should indeed be done very gently.

The word *recayet* is used for the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). As it has been said: "In expressions of wonder, dejection, wretchedness, emphasis, conciliation, and joy, a single sentence is repeated twice.
Regarding the phrase *kapālaśodhanam*: it is the purification, that which effects the cleansing, of the *kapāla*, which is the skull (the head).

It destroys the eighty types of wind-born disorders (vātadoṣa), thus it is "vātadoṣaghna"; it removes the disorder (doṣa) or affliction caused by worms born in the abdomen, thus it is "kṛmidoṣahṛt. It should be administered repeatedly, again and again.

By filling with the sun (sūrya) and retaining like a jar (kuṃbhita), and then exhaling through the moon (caṃdra)—in this manner, the yogis have described this as the supreme, most excellent practice called Sūryabheda; "by the yogis" is the understood subject. || 50 ||
He says [the following] with a half-verse regarding *ujjāyī*: "The mouth. This means having restrained—that is, made controlled—the mouth, which is the face;
the sense is that it has been sealed.
Root Text
As before, one should fill the breath into the kumbha and then exhale through the iḍā.
It removes the disorder of phlegm from the throat and increases the digestive fire of the body.

This kumbhaka, known as ujjāyī, which destroys defects located in the channels, water, the abdomen, and the bodily constituents (dhātus), should be performed by one whether walking or standing. || 53 ||
Commentary:
"From the throat"—beginning from the throat and ending at the heart;
that action for which the heart is the limit is described thus. "Accompanied by sound" (*svanena sahitam*)—both are adverbs. The wind (*pavana*) adheres or clings.

This is the meaning. Likewise, in that manner, having slowly and gently drawn in—that is, having inhaled—the wind or breath through the two channels, namely the iḍā and piṅgalā, one should fill [the abdomen]. || 51 ||

The *prāṇa* is as before, equal to the previously mentioned "piercing of the sun" (*sūryabheda*). One should perform *kumbhaka*—meaning one should restrain it—according to the method described, from the hair to the tips of the nails, until the cessation [of breath]. Then, after that *kumbhaka*, by means of the *iḍā*, the left channel...
One should practice it and abandon [other methods]. He states the qualities of *ujjāyī* in a verse and a half.

"Remover of phlegmatic disorders" (śleṣmadoṣahara) means: the "phlegmatic disorders" (śleṣmadoṣāḥ) are disorders of phlegm (śleṣman) in the throat, such as cough and so forth; that which removes them is the "remover of phlegmatic disorders. It is an "augmenter of the bodily fire" (dehānalavivardhana), meaning it increases the digestive fire (jāṭhara) located within the body.
The meaning is that "dīpana" refers specifically to causing increase. || 52 ||
Regarding the term *nāḍī*: *nāḍī* means a vessel or channel; *jala* means water that has been drunk; *udara* means the belly or abdomen;
and *dhātava ādhātavaḥ* refers to the constituent elements (dhātus) and the secondary elements (*ādhātus*) existing throughout the body.
These form a mutual *dvandva* compound. The "defect" (*doṣa*) or morbid change (*vikāra*) that has "gone to" or reached these [elements] is what is meant.

Because it destroys [impurities] specifically, it is called *nāḍījalodarādhātugatadoṣavināśana* (the destroyer of defects residing in the channels, water, abdomen, and bodily constituents). Whether by a man who is moving—performing locomotion—or even by one who is standing still, that which has the name *ujjāyī*—that whose designation is "Ujjāyī"—[is practiced]. By the word "tu" (but/however), its...

This indicates its distinctiveness. "Kāryam" means that which ought to be done. "Ujjāpī" is a reading found in some manuscripts. Whether walking or standing, one should remain free from attachment. The word *kumbhaka* is tri-gendered; however, in the masculine gender, it applies to the adjectives as well.
The reading should be made in the masculine gender. || 53 ||
p. 63) || Root Text ||
Now follows the practice of Sītkārī.
One should make a hissing sound with the mouth, and likewise yawn through the nose alone.
Through such practice and yoga, one becomes a second Kāmadeva. || 54 ||
Common to the circle of Yoginīs, he is the agent of creation and dissolution; neither hunger nor thirst, nor sleep nor even laziness arises [for him]. || 55 ||
Commentary:
