He describes the *sītkārī* breath-retention (*kumbhaka*): "The sound *sīt*" and so forth. One should produce the *sītkāra*, which is the sound "sīt" or "sīd," within the mouth (*vaktra*).
With the tongue pressed against the space between the lips, one should perform it through the mouth preceded by the *sītkāra*.
The meaning is that one should perform inhalation (*pūraka*).

By the phrase "by the nose alone" (*ghrāṇenaiva*), it is stated that exhalation (*recaka*) should be performed through both nostrils. The word "alone" (*eva*) excludes the mouth; [it means] not by the mouth.

The expulsion of air (recaka), however, should not be performed even after practice, because it causes a loss of strength. The phrase "one should perform the yawn-recaka" is also connected here. Although not explicitly mentioned, the retention (kumbhaka) should also be performed with a hissing sound (sītkāra).
It is to be understood precisely because of its nature as *kuṃbhaka* (retention). Now, the praise of the *sītkārya* (the practice of hissing):

practice (*abhyāsa*) in the manner described above—its repeated performance—is itself *yoga*, because it is a means to achieve *yoga*; by that [practice], the second [Kāmadeva] is indeed the "second" (*dvitīyaka*).
Kandarpa; because of his resemblance to the god of love (Kāmadeva) due to the excellence of his beauty and charm. || 54 ||

The "wheel of yoginīs" (*yoginīcakra*) is the assembly of yoginīs. Its "common [nature]" is that which is to be served; "emanation" (*sṛṣṭi*) is the arising of the phenomenal world, and "reabsorption" (*saṃhāra*) is its dissolution.
He is the "agent" (*kāraka*), the doer of both. There is no "hunger," meaning no desire to eat; there is no "thirst," meaning no desire to drink water.
Sleep is not deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Laziness is the absence of activity due to heaviness of body and mind;
heaviness of body arises from phlegm and the like, while heaviness of mind arises from the quality of darkness (*tamas*).
"It is neither produced nor does it manifest"—thus [it is said] by means of the yoga of practice, and [the word] "is produced" is used in this sense.
It is connected with each response. || 55 ||
p. 64) || Root Text ||
And by this method, the body shall become true and free from all afflictions; truly, by this rite, one becomes a lord of yogis upon the circle of the earth. || 56 ||
Now, Śītalī.
Having drawn in the air with the tongue, one performs the practice of retention (kumbhaka) as before.
The wise person should slowly exhale the breath through both nostrils.
It cures diseases such as abdominal tumors and splenic disorders, as well as fever, bile disorders, hunger, and thirst.
Indeed, this daughter of Kumbhika named Śītalā destroys poisons.
|| Commentary ||

"May it be so": may there be strength and vitality for the body, that is, the physical frame. By this aforementioned method, the method of practice, the lord of yogis—like Indra among yogis—becomes free from all afflictions upon the circle of the earth, being devoid of every calamity.
It would indeed be true; for according to the maxim that "every statement is restrictive," the meaning is that the result which has been stated is truly so. || 56 ||

He describes the *śītalī-kumbhaka*: "With the tongue"—meaning, having drawn in the air slowly by means of the tongue extended outside the lips, resembling the beak of a bird, one performs the inhalation (*pūraka*); as before, [one holds] the *kumbha*, that is, the *kumbhaka*, like the *sūryabheda*.

The phrase "having performed the practice (sādhana) and the ritual procedure (vidhāna)" is to be supplied as an ellipsis. "Sudhīḥ" means one whose intellect (dhī) is excellent; "ghrāṇasya randhre" refers to those two, namely the cavities of the nostrils; "śanakaiḥ śanaiḥ" means very slowly indeed.
The suffix *akac* is applied according to the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām*. One should exhale the wind, that is, the breath. || 57 ||

He states the qualities of *śītalī*: "Gulma and *plīha* (spleen) are specific diseases; those [diseases] beginning with *gulma* and *plīha* are the ailments (*āmayān*). Fever (*jvara*) refers to the disease known as fever. Pitta refers to a disorder of *pitta*. Hunger (*kṣudhā*)."

It destroys completely the desire to eat, thirst—the desire to drink water—and poisons, which are the disorders produced by the venom of snakes and other creatures; "śītalī" is an indeclinable with its meaning well-known [from common usage]. This aforementioned *kuṃbhikā* utterly destroys these.
It destroys. The word *kumbha* is also feminine in gender.
(p. 65) || Root Text ||
Now, the bellows.
Placing both soles of the feet auspiciously upon the thighs—this is the lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys all sins. || 59 ||

Having properly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) with the neck and abdomen held straight, the wise practitioner should carefully close the mouth and exhale through the nostril using the nostril itself.
Just as it resonates from the heart and throat up to the skull,
one should also forcefully fill the vital air (māruta) down to the heart-lotus.
Commentary:
The Liṅga [Purāṇa] also [confirms this]. And so says Śrī Harṣa: "Having cast up the jars made of refined gold... (58).

Since the practice of *bhastrā-kuṃbhaka* must be performed preceded by the *padmāsana*, he first describes the *padmāsana*: "Upon the thighs," etc. Having placed both soles—the lower parts of the two feet—upward, auspicious, and pure, firmly upon the thighs.

One should sit; this shall be the *padmāsana*. Of what nature is it? It is the supreme destroyer of all sins. Here, the indeclinable (*avyaya*) "upari" signifies "lying face upwards. Thus, in the *Manoramā* commentary on the *Kāraka* section, regarding the phrase "upary upari buddhīnām," [the word "upari" is used].
The commentary on the term "buddhīnām" has been made as "of those with shallow intellects. || 59 ||

He describes the *bhastrikā-kumbhaka*: "Properly," etc. "Neck and belly" (*grīvodara*)—since these are parts of a living being, they form a singular compound. One whose neck and belly are even is "one with even neck and belly" (*samagrīvodara*). One whose intellect (*dhī*) is well-established is "well-minded" (*sudhī*). [One should sit in] the *padmāsana*.

Having firmly and correctly assumed the posture, having restrained the mouth and made it fully controlled, one should with effort and exertion exhale the *prāṇa*— the air situated within the body— through the nose, specifically through one of its two apertures. || 60 ||

He describes the method of exhaling (recaka): "yathā" etc. "Hṛtkaṇṭhe" means at the heart and the throat; this is a collective copulative compound (samāhāra-dvandva). "Kapālāvadhi" means up to the skull; "sasvanam" means accompanied by sound—that is, in such a way that it is with sound. By which [means]... so that it may be thus.
In this manner (p. 66) || Root Text ||
One should likewise purge again and again, and fill [the body] again and again, just as a blacksmith moves the bellows with force. || 62 ||
In that very same way, one should mentally move the vital air (pavana) residing within one's own body; when fatigue arises in the body, then one should fill it with the solar breath (sūrya).
Just as the abdomen becomes full [of air], so too should one hold it firmly with the middle and index fingers, excluding the thumbs, while remaining light. 64.
Commentary:

The word "prāṇa" is to be supplied as the object; thus one should exhale. That action for which the heart-lotus is the limit—that is, one should fill the wind (māruta) with force and speed up to the heart-lotus.
The particle "ca" is used here merely to complete the meter. || 61 ||

Regarding the word "punar" (again): the grammatical connection is that, as before, one should again expel [the air] and repeatedly fill it. To illustrate the stated point, he provides an example with the words "yathaiva" (just as).
Just as the hide, which serves as the means for blowing the bellows-fire, is moved by the blacksmith— the maker of iron products— in a particular manner and with a particular velocity; || 62 ||
In that very same manner, by means of the intellect (dhi), one should move the vital air (pavana) or prāṇa situated within one's own body.
He states the limit of this movement through the continuous alternation of exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka): "When..."
Regarding "fatigue": when, at which time, fatigue— that is, exhaustion— should arise in the body (the physical frame) due to the continuous repetition of exhalation and inhalation, then at that time,
in such a manner (yathā) by means of which (yena) method, the abdomen becomes light and quickly full through the breath (pavana).
It should be so; in that manner, one should fill [the body] through the solar channel (*sūryanāḍī*).
Regarding the words *laghu*, *kṣipra*, *aram*, and *druta*, the *Amara-kośa* states: "light, swift, quick, and rapid. (63)
He states what is to be done immediately after the inhalation (*pūraka*) in the words: "One should retain" (*dhārayet*).
Using the two middle fingers and the two index fingers— excluding the thumbs, ring fingers, and little fingers— one should firmly hold the nose;
with the thumb, one should close the right nostril.
The meaning is that, having blocked the left nostril with the ring finger and the little finger, one should hold the nose firmly. || 64 ||
p. 67) || Root Text ||
Having performed the kumbhaka according to the rules, one should exhale the breath through the iḍā.
It pacifies wind, bile, and phlegm, and increases the digestive fire of the body. || 65 ||
|| Commentary ||

"According to rule" means: having performed *kumbhaka* preceded by *bandha*, one should exhale (*recayet*) the wind or air through the *iḍā*, the lunar channel. This is the procedure for the bellows-like *kumbhaka*. [Then] the left nostril—
Having blocked [the left nostril] with the ring and little fingers of the right hand,
one should perform exhalations and inhalations through the right nostril with the force of a bellows.
When fatigue arises, one should perform an inhalation through that same nostril using the thumb.
Having blocked the right nostril, one should hold the breath in *kuṃbhaka* according to one's capacity;
afterwards, one should exhale through the *iḍā*. Again, having blocked the right nostril with the thumb, one should perform rapid exhalations and inhalations through the left nostril like a bellows.

These should be performed. When fatigue arises, one should perform inhalation through that same nostril, close the left nostril with the ring finger and little finger, perform retention according to one's capacity, and exhale through the *piṅgalā* [right nostril]; this is one method.

Having performed inhalation through the right nostril using the ring and little fingers on the left nostril, one should suddenly block it with the thumb and exhale through the left nostril. Having performed this a hundred times, when fatigue occurs—
Once it has arisen, one should fill [the lungs] with that very [air]. Having performed the binding (bandha), one should exhale through the iḍā [nāḍī].
Again, having blocked the right nostril with the thumb and performed inhalation through the left nostril, [one should exhale] instantaneously.
Having blocked the left nostril with the ring and little fingers, one should exhale through the *piṅgalā* [right nostril] like a bellows. Having repeated this again and again,
when fatigue arises from the cycle of exhalation and inhalation, one should perform inhalation through the left nostril.

Having formed [the mudrā] with the ring and little fingers, holding it, and performing *kuṃbhaka*, one should exhale through the *piṅgalā*—this is the second method. He now states the qualities of the bellows (*bhastrikā*):

Regarding "vātapitta": wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman) constitute "vātapittaśleṣmāṇaḥ"; that which removes these is so described. It is the specific increase—that is, the stimulation—of that fire which is the digestive heat (jaṭharānala) within the body, the physical frame. || 65 ||
p. 68) || Root Text ||
It quickly awakens the kuṇḍalinī, is beneficial for the vital breath, and bestows happiness.
It destroys the obstructions of phlegm and other humors situated at the opening of the Brahma-nāḍī.
|| Commentary ||
It awakens the sleeping Kuṇḍalī quickly and swiftly;

it is called *pavana* because it purifies (*pavitrakāraka*) and bestows happiness (*sukhada*). It is beneficial (*hita*) because it removes the three *doṣas*, and it is always beneficial for everyone.

Although all *kumbhakas* are beneficial at all times, *sūryabheda* and *ujjāyī* are generally beneficial in cold weather, while *śītkārī* and *śītalī* are cool and generally beneficial in hot weather. *Bhastrikā* and *kumbhaka* are neutral regarding heat and cold and are beneficial for everyone at all times.

Although all *kumbhaka* breath-retentions remove all diseases, *sūryabheda* generally removes wind (*vāta*), *ujjāyī* generally removes phlegm (*śleṣman*), *sītkārī* generally removes bile (*pitta*) through its cooling nature, and the *kumbhaka* called *bhastrā* removes the three humors (*tridoṣa*).
Thus it should be understood. The *brahmanāḍī* is the *suṣumnā*, because it leads one to Brahman.
And so says the Śruti: "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head. Going upwards by that, one attains immortality."

The others are directed in every direction for the purpose of ascending. That which is situated—that is, properly positioned—at its mouth, at its forepart, is the bolt consisting of phlegm and other humors that obstructs the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa); [the mantra] is the destroyer, the agent of its destruction. || 66 ||
Root Text (Mūla) (p. 69)
This practice known as *bhastrā* (bellows) *kumbhaka* must especially be performed so as to break the three knots produced within the body. || 67 ||
Now follows the Bhrāmarī [mudrā].

Through the practice of yoga in this manner by the lords of yogis— [the breath] with speed as *ghoṣa*, *pūraka* (inhalation), *bhṛṅganāda* (the humming of a bee), *bhṛṅgīnāda* (the chirping of a female bee), and *recaka* (exhalation) very slowly— a certain play of bliss arose in the mind.
Commentary:

That which has become perfectly firm within the body, having properly arisen and emerged within the *suṣumnā* itself— that triad of knots (*granthitraya*) consisting of the Brahma-knot, the Viṣṇu-knot, and the Rudra-knot.

It specifically produces differentiation; for this very reason, this kumbhaka known as "bhastrā"—that which has the name *bhastrā*—must indeed be performed specifically, meaning it must necessarily be performed. However, [the practices] such as *sūryabheda* and others are to be performed according to their possibility.
They should be performed. || 67 ||
He describes the *bhrāmarī* breath-retention (*kumbhaka*). Regarding the phrase "with speed" (*vegāt*):

having performed the inhalation (*pūraka*) such that there is a sound—that is, with noise—just like the humming of a bee (*bhṛṅga*), which is to say, a sound like the buzzing of a bee (*bhramara*) during that action; [then] the bees...

That [practice] in which the sound is like the humming of bees is described as such; one should perform exhalation (*recaka*) very slowly. After inhalation (*pūraka*), the retention (*kumbhaka*) is established by its very nature as "the bee's" (*bhrāmarya*); therefore, it is not mentioned separately. However, regarding inhalation and exhalation:
"It is a distinction," thus those two were addressed. In the manner described above, *abhyāsa* is practice;
the *yoga*, or application, of that [practice]—from that, O lords of yogis, there arises (*jātā*) or comes into being a certain ineffable *ānandalīlā*, a play or sport in bliss. || 68 ||
p. 70) || Root Text ||
Now, fainting.
At the end of the inhalation, having firmly bound the Jālandhara lock, one should [proceed] slowly.
This state, known as *mūrcchanā*, is called the "fainting of the mind," which bestows happiness.
Now, the Plāvinī [meter].
With his interior filled by the noble wind set in motion within, he floats with ease even upon deep water like a lotus leaf. || 70 ||

Prāṇāyāma is said to be threefold, consisting of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka). Retention is considered to be of two kinds: sahita (accompanied) and kevala (unaccompanied). || 71 ||
Commentary:
He describes the *mūrchā-kuṃbhaka*: "At the end of the inhalation," and so forth.

At the end, at the conclusion of the *pūraka*, having firmly applied the lock known as *jālandhara-bandha*, one should exhale very slowly and gently. This is called *kumbhikā*; it is termed *mūrchanā* because it is so designated.

"What kind [of melody] enraptures the mind?"—this is *manomūrchā*. By this, the fruit of the *mūrchanā* is stated, preceded by a demonstration of its formal analysis (*vigraha*). Furthermore, what kind?
"Bestowing happiness" (*sukhapradā*), meaning it bestows (*pradadāti*) happiness (*sukham*). || 69 ||

He explains the *plāvinī-kumbhaka*: "Internally," etc. This refers to one by whom the abdomen is filled on all sides with that noble (*udāra*), i.e., excessive (*atiśayita*), wind (*māruta*) or air (*samīra*) which has been set in motion and filled within the interior of the body.
The person floats, crosses over, and moves through even unfathomable water that touches no bottom, as effortlessly and with ease as upon a lotus leaf. || 70 ||

Now he states the different types of *prāṇāyāma*: "Prāṇāyāma" [is defined as follows]. *Āyāma* is the stretching or restraint—that is, the cessation—of the *prāṇa*, which is the air moving within the body; thus it is called *prāṇāyāma*.
The definition of *prāṇāyāma* was stated by Gorakṣanātha:
Prāṇa is the life-force of one’s own body; āyāma is its restraint. It is threefold through these divisions: exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka). (p. 71)
Root Text
One should practice this combined method until complete perfection is attained;
it consists of the exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and the retention of the breath (kumbhaka) performed comfortably.
Commentary:
Breath control (prāṇāyāma) is of three kinds: exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka). Regarding the definition of exhalation, Yājñavalkya says:
"The outward expulsion of air from the abdomen is known as exhalation."

The definition of *recaka* breath control (*prāṇāyāma*): Having expelled the entire vital breath through the nostrils until it is as if empty outside by means of the wind, one remains with the breath restrained; this, wherein the air is blocked, is called *recaka*, the great restraint. The definition of *pūraka*:

The filling of air from the outside into the abdomen is indeed *pūraka* (inhalation). This is the definition of *pūraka-prāṇāyāma*. Having drawn in the air situated outside by means of the nostril, one should [fill] all the channels gradually and evenly with that very [air].
He who fulfills [the breath] is the one named *pūraka*, which is the great cessation (*mahānirodha*). Regarding the characteristic of *kuṃbhaka*:
having filled [the body] like a jar, the retention of the wind is *kuṃbhaka*.
This *kuṃbhaka* is not distinct from the *pūraka* breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), yet it is distinct [from others] in that it is neither exhalation (*recaka*) nor inhalation (*pūraka*).

And here, "filling" (pūraka) refers to holding the air situated within the nostrils perfectly motionless; those who know this call it "pot-like" (kumbhaka). Now, he divides prāṇāyāma by another method, beginning with "sahita" (combined). This is kumbhaka.

It is of two kinds: combined (*sahita*) and isolated (*kevala*). This is considered and accepted by yogis; the word "regarded" (*mata*) implies "by yogis. Among these, the combined [breath control] is of two types: that preceded by exhalation (*recaka*) and that preceded by retention (*kuṃbhaka*). As it has been said: "Whether having exhaled or having inhaled, one should perform it; that indeed is the combined *kuṃbhaka*. In that regard...

That which begins with *recaka* is non-different from *recaka-prāṇāyāma*; that which begins with *pūraka* is *kuṃbhaka*, and it is non-different from *pūraka-prāṇāyāma*; and *kevala-kuṃbhaka* is non-different from *kuṃbhaka-prāṇāyāma*. These include the previously mentioned [techniques] such as *sūryabheda* and others.
The [stages] of the kumbhaka preceded by pūraka are to be known. || 71 ||
He states the limit for the practice of *sahitakumbhaka*: "As long as... [referring to] the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the *kevala* [kumbhaka], that is, the *kevalakumbhaka*.
Root Text

This is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*; it is indeed the pure *kumbhaka*. When the pure *kumbhaka*, devoid of exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), is mastered, [then one is successful]. || 73 ||
For him, nothing whatsoever in the three worlds is difficult to obtain;
he is capable of sustaining the breath at will by means of the *kevalakumbhaka* alone.
And one also attains the state of Rājayoga; there is no doubt in this matter.
From the practice of *kumbhaka* comes the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī; from the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, [the supreme state] arises. || 75 ||
Commentary:

One should practice and perform the combined *kumbhaka* along with *sūryabheda* and other techniques until the attainment of *kevala-siddhi* (the independent perfection) is reached. After the piercing of the *suṣumnā*,
when the sounds of a jar (*ghaṭa-śabda*) arise within the *suṣumnā*, then the *kevala-kumbhaka* is perfected.
Immediately after that, ten or twenty combined kumbhakas should be performed;
the completion of the count of eighty must be accomplished by means of kevala-kumbhakas alone. If one has the capacity, more than eighty kevala-kumbhakas should be performed.

He states the definition of *kevala-kumbhaka* alone: "Having abandoned exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), that which is the retention of the breath (*vāyu-dhāraṇa*) such that it may be easy and effortless. (72)

"Sa-vā" means that this prāṇāyāma, which is a mixture of [exhalation and inhalation], is called "mixed kumbhaka"; they praise this as "pure" (kevala). Regarding "pure": exhalation is *reca*, and inhalation is *pūraka*; that which is devoid of or free from both exhalation and inhalation (*recapūrakau*) is "pure kumbhaka."
When [that] has been accomplished. || 73 ||

For that yogi, there exists nothing whatsoever—whether difficult to obtain or hard to attain—that is desired or wished for in the three worlds; even the retention of the vital breath (*vāyu-dhāraṇa*) is not [difficult] for him.
The meaning is that everything is easily obtained by him. "Capable" means by means of *kumbhaka* alone.

One who is capable and empowered through the practice of *kumbhaka* [can perform] the retention of the vital air (*vāyu*) as desired or according to one's wish; therefore, from that retention of the vital air... || 74 ||

One attains the state of Rājayoga, the state whose essence is Rājayoga; there is no doubt in this matter—this is the meaning of "it is certain. He states that the practice of *kumbhaka* (breath retention) is the cause of liberation (*kaivalya*) through a traditional sequence: "From *kumbhaka*," etc.
From *kuṃbhaka*—that is, from the practice of *kuṃbhaka*—the *kuṇḍalī* arises; she is the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*) of that [practice]. (p. 73) [Root Text]
The *suṣumnā* becomes unobstructed and the perfection of *haṭha* arises. Without *haṭha*, *rājayoga* does not succeed;
without *rājayoga*, *haṭha* does not succeed. Therefore, one should practice the pair until both are accomplished. (76)
At the conclusion of the retention of breath through *kuṃbhaka*, one should make the mind supportless.
By means of such practice through yoga, one shall attain the state of Rājayoga.
|| Commentary ||
Awakening is the breaking of sleep; awakening of Kuṇḍalī is *kuṇḍalībodha*; therefore, [it arises] from that awakening of Kuṇḍalī. || 75 ||

The *suṣumnā* channel becomes unobstructed, free from the blockages of phlegm and other humors. Through the sequence beginning with sensory withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the perfection of *haṭha*—that is, the perfection of the practice of *haṭha*—arises in the form of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). This pertains to the two means: *haṭhayoga* and *rājayoga*.

He states their mutual relationship as benefactor and beneficiary: "Without haṭha," etc. Without haṭha—that is, without haṭhayoga—rājayoga is not perfected; without rājayoga, haṭha is not perfected. Therefore, for one intent on only one of them, there is no accomplishment. Hence, [one should seek] completion...
Taking the attainment of the perfection of Rājayoga as the limit,
one should practice and perform the pair— namely, both Haṭhayoga and Rājayoga— until that perfection of Rājayoga is reached. Beyond Haṭha...
The term "rājayoga" here refers to the means for achieving rājayoga, whether directly or indirectly,
just as the word "life" (jīvana) is applied to a plough that is the means of sustaining life. And the means for achieving rājayoga is taught in the fourth chapter.

The forms of the Unmanī-Śāmbhavī-mudrā and others to be described hereafter have been stated in the *Aparokṣānubhūti* as consisting of fifteen limbs and ten limbs respectively; those consisting of the "interpenetrated by the visible" (*dṛśyānuviddha*) and so forth have been stated in the *Vākyasudhā*. || 76 ||
He describes the manner of attaining Rājayoga through the practice of Haṭha: "By means of Kumbhaka," and so forth.

At the end— that is, in the middle— of that restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through retention (*kuṃbhaka*), one should make the mind (*citta*), which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), supportless. The meaning is that once *samprajñāta-samādhi* has arisen, one should effect the dissolution of that state of abiding in the form of Brahman through supreme detachment (*vairāgya*).

In the manner thus described, by means of *yoga*—that is, by means of the practice (*abhyāsa*) which is the application (*yukti*) [of that method]—one shall go to, or attain, the state of *rājayoga*. According to the lexicon (*kośa*), "yoga" is used in the senses of conjunction, means, meditation, union, and application. || 77 ||
p. 74) || Root Text ||
Emaciation of the body, brightness in the face, clarity in the voice, and perfectly clear eyes; freedom from disease, mastery over the bindus, stimulation of the digestive fire,
and purification of the channels— these are the signs of Haṭhayoga.
Thus ends the second instruction in the Haṭhapradīpikā. || 2 ||
Commentary:

He states the indicators of the attainment of *haṭha*: "Emaciation of the body," and so forth. Emaciation (*kārśya*) of the body (*vapuḥ*), that is, the physical frame; serenity (*prasāda*) in the face (*vadana*), that is, the countenance;
clarity (*sphuṭatva*), that is, the manifestation of the internal sound (*nāda*); and the eyes (*nayane*) being perfectly stainless, as if one were free from disease.
The state [of health] is freedom from disease, which is well-being; it is the victory over the element of *bindu*, consisting in its non-depletion;

it is the kindling of the digestive fire (*audarya-agni*); and it is the specific purification of the channels, which is the removal of impurities—this is the future result of *haṭha*, that is, the perfection of the practice of *haṭha*.
That by which something is characterized is a "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa). || 78 ||
Thus ends the second instruction in the *Jyotsnā*, the commentary on the *Śrī Haṭhapradīpikā* composed by Brahmānanda. 2.
The Third Instruction.
Root Text.
Just as the serpent-king is the support for the earth with its mountains and forests, so indeed is Kuṇḍalinī the support for all the Yoga-tantras. || 1 ||
When Kuṇḍalinī, sleeping by the grace of the Guru, awakens, then all the lotuses and even the knots are pierced.
Then the path of the breath becomes like a royal highway to the state of emptiness; then the mind is without support, and then there is the deception of time.
|| Commentary ||
Now he states that Kuṇḍalī is the locus of all yogas: "saśailā... etc. "Saśailavanāḥ" means those which exist together with mountains (śaila) and forests (vana);
and these are the "dhātryaḥ," meaning the grounds. Although "dhātrī" is singular, [the plural is used here].

The plural number is used by taking into account the distinction between different regions. "Ahināyaka" means the leader or guide of snakes (*ahīnām*); just as Śeṣa is the support or substratum (*ādhāra*), so too [is he].
"Yogatantrāṇi" refers to the systems or methods (*tantra*) of yoga—that is, the means (*upāya*) for yoga—for all of them.
The Kuṇḍalinī is the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) and the support; the sense is that without the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī, all means of yoga are futile. || 1 ||
He states the fruit of awakening the Kuṇḍalinī in two verses, beginning with "suptā" (asleep).
When the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī awakens—that is, becomes conscious—by the grace of the Guru, then all the lotuses, namely the six cakras, are pierced; that is, they become opened. The knots as well...
And the knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are pierced; that is, they undergo dissolution—this is the grammatical connection. || 2 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the vital breath" (prāṇasya): at that time, the path of emptiness, the *suṣumnā*, acts like a royal road (*rājapatha*) for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is like a wind; it becomes a royal road (*rājayathāyate*), as it were, a highway (*rājamārgāyate*), because movement [along it] occurs with ease. At that time...

The mind has an object and a support; therefore, when it becomes objectless and supportless—having emerged from that—it becomes free from objective referents. At that time, there occurs the deception and evasion of Time, which is Death. || 3 ||
p. 76) || Root Text ||
Suṣumnā, Śūnyapadavī, Brahmaraṃdhra, Mahāpatha, Śmaśāna, Śāṃbhavī, and Madhyamārga—these are synonymous terms. || 4 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the application of mudrās in order to awaken the Goddess who is sleeping at the entrance of the door of Brahman. || 5 ||
Mahāmudrā, Mahābandha, Mahāvedha, Khecarī, Uḍyāna, Mūlabandha, and the bandha known as Jālandhara. (6)
Karaṇī, the one called Viparītā, Vajrolī, and Śakticālana—this indeed is the tenfold mudrā that destroys old age and death. || 7 ||
Commentary:
He states the synonyms of Suṣumnā: "Suṣumnā," etc. These words mentioned are denoters of a single object; that is, they are synonyms. The meaning of the verse is clear. || 4 ||
"Therefore" means: since the piercing of the six chakras and so forth occurs only through the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī,

therefore, by every effort— that is, by all possible exertion— one should [awaken her], for Suṣumnā is the door to Brahman, characterized as existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda), meaning it is the means of attaining it.
Having closed the opening of the *suṣumnā* with the mouth at its tip— that is, at its front part— one should perform the practice,
that is, the repeated exercise, of the *mudrās*, such as the *mahāmudrā* and others, in order to awaken, that is, to thoroughly rouse, the sleeping *kuṇḍalinī*, the Sovereign Lady.
One should practice; one should practice correctly. || 5 ||
He indicates the mudrās with the half-verse beginning with "mahāmudrā" and so forth. The meaning of this half-verse is clear. 6.
He states the fruit of the mudrās with two and a half verses: "This," etc. This aforementioned group of ten mudrās [overcomes] both old age and death.
Root Text
This divine [teaching] was proclaimed by Ādinātha; it bestows the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭaiśvarya), is beloved by all the Siddhas, and is difficult even for the gods to attain. || 8 ||
Commentary:
Regarding old age and death, it is their destroyer and preventer. || 7 ||
It was spoken—that is, declared—by Ādinātha Śambhu. "Divine" (divya) means existing in heaven (divi), and it is supreme. Furthermore, the eight sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya) are those known as:
atomization (aṇimā), magnification (mahimā), heaviness (garimā), lightness (laghimā), attainment (prāpti), irresistible will (prākāmya), sovereignty (īśitā), and mastery (vaśitā).

Among these, *aṇimā* is the subtlety of the body like that of an atom, resulting from the departure of *prakṛti* by mere volition. 1. *Mahimā* is the state of greatness like that of space and so forth, resulting from the filling out by *prakṛti*.
2. *Garimā* is the state of heaviness like that of a mountain and so forth, even for something as light as cotton-wool. 3.
4. *Laghimā* (levity) is the state of lightness, like that of cotton wool, even for something as heavy as a mountain.

5. *Prāpti* (attainment) is the proximity to all things; for example, while remaining on the ground, one touches the moon with the tip of a finger. 6. *Prākāmya* (efficacy) is the non-obstruction of one's will; for example, ...

6. Like water, one sinks into and emerges from the earth. 7. Sovereignty (*īśitā*) is the capacity for the specific creation, dissolution, and arrangement of the elements (*bhūta*) and elemental derivatives (*bhautika*). 8. Mastery (*vaśitva*) is the making of the elements and elemental derivatives subject to one’s own will. 9. Of these...

"Pradāyaka" means one who gives pre-eminently; thus, he is the beloved and dear one of all those perfected beings (siddhas) such as Kapila and others, and even for the Maruts—the gods—he is difficult to attain, let alone for others—this is the meaning. || 8 ||
p. 78) || Root Text ||
It should be guarded with great effort like a casket of jewels; it must never be told to anyone, just as one would not speak of the secret amorous dalliances of a woman of noble family.
Now, the Mahāmudrā.
Pressing the perineum with the left heel and extending the right leg,
one should hold [the posture] firmly with both hands.
Having placed the band around the neck, one should hold the breath upwards; just as a snake struck by a staff becomes straight like a staff. || 11 ||
Commentary:
"Should be kept secret" means it must be concealed with great and supreme effort.

To provide an illustration for its necessity of being kept secret, he says "just as": just as a casket for jewels—that is, a jewel-casket for diamonds and the like—is [kept]. By what? By that [effort].

It is concealed in such a manner; it must not be told to any person whatsoever, nor even to Brahmā himself—how much less to anyone else? In this regard, there is an illustration: *kulastriyaḥ surataṃ* means the sexual union (*saṃgamana*) of women of noble family.
*yathā* means "just as" or "in whatever manner. || 9 ||
Among the mudrās and so forth, since the Mahāmudrā was mentioned first, he now explains it.

Regarding the phrase *pādamūlena*: "the root of the foot" (*pādamūla*) refers to the heel (*pārṣṇi*) of the left or right foot; thus, by "the root of the foot," the meaning is "by the heel of the left foot. "The womb" (*yoni*) refers to the place of the womb, the region between the anus and the penis.
Having firmly pressed the root of the vagina with the heel of the contracted left foot— this is the meaning— the right foot, other than the left,
is extended with its heel touching the ground and its toes pointing upward.
Having formed it like a staff with both hands,
one should hold it firmly and tightly at the region of the thumb, grasping it with the index fingers of the two hands slightly bent. || 10 ||
Having properly applied—that is, having performed—the Jālandhara-bandha by binding at the throat, in the region of the throat; [one should draw] the wind, the vital air, upwards.
Root Text
When the Kuṇḍalinī power suddenly becomes straightened, then that state of death arises, which rests upon the two channels (nādīs). || 12 ||
Then one should exhale very slowly indeed, and not with force; by that very method, the best of the wise call it Mahāmudrā. || 13 ||

This very Mahāmudrā has indeed been revealed by the great adepts (mahāsiddhas); through it, the afflictions such as the great defilements, as well as death and other such states, are brought to exhaustion.
|| Commentary ||

One should fix [the mind] above in the *suṣumnā*. By this, the *mūlabandha* (root-lock) is indicated. The traditional teachers maintain that this is accomplished by the compression of the *yoni* and the binding of the tongue.
Just as a serpent struck with a staff—that is, beaten by a staff—is made to coil (*kuṇḍalinī*).

"Having the form of a staff" (*daṇḍākāraḥ*) means that which has a form like that of a staff; the meaning is that it becomes straight, having abandoned its curved shape. Likewise, the *kuṇḍalī-ādhāra-śakti* arises or comes forth pre-eminently, suddenly—that is, very quickly—as straight.
When she has become such, straightened out, and rendered upright, then it is as stated.
When the two channels, Iḍā and Piṅgalā, which serve as its support, [cease], that state of death arises;
for when Kuṇḍalinī is awakened and the vital breath has entered the Suṣumnā, there is separation from the breath in both [channels]. || 12 ||

Then, immediately after that, one should exhale the breath very slowly; the word "the breath" is understood here. However, one should not exhale with force, for if one exhales with force, there is the danger of loss of strength.
The particle *khalu* is used as an expletive. This is Mahāmudrā.
It was clearly demonstrated—that is, shown with excellence—by the great Siddhas, beginning with Ādinātha.
He explains the etymological meaning of *mahāmudrā*: "Great" (*mahān*) and they are "afflictions" (*kleśāḥ*), thus "great afflictions" (*mahākleśāḥ*);
these are ignorance, pride, attachment, aversion, and dogmatic adherence.
Root Text
And for that very reason, the best of the wise call it Mahāmudrā.
Having practiced on the lunar limb, one should practice again on the solar limb; when the count has become equal, one should then release the mudrā.
Commentary:

Those faults, such as grief and delusion, which have those five as their primary cause—that is, whose effects they are—are destroyed. Furthermore, death and the rest—namely old age and so forth—also perish and vanish. For this very reason, the wise are distinguished.
Among those, the wise are the best; they call [the state] the "Supreme Wisdom" (vibudhottama).

It is called "Great Seal" (mahāmudrā) because, according to its etymological derivation, it seals—that is, pacifies—the great afflictions and defects such as death and so forth. This is the meaning. || 14 ||
He describes the sequence for practicing Mahāmudrā: "In the lunar limb" (*caṃdrāṅge*). The "lunar limb" (*caṃdrāṅga*) refers to the limb characterized by the moon, that is, the lunar channel;
it is the left limb. The word "tu" (but/indeed) serves to complete the meter. Having practiced correctly [on the left], one [practices] with the sun.

The limb characterized by Piṅgalā is the solar limb (sūryāṅga). Within that solar limb, on the right side, following the practice of the left side, for as long as time continues, it remains equal upon the left side.

One should practice until the number [of breaths] becomes equal to the count of the *kumbhaka* exercises; thereafter, following that equality of count, one should release the *mudrā*, namely the *mahāmudrā*. The procedure here is as follows: having joined the heel of the contracted left foot to the place of the *yoni*.

Having grasped the big toe of the extended right foot with the two contracted index fingers, one practices on the left side; in this practice, the filled air remains in the left side. [Then] the heel of the contracted right foot is placed at the site of the *yoni*.

Having joined [the hands], one should grasp the big toe of the extended left foot with the two contracted index fingers; this is the practice on the right side. In this practice, the filled air remains in the right side. || 15 ||
p. 81) || Root Text ||
For there is nothing that is either wholesome or unwholesome; indeed, all tastes become tasteless. Even dreadful poison, once consumed, is digested, as is even nectar.
Consumption, leprosy, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, indigestion, and other such ailments—his humors (doṣas) go to destruction if he practices Mahāmudrā. || 17 ||
This Mahāmudrā, which brings about great accomplishment for human beings, has been taught; it should be guarded with effort and not given to just anyone. || 18 ||
|| Commentary ||
He states the qualities of Mahāmudrā in three [verses], beginning with "Not indeed... (na hi).

For the phrase "for one who practices Mahāmudrā" is to be supplied [as the subject]. "Neither wholesome nor unwholesome" means that there is no consideration of what is wholesome or unwholesome. Therefore, the construction is to be understood by changing the case-ending: "therefore, all tastes consumed—whether pungent, sour, and so forth—are digested."
"Flavorless" means those things from which the essence has departed; such stale objects are digested.

Even food that is "terrible"—meaning difficult to digest—when eaten, is digested and becomes assimilated like poison, like venom, or even like nectar (pīyūṣa). How much more so, then, other [ordinary] things?
The state of being. || 16 ||
For that person who practices Mahāmudrā, consumption, royal diseases,
leprosy, anal prolapse, abdominal tumors, and other specific ailments— of which indigestion,
the failure to digest consumed food, is the foremost or precursor— [shall perish].
Likewise, such defects as mahodara, fever, and others—diseases produced by the humors (doṣas)—go to their end, that is, they reach destruction. || 17 ||
While introducing the Mahāmudrā, he speaks of its secrecy: "It has been told," etc.
This very Mahāmudrā has been told—that is, explained. (p. 82)
Root Text
One should place the heel of the left foot in the region of the vagina;
likewise, one should place the right foot upon the left thigh. (19)
Thus ends the Mahābandha.
Then, having filled the breath, pressing the chin firmly against the heart, and contracting the breath, one should fix the mind in the center. || 20 ||
Having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, one should slowly exhale the air; having practiced on the left side, one should then practice on the right side. (21)
Commentary:

The word "mayi" (in me) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Of what nature is she? She is the one who brings about (*karī*) the great *siddhis*—such as *aṇimā* and the rest—for men who practice;
she is to be concealed by that supreme effort (*prayatna*), being worthy of concealment through such exertion.
"To anyone whatsoever"—meaning to any person who is unqualified and unrelated; the genitive case is used here in a general sense. "Should not be given" means it is not fit to be bestowed. || 18 ||

He describes the *mahābandha*: "The heel," and so forth. The *pārṣṇi* is the lower part of the ankles of the left (*vāma*) foot—that is, the *savya* foot. As Amara states: "The two ankle-joints are called *granthi*; the male [term] is *gulpha*;
the part below those two is the *pārṣṇi*. It is placed in the region of the *yoni*, that is, in the space between the anus and the genitals.

"Should apply intensely" means he should join [the limbs] together. Having placed—that is, having properly positioned—the right foot upon that left thigh, which is the "left" or "savya" one; the word "tathā" (so) is used here for the purpose of completing the meter. || 19 ||

"Having filled" means: thereafter, having filled [the body] with air, one should firmly press the chin against the heart, placing it there tightly; by this, the Jālandhara-bandha is described. [Then] the yoni...

Contracting the space between the anus and the genitals—by this, the *mūlabandha* is indicated; however, since its purpose is already served by the *jihvābandha*, it need not be performed separately. One should fix and direct the mind (*svānta*) into the center, that is, into the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*). || 20 ||

"Having retained" means: having retained—that is, having performed *kumbhaka* (retention)—according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*) without exceeding one's power, [one should exhale] the breath very slowly and gently.
Root Text
However, it is the opinion of some that one should avoid tying [the thread] around the neck.
The binding of the tongue against the upper teeth is said to be recommended. || 22 ||
But this [bandha] is the obstructer of the upward movement of all the channels;
indeed, this is the Great Bandha, the bestower of great siddhis. || 23 ||
He is expert in liberating [beings] from the great bondage of the noose of Time.
Commentary:

One should exhale the breath. Having practiced correctly on the left side and the right side, and having turned [the breath] properly, one should practice again on the right side and the left side for exactly the same number of times. || 21 ||
Now, he states the lack of utility for the constriction of the throat within the Jālandhara-bandha: "The opinion... etc.
This is the opinion of certain teachers. What is it? He says: here, in this Jālandhara-bandha, "bandha" refers to the binding of the throat.
One should avoid contracting [the tongue], and one should especially avoid it. Why?

Because the "kings of the teeth" (dantarājānaḥ) are the front teeth; those situated upon the front teeth are called "situated on the king-teeth" (rājadaṃtasthāḥ), and that which is the tongue is thus "situated on the king-teeth."

In that [practice], the binding—meaning the contact—of the upper part of the tongue against the palate (the "king's tooth") is recommended; this is because it is more excellent than relying on the contraction of the throat. || 22 ||

Regarding the phrase "But this": "this," however, refers to the binding of the tongue situated at the "king's tooth" (the uvula). Furthermore, "all those channels" (*sarvanāḍyaḥ*) refers to the seventy-two thousand channels; of these, excluding the *suṣumnā*, there is an upward movement of the vital air (*vāyu*) above, that is, in the upper direction, which constitutes its "upward motion" (*ūrdhvagati*). Of that [motion]...

The term *nirodhaka* means "obstructive. By this, it is indicated that the result described for *jālandhara*—namely, "for by this one binds the network of vessels" (*badhnāti hi śirājālam*)—is established through this very [practice]. He states the fruit of *mahābandha*: "This indeed... This refers to the aforementioned [bandha], which is well-known (*prasiddha*).
It is so called because it bestows great accomplishments (mahāsiddhi) preeminently. || 23 ||
The noose or snare of Time—that is, of Death—is the great bond; [he is skilled] specifically in the liberation from that bondage. (p. 84)
Root Text
It maintains the confluence of the three rivers (Triveṇī) and causes the mind to reach Kedāra.
Just as a woman endowed with beauty and charm is [unfulfilled] without a man.
The great seal (mahāmudrā) and the great bond (mahābandha) are fruitless when devoid of piercing (vedha). || 25 ||
Now, the Great Piercing (Mahāvedha).
The yogi, established in the great bandha, being single-minded, performs pūraka and restrains the movement of the vital airs by means of the kaṇṭhamudrā.
Commentary:
Expert and skilled in liberation; he maintains—that is, ordains—the confluence, which is the union of the three rivers, at Prayāga.
He holds that sacred site of Śiva called Kedāra, located between the two eyebrows, within his mind.

One should cause [the mind] to reach its own state. By the rule beginning with *gati-buddhi-*, that which is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the sense of the root *aṇ* (the causative base) becomes the object (*karman*) in the sense of the root *ṇi* (the causative). || 24 ||

In order to speak first of the Great Piercing (mahāvedha), he describes its excellence: "Form," etc. Form is beauty; the quality dear to the eye is *lāvaṇya*, a particular kind of luster. As it has been said: "Like the internal shimmering of a shadow within pearls..."

"That which shines forth within the limbs is here called *lāvaṇya* (grace). A distinguished young woman endowed with these two [qualities] is as fruitless without a husband as a man is without a wife; likewise are *mahāmudrā* and *mahābandha*.

By means of the "great piercing" (mahāvedha). According to the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya that "the elision of the preceding and following members [of a compound] should also be stated even without an external cause," there is the elision of the word *mahat*. The meaning is that they are excluded, devoid, fruitless, and useless. || 25 ||

He speaks of the *mahāvedha*: "In the *mahābandha*" means situated in the *mahābandha-mudrā*. The one whose intellect (*dhī*) is single-pointed (*ekāgra*) is the "single-pointed-minded" (*ekāgradhī*) yogi, the practitioner of yoga; [he performs] the *pūraka* (inhalation).
Having performed the inhalation of air through both nostrils, one applies the throat-seal (kaṇṭhamudrā);
by means of that Jālandhara-mudrā, [one restrains] the movement— consisting of upward, downward, and other directions— of the vital winds such as prāṇa.
p. 85) || Root Text ||
With both hands joined together, one should gently strike the buttocks against the ground.
Having transcended the two petals, the wind throbs while moving in the center. || 27 ||
Indeed, a connection between the moon, the sun, and fire arises for the sake of immortality; once the state of death has arisen, one should then exhale the vital air (vāyu). || 28 ||
Through practice, this Great Piercing bestows the great accomplishment.
Commentary:
The meaning is: having turned [the breath] so that it is quiet and motionless, having restrained it, that is to say, having performed *kumbhaka* (retention). || 26 ||

Regarding the term *samahasta*: "one whose pair of hands is level on the ground" (*bhūmau*) means one whose pair of hands (*hastayuga*)—that is, the two hands—is level upon the earth; the sense is that he is one whose two hands have their palms pressed flat against the ground and are straight. *Sphicau* refers to the buttocks (*kaṭiprothau*). [In the feminine...]
According to Amara, *sphic* refers to the buttocks (*kaṭiprotha*).
By means of supporting the hands, whose palms are pressed against the ground,
together with the left foot, the heel of which is joined to the region of the vulva, [one remains] upon the earth.
Having slightly raised [the breath], one should strike it slowly and gently; one should strike it properly.

Having transcended—that is, having passed beyond—the pair of the two channels, Iḍā and Piṅgalā, right there on the ground, the wind moves in the middle, vibrating within the center of the Suṣumnā. || 27 ||
"Soma, Sūrya, and Agni" refers to the channels (nāḍīs) presided over by them— namely Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā— which are to be understood by the terms Soma, Sūrya, and Agni;
their connection [is established] through their connection with those [deities] via the vital air (vāyu).
The connection [is as follows]: it arises for the sake of immortality, that is, for liberation (*mokṣa*). The indeclinable *vai* is used for emphasis.

The state of death—the condition of one who has died, being separated from the vital breaths—comes into existence because of the absence of the movement of the vital breath in the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels. Then, immediately after that:
One should expel the air through both nostrils, releasing it slowly. || 28 ||
Regarding "the great penetration" (mahāvedha):
through this great penetration, by repeated practice— that is, by its constant repetition— the great supernatural powers (mahāsiddhi), such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, arise.
p. 86) || Root Text ||
It destroys wrinkles, gray hair, and disease, and is practiced by the most excellent of adepts. || 29 ||
This triad is a great secret that destroys old age and death; it increases the digestive fire and bestows qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. || 30 ||
And it is performed eightfold, every watch, day after day.
It always sustains the accumulation of merit and shatters the flood of evil.
Commentary:
A *pradāyaka* is one who bestows abundantly. *Valī* is the wrinkling of the skin due to old age;

*palita* is the whiteness of the hair caused by aging; and *vepa* is trembling. He is called *valī-palita-vepa-ghna* because he destroys these. For this very reason, he is the most excellent among practitioners (*sādhakas*) and those who engage in spiritual training (*abhyāsins*).
The meaning is that it is served—that is, practiced—by the most excellent practitioners. || 29 ||

He states the extreme secrecy of the three, beginning with Mahāmudrā: "This" refers to this triad, the triad beginning with Mahāmudrā, which is a great secret (*mahāguhya*) and an extreme mystery (*atirahasya*). Here, the qualifiers contain the reason: for since old age (*jarā*), that is decrepitude, and death (*mṛtyu*), the final end...
The separation of the vital breath from the body, the specific destruction of those two [the breath and the body],

the increase and radiance of the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), and the agent that effects this— namely, the qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā) and so forth— these qualities he brings to excellence.

"Dadāti" means it bestows qualities such as *aṇimā* and so forth. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of including health, the *bindu*, victory, and so on; the word "eva" (only/verily) has the sense of restriction.
30. Now he states the specific means for each of these three separately: "In eight ways," [and] "during the day."

"Daily" means every day. "In every watch" means in every *prahara*; the repetition [of the word] indicates frequency. "In eight ways" means it is performed in eight modes. The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
It is also connected with the phrase "these three. Of what nature is it? It is a "mass of merit" (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*).
What kind of thing is it that is joined together and fashioned as a mass— a flood, a torrent, or a multitude, so to speak— of sins? That which is like a thunderbolt, the destroyer of such a mass,
when practiced at all times, then and there becomes the destroyer of sins.
p. 87) || Root Text ||
Thus, for those who possess the right training, even a very small amount constitutes the first accomplishment.
Now, the Khecarī [mudrā].
When the tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in reverse, and the gaze is directed between the eyebrows,
that is the Khecarī Mudrā.
One should gradually increase the *kalā* by means of cutting, moving, and milking, until it touches the space between the eyebrows; then, the perfection of *khecarī* is attained. || 33 ||
|| Commentary ||
Those who possess the instruction handed down through the authentic tradition— that is, the teacher’s oral guidance—
should perform the preliminary practice in the manner described, namely eight times every day and every watch, though in ever-increasingly small measures. || 31 ||

Desiring to explain Khecarī, he first describes its essential nature: "In the skull... and so forth. In the skull—that is, at the head—there is a cavity or hollow; in that skull-cavity, the tongue (rasanā) should be "moving in reverse," meaning it moves upward, having turned its face away [from the mouth].
The gaze that has entered between the eyebrows, having gone into the middle of the eyebrows, is the vision [of Khecarī].

That becomes the Khecarī Mudrā. The definition of Khecarī is established as the vision between the eyebrows preceded by the insertion of the tongue into the cavity of the skull (kapālakuhara). || 32 ||

He states the characteristics of the accomplishment of *khecarī*: "Cutting," etc. "Cutting" (*chedana*) is that which will be described immediately below. "Moving" (*cālana*) is grasping the tongue with the thumbs and index fingers of both hands and rotating it from left to right and right to left. "Milking" (*doha*) [is as follows].
With the thumb and forefinger of both hands, one should milk that [channel] like a cow-milking vessel;

by means of those [fingers], one should gradually lengthen the tongue—that is, make it long—until that tip of the tongue touches the space between the eyebrows, the exterior point between the two eyebrows. When that occurs, then...
The perfection of Khecarī is the attainment of Khecarīsiddhi. || 33 ||
p. 88) || Root Text ||
Then, taking up a very sharp, smooth, and stainless blade resembling the leaf of the Snuhī plant,
one should cut off a portion the size of a single hair with it.
Then, one should rub [the area] with powdered saindhava and pathyā;
when seven days have passed again, one should shave it down to the level of the hair.
In this manner, one who is constantly disciplined should practice for six months in succession.
Within six months, the stone-binding at the root of the tongue is destroyed.
Commentary:
He states the means for achieving that: "Snuhī," etc. Snuhī is *guḍā*; its leaf is its petal.

A weapon resembling a *snuhī* leaf—that is, like a *snuhī* leaf—is very sharp (*sutīkṣṇa*), meaning exceedingly sharp, and it is both glossy (*snigdha*) and stainless (*nirmala*), thus being "glossy and stainless" (*snigdhanirmala*). Such is the weapon.

Having taken up the instrument for cutting, having properly taken it and grasped it, then immediately after seizing the blade, one should cut— meaning one should properly excise and sever— a portion the size of a hair (*romapramāṇa*), that is, merely a hair’s breadth,
[at the vessel] called the "vein at the root of the tongue."
The word *karma* is to be supplied [from the previous verse]. According to Amara: "Siṃhuṇḍa, vajrasruk, strī, snuhī, and guḍā are synonyms for miśreyā. (34)
Then, immediately after the excision, one should vigorously rub the severed site of the vessel with powdered *saindhava* salt— originating from the Sindhu region— and *harītakī*.

For up to seven days, scraping and rubbing with rock salt (*saindhava*) and *pathyā* should be performed morning and evening. Since practitioners of yoga are prohibited from using salt, they take the powder of *khadira* and *pathyā*. [End of] Root [section].
The mention of "Saindhava" (rock salt) is intended for the practice of Khecarī prior to the practice of Haṭha.

"Saptadina" is a collective term for seven days; when that has arrived—that is, when it has passed—the meaning is on the eighth day. Verbs signifying "attainment" are synonymous with verbs signifying "going."
Previously, in comparison to cutting, one should cut off even more than a hair's breadth. || 35 ||

"Thus" means: in this manner, by this sequence, first there is the cutting of [hair] the measure of a single hair for seven days, and during that same period, the cutting is performed both evening and morning. (p.
Root Text
Having turned the *kalā* away from oneself, one should join it at the triple path (*tripatha*).
That becomes the *khecarī-mudrā*, and it is called the *vyomacakra*. || 37 ||
Having turned the tongue upward, he remains so for even half a moment.
The yogi is liberated from poisons, as well as from disease, death, old age, and the like. || 38 ||
Commentary:

And rubbing. On the eighth day, there is further cutting; following this stated sequence, being constantly disciplined, one should perform and practice correctly for six months, up to the end of six months. The words "cutting and rubbing" are supplied as the objects of the action.
After six months,

the binding— the fetter— by means of that channel (nāḍī) which acts as an obstruction at the junction of the palate-cavity and the tongue (rasanā), specifically at the root of the tongue (rasanāmūla) in its lower part, shall perish.
It is destroyed completely. || 36 ||
He states what must be done when the tongue has grown large due to cutting and so forth: "The digit," etc.

Having turned her face away— she whose tongue is a mere fraction and whose mouth is averted— one should make her face toward oneself and join her to the "threefold path," that is, the cavity of the skull where the paths of the three channels meet. One should unite her there.
That Khecarī Mudrā, which has the form of a triple-path extending for a yojana, is called the Vyomacakra;
it is designated by the term "Vyomacakra. || 37 ||

Now, the qualities of Khecarī: "The tongue," etc. Having placed the tongue—so called because it moves upward into the cavity above the palate—in such a manner for half a moment (kṣaṇārdham), that is, for half of a moment or muhūrta, even for just a ghaṭikā; [one should remain thus].
If the Khecarī Mudrā is maintained, then the yogi is liberated from poisons— specifically liberated from the poisons of snakes, scorpions, and the like; he is also freed from disease,
which is the imbalance of the bodily constituents, and from death, the final separation of the vital breath from the body, and from old age.
And one is liberated from those things beginning with old age, such as wrinkles and the like.

Regarding the word *kṣaṇa*, it is used in various senses: in the sense of a festival (*utsava*), the forearm (*prakoṣṭha*), a moment (*muhūrta*), a religious observance (*niyama*), a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*), and also time (*samaya*). Thus it has multiple meanings. || 38 ||
p. 90) || Root Text ||
Neither disease, nor death, nor lassitude, nor sleep, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor even fainting shall befall him who knows the Khecarī Mudrā. (39)
He who knows the Khecarī Mudrā is not afflicted by disease, is not tainted by karma, and is not constrained by time. (40)
Because the mind moves in the void and the tongue has gone to move in the void, this mudrā is designated by the perfected ones (siddhas) as "Khecarī" (the Sky-farer). || 41 ||
He by whom the aperture above the uvula is sealed by the Khecarī [mudrā], his bindu does not leak even when embraced by a passionate woman. 42.
|| Commentary ||

"Regarding 'no disease': for one who knows the khecarī mudrā, there is no disease, no death, no *tandrā*— which is a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) characterized by *tamas*— no sleep, no hunger, no thirst (*pipāsā*), and no fainting of the mind."
And there would not be a particular state characterized by being overwhelmed by *tamas*. || 39 ||
Regarding the phrase "is afflicted": he who knows the khecarī mudrā is not joined with disease, such as fever and the like. || 40 ||

Regarding the term *citta*: because the mind (*citta*), which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), moves in the sky (*khe*)—that is, in the space between the eyebrows—and the tongue, having gone to that very same sky, moves there;
for that reason, this is called the *mudrā* named *Khecarī*, renowned as *Khecarī*.

The word *nāma* is an indeclinable used in the sense of "well-known. She is described by the perfected ones (*siddhas*) such as Kapila and others. She is etymologically derived from her parts as *khecarī*—she in whom the mind and the tongue move or travel in the *kha*, that is, in the space between the eyebrows within the void. This has been stated in the three preceding verses.
Furthermore, the repetition of [the mention of] diseases and so forth is not a fault, because those verses have been summarized. || 41 ||
Regarding the term *khecaryā*: by which yogin, through the *mudrā* called *khecarī*, [the breath is directed] "above the *laṃbikā*," that is, from above the *laṃbikā*.
p. 91) || Root Text ||
Even when the bindu has moved and reached the circle of the yoni, it goes upward, drawn by Śakti and bound by the Yonimudrā. || 43 ||
The knower of yoga who, having become steady, performs the drinking of soma with the tongue turned upward, undoubtedly conquers death within half a month. || 44 ||
That yogi whose body is eternally filled with the digits of the moon.
|| Commentary ||

The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). The uvula (*laṃbikā*) is the palate; the aperture or cavity situated above it, in its upper portion, is sealed or closed. Even though [the practitioner] is embraced or embraced by a passionate young woman—the word "ca" (and) having the sense of "even" (*api*)—of that [aperture].
The bindu does not leak; it does not falter. || 42 ||
Regarding the word "calita": when the *bindu*, even though moved or slipped, reaches— that is, arrives at— the *yonimaṇḍala*, which is the location of the *yoni*, at that very moment,
by means of the *yonimudrā* consisting of the contraction of the genitals (*meḍhra-ākuñcana*), this indicates the *vajrolīmudrā*.
Firmly bound and drawn upward by the power of attraction, it ascends excellently; through the path of the Suṣumṇā, it goes to the station of the Bindu. || 43 ||
Regarding the term "ūrdhvajihva": he whose tongue is turned upward, hanging down, and directed toward the upper cavity is "ūrdhvajihva.

Having become steady and motionless, he performs the drinking of *soma*—that is, the drinking of the lunar nectar (*caṃdrāmṛta*) flowing from the upper cavity of the hanging tongue. He who [does this] is the one described.

A person who knows yoga—that is, one who understands yoga—conquers and overcomes death, which is to say mortality, within half a month, that is, within a fortnight; of this there is no doubt, meaning this is certain. || 44 ||
"Perpetually": for that yogin whose body is perpetually—every day—filled with the digits of the moon, that is, filled with the nectar of the lunar digits.
Root Text
Even when bitten by Takṣaka, the poison does not spread through him.
Just as fire does not leave its fuel, nor a lamp its oil and wick,
so too the embodied soul does not abandon the body filled with the digits of the moon.
I consider him to be of noble birth who constantly eats beef and drinks the nectar of the celestial vine;
others are destroyers of their lineage.
|| Commentary ||
Even when that yogi has been bitten or stung by Takṣaka, a particular species of serpent,
the poison— the venom— and the suffering produced by it do not spread or circulate through his body;
just as a lamp does not consume its fuel, such as wood and the like.
Just as one does not abandon a wick filled with oil, so too the embodied soul (dehī),
which is the living being (jīva), does not abandon or leave behind the body (deha), which is filled with the digits of the moon— that is, filled with the nectar of the lunar digits. || 46 ||
"Omnivorous flesh" (*gomāṃsa*) refers to that which is about to be described as the technical term for "beef.
He who would constantly— every single day— consume this and drink the "divine wine" (*amaravāruṇī*), also to be described,
that yogi I [the author] call "noble-born" (*kulīna*), meaning one born into the [spiritual] lineage.
I consider him to be born of a noble family; as it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"By him his parents have achieved their purpose, blessed is that land and that lineage, wherein one who possesses yoga is born, and wherein what is given becomes inexhaustible."
One who possesses discernment between the male organ and its nature purifies the sins of men that would otherwise lead to hundreds of millions of births, merely by being seen, spoken to, or touched.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "A practitioner of yoga excels over a thousand householders, a hundred forest-dwellers, and a thousand celibate students."
The words of Śiva to Vāmadeva regarding Rājayoga:
"Who truly understands the greatness of Rājayoga? That place where a knower of it dwells is a vessel of merit."
By seeing and worshipping this [liṅga], even the ignorant, together with twenty-one generations of their lineage, attain the state of liberation; how much more so those who are devoted to it?
He who understands specifically the internal yoga and the external yoga—
[this is the root].
The tongue is denoted by the word "go" (cow), for its entry into the palate is indeed the eating of "gomāṃsa" (cow-flesh);
that [act] destroys even the most heinous sins. 48.
Indeed, that essence which flows from the moon, produced by the fire generated through the entry of the tongue, is the nectar of the immortals (amaravāruṇī). || 49 ||
If the tongue, dripping with saliva and salty, constantly kisses the tip of the uvula; [this is the practice].
Commentary:
"This bondage must be understood by you, by me, and by the rest; how much more so by others!
Thus it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Those who practice [this yoga] once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or even constantly..."
They should be known as Mahāyogas, the Great Lords.

Others— those who abstain from eating beef and drinking *amaravāruṇī* as will be described, yet are not practitioners of yoga— are destroyers of their lineage and ruiners of their family, because the birth of one born into a noble family has become utterly futile. || 47 ||

He states the meaning of the word *gomāṃsa* (cow-flesh): "By the word *go*" means by the word in the form of "go," that is, by the term *go*. "The tongue" is said to arise from the palate (*rasanā*). The locative case in *tāluni* is used in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpikādhāra*); it refers to the opening above near the palate for that tongue.
"Entry" refers to the consumption of cow-flesh— the term "consumption of cow-flesh" being used figuratively—
and such consumption of cow-flesh is the destroyer of great sins (mahāpātakas), such as the theft of gold and others. || 48 ||

He explains the meaning of the term *amaravāruṇī*: "The tongue... and so forth. The entry of the tongue is its insertion into the upper opening of the *laṃbikā* (the uvula); the fire (*vahni*) produced from that—that is, the heat (*uṣman*) generated by it—is what brings [the nectar] forth and produces it. Here, by the word "fire," heat is indicated.
That essence which flows and trickles from the moon situated on the left side between the eyebrows—that shall be the *amaravāruṇī*, the one denoted by the term *amaravāruṇī*. || 49 ||
"Kissing": if [the tongue] kisses—that is, touches—the tip of the *laṃbikā*, which is the opening above the *laṃbikā*, constantly and without interruption.
Root Text
Resembling bitter, sour, and milk-like [tastes], and likewise similar to honey and clarified butter;

it is the remover of diseases, the ender of old age, the provoker of the onset of weapons, and for him there shall be eightfold immortality, including the power to attract the wives of the Siddhas. || 50 ||

With the face turned upward, having forcefully restrained the tongue within the cavity and contemplating the supreme Śakti, he who drinks the pure, wave-like water in the form of a stream that has fallen from the sixteen-petaled lotus at the crown and is obtained through the vital breath (prāṇa), becomes free from disease.
That yogi, whose body is as tender as a lotus stalk, lives for a long time. || 51 ||
Commentary:

Therefore, *rasaspandinī* refers to one whose tongue possesses the vibration, movement, or flow of *rasa*, which is the nectar of the lunar digit (*somakalāmṛta*). *Sakṣārā* means accompanied by salt (*kṣāra*), that is, the salty taste; *kaṭukaṃ* refers to black pepper and the like; *amlaṃ* refers to the sour.

The milk [is] similar to, that is, equal to, the *ciñcā* fruit and so forth; honey (*madhu*) is the nectar of bees, and clarified butter (*ājya*) is ghee; it is equal to those two. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) is used in a conjunctive sense. By these qualifiers—

Because rasa possesses manifold flavors, and because it is sweet and unctuous, the tongue likewise is described as being characterized by the vibration of rasa. Therefore, its removal of diseases— that is, the disappearance of ailments— and its bringing about of the end of old age— that is, its destruction— is established.

The arrival (*āgama*) of weapons—that is, the coming of arms from the presence of their owners—and the provocation (*udīraṇa*) or warding off thereof; the eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā* which have arisen in him, thus constituting the eightfold immortality (*amaratva*), the state of being immortal; and the women of the Siddhas.
The Siddhas are perfected beings, and they are also women; thus, "siddhāṅganāḥ" refers to them.
Their power of attraction (ārṣaṇam) would be the capacity for drawing [others] toward themselves. || 50 ||

Regarding the word "mūrdhni" (on the crown): having restrained—that is, joined—the tongue (*rasanā*) within the cavity of the skull (*kapālakuhara*), he is one whose mouth is turned upward (*ūrdhvam-uttānam*).
Root Text

The wise declare that the essence within the hollow space of the moon situated upon the summit of Mount Meru is the source of all rivers; from the moon, a vital fluid flows from its body, and by that, death comes to men. Therefore, one should secure it through an auspicious rite, for otherwise it cannot be done.
The accomplishment of the body. || 52 ||
Commentary:

By the phrase "with face turned upward," the *viparītakaraṇī* (the inverted posture) is indicated. While contemplating—that is, meditating upon—the supreme power *Kuṇḍalinī*, one [should restrain] the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) which serve as the means of accomplishment.
That which has sixteen petals or leaves is the "sixteen-petaled"; and that is the lotus (*padma*).
That stainless, pure water of the lunar digit— situated in the region of the throat, forcefully released there, obtained through Haṭhayoga,
consisting of a continuous stream, surging with great waves and high crests— is the essence of the moon's digit.

That man who drinks and drinks [it] is a yogi; being free from diseases such as fever and the like, he is "nirvyādhi"; or rather, being one from whom various mental afflictions (*ādhi*) have departed, he possesses a body as delicate and soft as a lotus fiber (*mṛṇāla*).

He whose body possesses a form as tender as a lotus stalk lives for a long time—that is, he sustains his life-force—through *haṭha*, meaning through *haṭhayoga*; or alternatively, the construction may be understood as "attained from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which serves as the means. Thus, [the phrase] "by means of the vital breaths" (*prāṇaiḥ*).
In some places, there is a different reading. || 51 ||
Regarding the phrase *yatprāleya* and so forth: like the desert (*maru*), Suṣumnā is elevated above all; Meru is its summit or upper portion.

That which stands within its interior—that is, in the middle—is "situated within the summit of Meru" (*merumūrdhāntarastham*). This refers to the "snow" (*prāleyam*), the water of the digits of the moon (*somakalā*) that has been sent forth.

That in which [the Self] is deposited is "tathā"; that which is such is a hollow or cavity (*suṣira*). In that cavity, the wise one—whose intellect (*dhī*) or consciousness (*buddhi*) is excellent (*sudhī*), meaning it is not overcome by *rajas* and *tamas*—proclaims (*pravadati*), that is, speaks with excellence, the Reality (*tatva*), namely the reality of the Self (*ātmatatva*). Of that...

According to the Śruti, "The Supreme Self is situated in the center of the crest-lock (śikhā). Since the Self is all-pervasive, its manifestation occurs there during the khecarīmudrā; thus it is said that the Reality (tatva) resides therein.
Root Text
The hollow space that generates knowledge and is endowed with five channels—therein, in that void which is stainless, the Khecarī Mudrā abides. || 53 ||
There is one seed-syllable consisting of creation, and one mudrā, which is khecarī;
there is one god who is without support, and one state, which is manonmanī.
Commentary:
Of the rivers—
namely those denoted by the words Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, and so forth, which are [the channels] such as iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā, and gāndhārī— in that particular cavity or in its vicinity.

The mouth is the foremost part; from the moon, which is the essence (*sāra*) of the body, [nectar] flows and trickles, and by that flow of the moon’s essence, death occurs for men, that is, for human beings. Therefore, for this reason, that aforementioned auspicious rite (*sukaraṇa*) [should be performed].

One should bind the excellent instrument known as the khecarīmudrā. The sense is that when this excellent instrument is bound, death will not occur due to the absence of the flow of the essence of the moon (semen). Otherwise, in the absence of binding this excellent instrument, there can be no perfection of the body (kāya).
She would not possess a form endowed with beauty, charm, strength, and a vajra-like constitution. || 52 ||

Regarding the term *suṣira*: it is that which is endowed with, or properly followed by, the five channels (*srotas*) which are the flows of *iḍā* and the others. Although there is a reading in some places as "endowed with seven channels," [the meaning remains the same].
It is the cavity (*suṣira*) that produces knowledge—that is, that which generates the extraordinary awakening consisting of the direct realization of the Self.

In that cavity, which is free from *añjana*— meaning ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects such as grief and delusion (*moha*) have departed from it— that is the stainless (*nirañjana*). Within that stainless void,
within the space of the hollow, the Khecarī Mudrā abides and becomes firm.
And the ātmanepada [suffix] is used in the sense of "making public" and "being an arbitrator. (53)
"One" means: the one primary seed-syllable called *praṇava*, which consists of emanation and has the form of emanation.

As it is stated in the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad*: "The syllable *om*—this entire [universe] is this. The *khecarī mudrā* is the one primary [mudrā], which is supportless, being devoid of any objective support (*ālambana*).
The one is the principal deity, because by abandoning all supports, one abides in one's own true nature.
The state of *unmanī* alone is the principal; according to Amara, "the word *eka* means 'principal' or 'exclusive'.
The meaning is that among the mudrās, such as *khecarī*, [this] is the principal, just as the *praṇava* is among the seed-syllables (*bīja*). || 54 ||
p. 97) || Root Text ||
Now, the uḍḍīyānabandha.
By means of this [bandha], the vital breath bound within the Suṣumnā is made to soar upward.
Therefore, this is proclaimed by yogis as "the flight" (uḍḍīyāna). || 55 ||
Because that great bird flies without rest, it is called Uḍḍīyāna; the binding [of the breath] therein is designated as the Uḍḍīyāna Bandha. || 56 ||
One should perform the final contraction in the abdomen above the navel;
this is indeed the Uḍḍīyāna Bandha, the lion to the elephant of death. || 57 ||
Commentary:
Desiring now to explain the *uḍḍīyānabandha*, he first states the meaning of the word *uḍḍīyāna*.
Regarding the term "bound": because the vital breath (*prāṇa*), bound— that is, restrained— by this particular bond, rises up within the *suṣumnā*, the central channel,
and flies through the sky [of the *suṣumnā*], for that reason this is called a "bond" (*bandha*).
That which is called Uḍḍīyana is correctly explained and described by yogis such as Matsyendra and others;
it is so named because the vital breath (prāṇa), when bound by means of this [bandha], flies upward (uḍḍīyate) within the Suṣumnā.
The word [ākāśa] is derived from the root *ḍīṅ* (to fly) preceded by the prefix *ut*, in the sense of "motion through the air," with the suffix *lyuṭ* denoting the instrument (*karaṇe*). || 55 ||

Regarding the term *uḍḍīnam*: the "great bird" (*mahākhaga*) is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), because it is always in motion within the space of the body. From whatever bond it may be, it performs the flight of a bird (*vihaṅgamagati*) so as to remain unceasingly soaring upward.
