The word "in the Suṣumnā" is to be supplied [as the context]. That very specific type of lock (bandha) shall be called Uḍḍīyāna, named after Uḍḍīyāna. Regarding that subject, the lock is being described; its essential nature is being stated by me.
The remainder. || 56 ||

He explains the Uḍḍiyāna-bandha: "In the abdomen," etc. In the abdomen—that is, in the belly—above the navel and, by the word "and" (ca), also below it; in both the upper and lower portions, there is a posterior stretch, meaning a backward contraction, such that the upper and lower parts of the navel [are drawn together].

The two [shoulders] should be attached to the back; likewise, one should cause the stretching known as *tānana* to be performed—that is, one should perform it. The causative sense (*ṇij-artha*) is not intended here. This *uḍḍīyāna*, called by the name *uḍḍīyāna*, consists of the stretching of the upper and lower portions above the navel.
Bondage! Of what nature? He is like a lion that turns back the elephant—the elephant being death itself—just as a lion repels a wild elephant. || 57 ||
p. 98) || Root Text ||
Uḍḍiyāna is indeed the innate [state], as always taught by the Guru; he who practices it constantly becomes youthful even if he is old. (58)
One should diligently perform the expansion of the body both above and below the navel.
If one practices for six months, one certainly conquers death; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, among all the bandhas, Uḍḍiyānaka is the supreme;
when the Uḍḍiyāna bandha is firmly established, liberation becomes natural. || 60 ||
|| Commentary ||

Regarding "Uḍḍīyāna, however": the Guru is the one who gives beneficial instruction; by that Guru, Uḍḍīyāna is said to be always—that is, at all times—the innate (*sahaja*) or natural (*svābhāvika*) outward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This is because it occurs for everyone at all times. As for whoever...

A person, however, should practice this constantly and without interruption; here too, the term "Uḍḍīyāna" is to be understood as connected. Indeed, even if he is old or aged, he acts like a youth—he behaves as a youth does. || 58 ||

Regarding the phrase "from the navel": above the navel, in the upper part, and also below, in the lower part, one should perform *tāna*— that is, *paścimatāna* (backward extension)— with *prayatna*, meaning with a supreme effort (*prakṛṣṭa-yatna*),
that is, through a specific exertion.
The nature of Uḍḍīyāna has been described in the first half [of the verse]. Now follows its praise:

"For six months"—meaning for a period of six months; the word "Uḍḍīyāna" is to be supplied [to the sentence]. "One should practice"—that is, one should perform it repeatedly—he certainly conquers death; there is no doubt about this. In this regard:
The meaning is that there is no doubt. || 59 ||
"Of all"— that is, among all the bindings (*bandhas*), the *uḍḍiyānaka*,

which is the *uḍḍiyāna-bandha* itself (the suffix *ka* being used in the sense of the base word), is the best, meaning the most excellent; for when the *uḍḍiyāna-bandha* is firm, [the state] is natural.

Liberation would indeed be established by its very nature; for when the Uḍḍiyāna-bandha is performed, the vital breath (prāṇa) proceeds to the crown of the head through the Suṣumnā via the flight of a bird. According to the scriptural statement, "One attains liberation in Samādhi," the implication is that liberation is innate (sahaja). || 60 ||
p. 99) || Root Text ||
Now, the root-lock (mūlabandha).
Pressing with the heel, one should contract the anus and the vaginal passage.
Drawing the downward breath upward is called the root-lock (mūlabandha). || 61 ||
By means of contraction, one forcibly causes the downward-moving apāna to go upward;
yogins indeed call this the mūlabandha.
Pressing the anus with the heel, one should forcefully contract the wind (vāyu).
Commentary:

He describes the root-lock (mūlabandha): "With the part of the heel," etc. The "part of the heel" is the region below the two ankles; with that, having firmly pressed—that is, thoroughly compressed—the "yoni," which is the site of the yoni, the middle portion between the anus and the genitals, [one should press] the anus.
One should contract, that is, draw in, the anus;
having drawn upward—that is, pulled up—the downward-moving *apāna* wind, it is called and described as the *mūlabandha*. [This is done] by means of the heel.
The meaning is that the contraction of the anus, preceded by the compression of the region of the womb, is called *mūlabandha*. || 61 ||
"Going downwards" (adhogatim): he whose movement is downward or toward the lower regions is "downward-moving"; that downward-moving [wind] is the *apāna* wind.
By means of contraction—that is, by the contraction of the *mūlādhāra*—it goes upward with force or by constraint; thus it is "upward-moving," and [the text refers to] that upward-moving [wind].

It causes [the breath] to move upward through the *suṣumnā*. The indeclinable *vai* is used here for emphasis. Yogins—those who practice yoga—call that "root-lock" (*mūlabandha*), because it is the binding (*bandhana*) of the root (*mūla*), which is the root location; thus they call it "root-lock" according to its etymological meaning.
By this, the meaning of the term *mūlabandha* has been stated; however, by the preceding verse, the manner of its binding was described, so there is no redundancy. || 62 ||
Now, according to the method described in the *Yogabīja*, he explains the root-lock (*mūlabandha*): "The anus," and so forth.

Having firmly pressed—that is, having properly compressed and joined—the anus with the lower part of the heels and the ankles; the word *tu* (but/however) [indicates] its distinction from the previous [method].
Root Text
And just as the vital air repeatedly rises upward again and again. || 63 ||
The prāṇa and apāna, as well as nāda and bindu, attain oneness through the mūlabandha; they bestow the perfect accomplishment of yoga—of this there is no doubt.
The unification of the downward and upward breaths, and the cessation of urine and feces.
Commentary:
It indicates a specific distinction. Just as, in whatever manner the wind (samīraṇa) moves upward in the upper portion of the Suṣumnā, in that same manner, by force or by effort, again and again—

One should repeatedly contract the downward-moving breath (apāna) by means of the contraction of the anus; one should draw it upward. "This is the mūlabandha"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied to the sentence. || 63 ||
Next, he describes the qualities of the *mūlabandha*: "The *prāṇa* and *apāna*," and so forth.
Prāṇa and apāna are the upward- and downward-moving breaths;

nāda is the unstruck sound (anāhata-dhvani), and bindu is the anusvāra. When these two, having attained oneness through mūlabandha, become unified, there is the complete perfection (saṃsiddhi) of yoga—that is, its perfect accomplishment.
"To one who bestows—that is, grants—the perfection of yoga; the word 'practitioner' is to be supplied as the subject.
In this matter, there is no doubt; the meaning is that there is no uncertainty. This is the intended sense:
when the *mūlabandha* is performed, the *apāna* becomes unified with the *prāṇa*."

It enters into the *suṣumnā*. Thereupon, the manifestation of the *nāda* occurs. Then, together with the *nāda*, the *prāṇa* and *apāna* go above the heart; having established the unity of the *nāda* with the *bindu*, they proceed to the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*). From that, the perfection of yoga (*yogasiddhi*) arises. || 64 ||
Regarding "of the apāna and prāṇa": through constant *mūlabandha*—that is, by performing the *mūlabandha-mudrā*—there occurs the unification of the apāna and prāṇa. (p.
Root Text
Even an old man becomes young through the constant practice of *mūlabandha*.
When the apāna wind moves upward and enters the sphere of fire,
then a long flame of fire arises, struck by the wind.
Then, having gone from there, he [reached] fire and the downward-breath (apāna), and the upward-breath (prāṇa) whose nature is heat.
By that, the fire born of his body became exceedingly blazing.
|| Commentary ||
It occurs: there is the depletion and falling away of accumulated urine and feces;
even one who is old or aged becomes young and youthful. || 65 ||

Regarding "apāna": through the *mūlabandha*, when the *apāna*—the wind whose nature is to move downward—becomes upward-moving (*ūrdhvaga*), that is, moving upwards; at that time, in the fire-mandala—the triangular mandala of fire located in the region below the navel—it is said: [The source text continues: "It is said..."
Yājñavalkya said: Within the body, O humans, is the seat of the flame (śikhī), possessing the luster of molten gold;

it is triangular for humans, quadrangular for four-footed creatures, and circular for winged insects—I tell you this as the truth. In its center, however, is the subtle crest (śikhā) that is ever-present.

"It remains in the fire. At that time, struck by the downward-moving wind (apāna) and joined with it, the flame of the true fire—the flame of the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni)—becomes long and extended.
In some recensions, the reading is "it increases" (vardhate). || 66 ||

"Then": after that, *vahnyapānau* refers to fire (*vahni*) and downward breath (*apāna*). He went to that fire, whose nature is heat, and to the upward-moving wind (*anila*), which is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), characterized by the length of its flame. It is of a hot nature due to the elongation of its crest. He went to that [fire].

"Of those going"—the construction may be understood as "from the length of the flame of fire," or "from that which has heat as its nature. By that union with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the fire born in the body—*dehaja*—becomes exceedingly and intensely ignited. The word *tathā* is used for the purpose of completing the meter.
The meaning is that when the apāna moves upward, the fire, already ignited, becomes intensely inflamed through its union with the prāṇa. || 67 ||
p. 102) || Root Text ||
By that [heat], the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī is thoroughly awakened;
like a female serpent struck by a staff, she hisses and attains straightness. || 68 ||
Then, as if entering a cave, one should proceed into the interior of the Brahma-nāḍī. Therefore, the root-lock (mūlabandha) must always be performed by yogis at all times. || 69 ||
Contracting the throat, one should firmly place the chin against the heart;
this is the lock known as Jālandhara, which destroys old age and death. || 70 ||
Commentary:

"By that" means: by that extreme blazing of the fire, being thoroughly heated—that is, perfectly incandescent—the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī power becomes fully awakened; she is completely enlightened. And she is "struck by the staff," meaning struck with a staff.
Like a female serpent or a hissing snake, having sighed—that is, having exhaled—she would attain or go toward uprightness and straightforwardness. || 68 ||

"Having entered the cavity": thereafter, immediately following the attainment of straightness, one should go into the interior—the middle—of that *brahmanāḍī*, the *suṣumnā*, which is like a female serpent (*bhujaṅgī*) that has entered a hole or cavity (*bila*); for that reason, the *mūlabandha* [should be performed] by yogis who practice yoga.
It should be performed constantly, every day, always, at all times; it is fit to be done.

He describes the Jālandhara-bandha: "The throat," etc. Having contracted the cavity at the throat (gale), one should firmly and steadily place the chin—the jaw—at the region four finger-breadths away from the heart, near the chest. This...

It is called Jālandhara because it consists of placing the chin near the heart, at a distance of four finger-breadths, by first contracting the throat and exerting effort to bend the head downward; thus it is known as Jālandhara.

The bond named Jālandhara: of what nature is it? It is the destroyer of old age—meaning the state of decrepitude—and death—meaning dying; it is a "destroyer" (vināśaka), one who specifically brings about their destruction. || 70 ||
p. 103) || Root Text ||
For it binds the network of vessels through which the water from the sky flows downward; therefore, Jālandhara-bandha is the destroyer of the multitude of sufferings in the throat. (71)
When the Jālandhara band, characterized by the constriction of the throat, is performed, the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the vital wind become agitated. || 72 ||
By means of constricting the throat alone, one should firmly arrest the two channels.
Commentary:

He explains the meaning of the term *jālandhara*: "It binds," because it binds (*badhnāti*) the net—that is, the collection—of the channels (*śirā*). It is called *adhogāmī* (downward-moving) because its nature is to go downwards; and it [holds] the water and the nectar (*amṛta*) of the sky, which is the hollow of the cranial vault.

It binds and obstructs. Therefore, from that [reason], *jālandhara*—the one named Jālandhara—is a bond whose name is significant (*anvartha*). It is called *jālandhara* because it "holds" (*dharati*) the "net" (*jālam*); here, "net" refers to a snare (*daśājālam*), or a collection of waters (*jalānāṃ samūhaḥ*). Of what kind is it? [It is located] in the throat.
He is the destroyer, the one who brings about the destruction, of that flood of suffering—the mass of misery born of transformation—that exists in the region of the throat. || 71 ||

He states the qualities of Jālandhara: "Jālandhara" means that which has the contraction of the throat—that is, the constriction or narrowing of the cavity of the gullet—as its defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) or essential nature (svarūpa); in such a [bandha] is Jālandhara.

When the bond known as Jālandhara-bandha is performed, the nectar (pīyūṣa), which is the immortal essence, does not fall—that is, it does not flow—into the fire of the stomach (jāṭhara-anala). Furthermore, the vital breath (prāṇa) does not become agitated;
the meaning is that it does not cause the movement or agitation of the wind within the channels (nāḍī). || 72 ||

"By the contraction of the throat": by means of a firm, tight contraction of the throat—by the mere contraction of the throat—one should paralyze the two channels, Iḍā and Piṅgalā; "this is Jālandhara"—thus one must supply the subject. This [occurs] at the location of the throat.
[It is] established.
(p. 104) || Root Text ||
This middle wheel is to be known as the binding of the sixteen supports.
Having firmly contracted the root-seat (mūlasthāna), one should perform the uḍḍiyāna lock; having bound the iḍā and piṅgalā, one should cause [the breath] to flow along the western path.
By this very method, the vital breath (pavana) goes to dissolution; consequently, neither birth nor death, nor old age, disease, and the like, arise. || 75 ||
Commentary:
The wheel known as Viśuddha is to be understood as the central wheel, the middle wheel.

Of what nature is it? It is the "binding of the sixteen supports" (ṣoḍaśādhārabaṃdhana), meaning the binding of those supports numbering sixteen, beginning with the support of the big toe and ending with the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

The binder: the thumb, the ankle, the knee, the thigh, the suture, the genitals, the navel, the heart, the neck, the region of the throat, the uvula, the nose, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, the head, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmaraṃdhra). These indeed...
Sixteen supports (ādhāras) have been described by the best of yogis;
the specific fruits of concentration (dhāraṇā) upon those supports, however, are to be understood from the Gorakṣasiddhānta.
He states the application of the three aforementioned bonds: "The root station," and so forth.

Having properly contracted—that is, thoroughly drawn up—the root station (*mūlasthāna*), which is the foundational support and the locus of the base, one should perform the *uḍḍiyāna* lock, which consists of a backward contraction. The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not intended here. [One should likewise contract] the *iḍā*, the *piṅgalā*, and the *gaṅgā*.
"And having bound the Yamunā"—the meaning is by means of the Jālandhara-bandha;

for it is said that by the mere constriction of the throat, one should paralyze the two channels (nāḍīs). One should cause the prāṇa to flow—that is, to go—along the western path, which is the course of the Suṣumṇā; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 74 ||

"By this": by this very method thus described, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the wind, attains dissolution, that is, stability. Dissolution (*laya*) of the breath is its abiding within the [central] aperture preceded by the cessation of movement. From that dissolution of the breath, death, old age, disease, and so forth [are eliminated].
p. 105) || Root Text ||
This triad of bonds is excellent and practiced by the great Siddhas; yogis know it to be the means of accomplishment for all Haṭha-tantras. (76)
Whatever nectar flows from the moon, which possesses a divine form, the sun swallows it all; by that means, the physical body becomes subject to old age.
|| Commentary ||
And likewise in the sense [of the verse]: "it is not born, it does not arise. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), wrinkles, gray hair, drowsiness, laziness, and so forth are to be understood. || 75 ||
Regarding "the threefold binding": this aforementioned threefold binding is excellent;

it is highly praised in the sixteen-fold binding of the foundations (*ādhāra-bandha*), and was practiced by the great adepts (*mahāsiddhas*) such as Matsyendra and others, and—by the word "and"—by sages such as Vasiṣṭha.
The yogis, beginning with Gorakṣa, know—that is, they understand—the practice of all Haṭha-tantras and Haṭha-methods which produces spiritual accomplishment (siddhi). || 76 ||

Desiring to explain that which effects transformation, he first describes the aging of the physical body as an introductory premise, saying: "Whatever... [and so on]. He who possesses a divine, excellent, and nectar-like form is described as such.

Therefore, whatever nectar— whatever *amṛta* or *pīyūṣa*— flows or falls from that divine-formed Moon (*soma*) situated at the root of the palate, all of that nectar is swallowed— that is, made into a morsel— by the Sun, who resides in the navel and consists of fire. As it has been said:
By Gorakṣanātha: "The sun, whose nature is fire, resides eternally in the region of the navel;
and the moon, whose nature is nectar, resides eternally at the root of the palate.
The downward-facing moon rains [nectar], and the upward-facing sun devours it. And that is the *karaṇa*."
"By that which [is performed], nectar is obtained.
By that swallowing of nectar performed by the Sun, the *piṇḍa*—the body—becomes possessed of old age; it becomes joined with decay. || 77 ||
p. 106) || Root Text ||
In that regard, there exists a divine method for deceiving the face of the Sun; it is to be known through the instruction of a guru, and not by means of millions of scriptural doctrines. (78)
Above the navel and below the palate, the sun is above and the moon is below;
this practice called "the reversal" is obtained through the word of the Guru. (79)
For the practitioner who is constantly engaged in practice, abundant food that increases the digestive fire should be provided. 80.
Commentary:

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): in that context, with respect to that subject, there exists a divine and supreme instrument called *mudrā*, which will be described hereafter and by which the mouth of the Sun situated at the navel is deceived; that [instrument] is to be known through the instruction of the Guru (*gurūpadeśataḥ*).
It is possible to know [it] through millions of scriptural meanings, yet it is not at all impossible to know. || 78 ||
He speaks of that which effects the reversal: "Above the navel.
One whose navel is above—that is, in the upper part—is "above-naveled" (*ūrdhvanābhi*). Below that above-naveled one, in the lower part, is the palate;
one for whom the palate is below is "below-palated" (*adhastālu*). [This refers to] the yogin who is below-palated.

Above, in the upper part, the sun, whose nature is burning, becomes the *bhānu*; below, in the lower part, the moon, whose nature is nectar, becomes the *śaśya*. However, according to the first reading of the end of the verse, when the yogi has his navel above and his palate below, then the sun is above and [the moon] below.

It becomes the moon (*śaśī*). The connection [of the words] occurs through the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of "when" and "then. This is the *karaṇī* called "inverted" (*viparītā*), so named because it is meaningful (*anvarthā*) due to the downward and upward positioning of the moon and sun, which are originally situated above and below.
It is obtained and attained solely by the word of the guru, by the guru’s very speech, and not otherwise. || 79 ||
"Constantly" means daily; "practice" refers to the act of training. For one who is "engaged," that is, attentive, in that [practice], the "gastric fire" is the digestive fire within the abdomen.
Root Text
If the digestive fire should become weak due to insufficient food, it will burn [the body] at that very moment.
On the first day, he should remain for a moment with his head downward and his feet upward.

One should practice for even slightly more than a moment day after day; after six months, wrinkles and grey hair will no longer be seen. He who practices this constantly for just one watch (yāma) is a conqueror of time. 82.
Commentary:
"Vivardhinī" means specifically "increasing"; it is an epithet for *viparītakaraṇī*.

For that practitioner who practices *viparītakaraṇī*, food—that is, eating—should be provided in abundance according to his desire; it must be made available. The particle *ca* is used for metrical filling. || 80 ||

Regarding the phrase "one who eats little": if one were such that their food—the consumption of desired food—is meager, then the fire, the digestive heat (*jatharānala*), would burn the body in a mere moment; that is to say, it would burn it quickly.
He now describes the action of making the moon and sun, which are situated above and below, [respectively] below and above.

"Head-downward" (adhaḥśirā) means one whose head is downward, that is, on the ground; having supported the region of the hips with both hands, [he remains] with his two arms extending from the armpits to the elbows.

Pressing the ground with both shoulders and the back parts of the neck and head, one should have the head downwards; he whose feet are upwards in the space above is "ūrdhvapādaḥ" (feet-up), for a moment on the first day, the day of commencement.
It would exist for only a single moment. || 8 ||

Day by day, every single day, he should practice— that is, perform the exercise— increasing it by one day at a time, from slightly more than a moment (kṣaṇa) up to two moments, three moments, and so on.
He states the qualities that cause reversal: "wrinkled," etc. "Wrinkled" means the contraction of the skin;
"gray-haired" means whiteness in the hair. "Six months" is a collective term for six months; beyond that—that is, after it—[the reversal] certainly does not occur.
p. 108) || Root Text ||
Now, Vajrolī.
Even if he conducts himself according to his own will, without the restraints prescribed for yoga, he who understands Vajrolī is a yogi who becomes a vessel for spiritual perfection.
In this regard, I shall describe two things that are difficult for anyone to obtain: first, milk; and second, a woman who is submissive. (84)
|| Commentary ||
"It is not seen" means it is not perceived; the phrase "the body of the practitioner" is to be supplied to complete the sentence.
But that practitioner who practices constantly for even a single watch (yāma) or a single hour (prahara) becomes a conqueror of time;
he conquers time, that is, death, and thus becomes a conqueror of death. By this, it is also indicated that yoga acts as an obstacle to the fruition of *prārabdha* karma. As it has been said:

In the *Viṣṇudharma*: "O protector of the earth, listen also to the characteristics of that yoga which brings about the complete destruction even of the karma that initiated one's own body. Thus it was also stated by Vidyāraṇya in his *Jīvanmukti* [treatise]: as follows—

The practice of yoga is more powerful than even that karma which is stronger than the knowledge of the truth regarding *prārabdha* karma; for this very reason, the voluntary casting off of the body by yogis such as Uddālaka, Vītahavya, and others, is logically established. This is also stated in the *Bhāgavata*: "The body..."
One should abandon [it] through meditative absorption. || 82 ||
In order to generate engagement in the *vajrolī* practice, he first states its fruit: "By one's own will," and so forth.
The yogi who practices *vajrolī*— who specifically knows the *vajrolī-mudrā* through his own direct experience— that yogi,
by his own will and without the observances prescribed in Yoga, such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the other rules mentioned in the Yoga scriptures, [attains success].

Even while acting according to his own will and engaging in worldly affairs, he becomes a vessel—a worthy recipient—of the supernatural powers (siddhis), such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. || 83 ||

He states the two things useful for its accomplishment: "In that regard" (*tatra*). In that context, regarding the semblance of *vajrolī*, there are two things; these two things constitute the "pair of things" (*vastudvaya*).
Root Text
With effort, one should gradually and correctly practice the upward contraction; thus, whether a man or a woman, one shall attain the perfection of Vajroli.
One should slowly and with effort produce a whistling sound through a well-blown tube into the vajra-cave, for the purpose of setting the vital winds (vāyu) in motion. 86.
Commentary:

I shall speak; I shall tell. Of what kind are these two things? They are for anyone whatsoever—be they poor or not—difficult to obtain, meaning they can be acquired with great hardship, or even impossible to acquire despite such hardship. [The word *duḥ* is used in the senses of "suffering" (*kaṣṭa*) and "prohibition" (*niṣedha*).]
From the Treasury [of Abhidharma]. In response to the inquiry, "What are those two things?", he says: "Milk."
There is one thing: milk.
After urination, because of the weakness of the senses, it is appropriate to drink milk for the sake of strengthening them.
Some, however, say that it is for the purpose of drawing [the vital energy] upward during the time of practice. Of that which has entered therein—

In the case of solidification, emergence is impossible; therefore, that [first option] is untenable. As for the second, it refers to a woman—a wife—who is submissive and under one's own control. || 84 ||

He describes the method of the Vajrolīmudrā: "By means of the penis" (mehanena). By means of the penis—that is, by the emission of the bindu following sexual union with a woman, which serves as the means of practice—a man (pumān) or even a woman (yoṣit), slowly and gently, [should perform it] correctly.
One should practice the upward contraction with effort—
the drawing upward of the *bindu* by contracting the penis— to attain the perfection of the Vajroli-mudrā.
One should go. || 85 ||

Now he describes the preliminary procedure for Vajrolī: "With effort," etc. "With a praised tube" means with a highly recommended tube made of lead or other materials; "gradually" means slowly, so that a puffing sound is produced for the purpose of blowing upon the fire.

One should perform such a hissing sound in the *vajrakandara* (the urethral opening), where the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*) occurs correctly within the *vajrakandara*; for that reason and by that cause, one should practice it intensely and repeatedly.
Now follows the procedure for the practice of Vajrolī.
p. 110) || Root Text ||
By practice, one should draw upward the drop falling from the female organ; and having drawn upward one's own drop when it has moved, one should preserve it.
|| Commentary ||

Having had a probe made of lead— smooth, suitable for insertion into the penis, and measuring fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length— one should practice inserting it into the penis. On the first day, one should insert it to a depth of only one finger-breadth.
On the second day, [insert] two finger-breadths; on the third day, three finger-breadths.
In this manner, as the size increases gradually until it reaches twelve finger-breadths, the vaginal passage becomes purified. Then, [insert] one of that same kind measuring fourteen finger-breadths.

Having caused it to be made with a bend of two finger-breadths and facing upwards, one should insert that [tube] measuring twelve finger-breadths; one should leave the two-finger-breadth bend facing upwards outside. Then, [the work of] the goldsmith...

Taking a tube resembling a reed, which serves as the means for fanning the fire, one should insert its tip into the middle of the two-finger-width opening at the end of the twelve-finger-long tube inserted into the penis; that opening should be curved, facing upward, and then one should blow through it. By that—

The purification of the right path occurs. Then, one should practice drawing up water by means of the *meṇḍhra*. Once the drawing up of water is mastered, one should practice drawing the *bindu* upward according to the method described in the previously cited verse.
When the extraction of the bindu is accomplished, the perfection of the Vajroli-mudrā is attained;
this succeeds only for one who has conquered the vital breath (prāṇa), and not for anyone else.
However, when both Khecarī-mudrā and the conquest of prāṇa are perfected, it becomes truly complete.
Thus, once the practice of *vajrolī* has been mastered, he describes the subsequent means of accomplishment: "In the vulva of the woman" (*nārībhage*). This refers to the female womb (*strīyoni*).
Root Text
Thus one should protect the bindu; the knower of yoga conquers death. Death occurs through the falling of the bindu; life comes from the retention of the bindu. 88.
A fragrant scent arises in the body of the yogi from the retention of the *bindu*. As long as the *bindu* remains stable in the body, how can there be any fear of death? (89)
Commentary:

"Patat" means falling; "patadbindu" refers to that falling drop. During the time of sexual union, one should, through practice, draw upward—that is, attract—the falling drop by means of the practice of the Vajroli-mudra.

Precisely before falling. He says "and if it has moved" because if there were no attraction of the drop (*bindu*) prior to its falling, then one would have to attract it once it had already fallen. "Moved" means the drop belonging to oneself—one's own—that has fallen into the female organ; by the word "and" (*ca*), her menstrual blood (*rajas*) is also included.
Having drawn up and brought upward, one should protect—that is, one should establish [it]. || 87 ||

He states the benefits of Vajroli: "In this way," etc. He who would properly preserve—that is, thoroughly protect—the *bindu* in the manner described above is a knower of Yoga, one proficient in yoga; he conquers, that is, overcomes, death. For death occurs through the falling, the discharge, of the *bindu*, which is the semen (*śukra*).
It comes to pass. "Retention of the bindu" means *bindudhāraṇa*;
from that retention of the bindu, life arises. Therefore, the meaning is that one should protect the bindu. || 88 ||

Regarding "sugandha" (fragrance): for the yogin who practices *vajrolī*, the retention of the *bindu*—that is, the semen—is called *bindudhāraṇa*. From that, a beautiful fragrance (*sugaṃdha*) arises and becomes manifest in the body. As long as the *bindu* remains stable in the body, there is no fear of death for that duration of time.
Whence is the fear of death? The meaning is: from nowhere at all. || 89 ||
p. 112) || Root Text ||
The semen of men is dependent on the mind, and life is dependent on the semen.
Therefore, one must protect both the semen and the mind with great effort.
Likewise, during her fertile period, she should protect both the menstrual flow (rajas) and the seed-drop (bindu).
One who knows the yoga of proper practice should draw [the breath] upward by means of the *meḍhra*.
The Sahajoli, Cāmaroli, and Vajroli are unified as one; having cast fine ashes produced from burnt cow dung into water. (92)
Commentary:

"Citta-dependent" means: because for human beings, semen (*śukra*) and vitality (*vīrya*) are dependent on the mind; since [semen] moves when the mind moves and is stable when the mind is stable, life—that is, living—is dependent on the mind.
Life is dependent on semen; as long as semen is stable there is life, but when semen is lost, there is death.

Therefore, semen is dependent [on the mind]; thus, semen—the drop—and the mind, which is mental, must be protected through supreme effort—that is, with great exertion. The meaning is that it must certainly be protected. The word "eva" (certainly) is placed out of its logical order. || 90 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the woman in her season": thus, by means of the aforementioned practice, one should protect the semen—the innate, personal drop—of a woman who is *ṛtumatī*, that is, one in whom the fertile period (*ṛtu*) has occurred, specifically when she has bathed after her menses. He demonstrates the aforementioned practice:
Regarding the phrase "with the *meṇḍhra*": the practice is the practice of *vajrolī*; that itself is the yoga because it is the means for achieving yoga.

One who knows this is a "knower of the yoga of practice. With the *meṇḍhra*, which is the secret organ, one should properly and with great effort draw [the *rajas*] upward, toward the top. The *rajas*...
The word "bindu" is to be supplied [from the previous verse] as the object of the action; this verse has been interpolated. || 91 ||
Desiring to speak of Sahajolī and Amarolī, he states that Vajrolī is a specific variety of those two.
"And Sahajoli. The distinction or specific feature of Sahajoli and Amaroli is their difference from Vajrolī.
The reason for this is "ekatā," which means "oneness" or "having a single fruit.
The suffix *tasi* is applied to the word *eka* in the sense of an abstract quality (*bhāvapradhāna*) in the ablative case. He now describes Sahajoli:
"In the waters," etc.: cow-dung refers to the excrement of cows; those same cow-dungs when burnt are "burnt cow-dungs"; [be] born from them. (p. 13)
Root Text

After sexual union through Vajrolī, the bodies of both the man and the woman are smeared with [the fluid]; while they remain seated in comfort, having ceased all exertion, [this occurs] in an instant.
This is declared to be Sahajoli, which should always be trusted by yogis. This auspicious yoga bestows liberation even while one is engaged in worldly enjoyment. 94.
This yoga belongs to those who are meritorious, steadfast, and seers of reality.
It shall succeed for those free from envy, but not for those possessed by envy. || 95 ||
|| Commentary ||
That beautiful ash (vibhūti), which is produced from burnt cow-dung and whose origin is such, having been cast into water— that is, mixed with water— is connected with the following verse.

Regarding "Vajrolī": for the sake of the Vajrolī-mudrā, there is sexual union; thereafter, immediately following that, while the two are seated comfortably with joy alone, their activity—the act of passion—is released and abandoned in an instant due to the festival of rati.
"Of those two whose activities have ceased":
"woman and man" is *strīpuṃsau*; "of those two" is *tayoḥ*. "Anointing one's own limbs" (*svāṅgalepanam*):
"one's own limbs" (*svāṅgāni*) refers to beautiful parts of the body, such as the head, forehead, eyes, heart, shoulders, arms, and so forth; "in those" refers to them.
The anointing. || 93 ||

Regarding "the innate method" (sahajoli): this aforementioned practice is called and taught as the "innate method" by the masters of yoga, such as Matsyendra and others. Of what nature is it? It is always worthy of faith, meaning it is fit to be believed at all times. This yoga known as the innate method is an auspicious means.

One who performs what is auspicious and beneficial is called *śubhakara*. According to the lexicon, *yoga* refers to union, means, meditation, conjunction, and application. What kind of *yoga* is it? It is that which, even when joined with worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*), bestows liberation (*muktidah*). || 94 ||
"This is yoga"—this is what has been called yoga. Those who possess merit are "meritorious" (*puṇyavantaḥ*); they are the doers of good deeds (*sukṛtinaḥ*). For them...
Root Text
Now, Amarolī.

In the Kāpālika system of the Khaṇḍamata, the first stream of water is avoided due to its predominance of bile (pitta), and the final stream is rejected because of its lack of essence; instead, the cool middle stream is practiced—
this is known as Amarolī.
He who drinks the immortal elixir daily and applies it as a nasal drop day after day.
One should practice Vajrolī correctly; it is called Amarolī. || 17 ||
|| Commentary ||
Those who see reality— meaning those who perceive the true nature of things— are the meritorious, the steadfast, and the courageous; for them, the seers of reality,
there are those who have emerged from envy, namely the non-envious.

For those men who are free from envy—that is, devoid of hatred toward the virtues of others (according to Amara, *matsara* is "hatred of another's virtues")—success shall be attained; however, for those possessed of envy, success shall not be achieved. || 95 ||
He speaks of Amaroli: "Because of the predominance of bile" (*pittolbaṇatvāt*). "Bile-predominant" (*pittolbaṇā*) means that which is intense or excessive due to bile;
the state of being so is "bile-predominance," and it is because of that. Just as one might leave behind the first, initial stream of water—that is, the stream of auspicious water (*śivāmbu*).
At the time of the emergence of the auspicious water, having abandoned a small portion of the preceding stream,

that which has had its essence extracted is "niḥsārā" (essence-less); the state of being such is "niḥsāratā," and by that "niḥsāratā"— that is, by way of being essence-less— the final stream, which is the last and ultimate stream.

Having abandoned that final stream, and having discarded it, that middle stream— which is cool and devoid of the intensity of the humors such as bile— is thoroughly utilized; for he for whom this is considered and desired is one who favors the *khaṇḍa* (the broken or middle) yoga.
"Khaṇḍamata" refers to that [tradition]; "in that Khaṇḍamata" means belonging to a Kāpālika; "this Kāpālika" refers to that Kāpālika;
"in that Kāpālika" means in the Khaṇḍakāpālika tradition—this is the meaning. It is understood that *amarolī* is well-known [there]. || 96 ||
Regarding "amarolī": the man who daily drinks the *amarī* (the water of Śiva), performing it as a nasal inhalation (*nasya*) during [an attack of] asthma...
Root Text
One should mix the lunar [substance] that has emerged from practice with the divine power (vibhūti).
If one wears it upon the head, divine vision is produced.
If a woman, by properly contracting her seminal essence (bindu) through proficiency in practice, can preserve her menses, she too is a Vajrolī Yoginī. || 99 ||
Commentary:

One who is not unrefined (*nāmaryā*), while performing the internal grasping within the nose, should practice correctly day after day—that which is described in the verse beginning with "gradually by means of the *mehana* (penis)" as *vajrolī*; this is called *amarolī*. The word "by the Kāpālikas" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
The "immortal drink" (amarī) is the nectar; the meaning is that the practice preceded by nasal inhalation (nasya-pūrvikā) is designated by the terms Vajrolī and Amarolī. || 97 ||
"From practice" means: from the practice of *amarolī*, one should mix— that is, join together— the lunar nectar (*cāndrī sudhā*) which has emerged or issued forth,
along with the ashes (*vibhūti*), upon the head.
One should apply [the ash] to the skull, eyes, shoulders, throat, heart, arms, and so forth;
the remainder is that it is mixed with ashes and is lunar (cāndrī). It is divine (divyā), meaning it is capable of perceiving objects that are past, future, present, concealed, or distant.
The vision of one who possesses it becomes a divine vision; it arises, that is, it is produced in its excellence.
The specific methods for practicing *amarī* (the immortal) are to be understood from the *Śivāmbu-kalpa*.
Having explained the practice of *vajrolī* for men, he now speaks of it for women: "The man's drop... and so forth.

If, through the proficiency— that is, the skill— of correct practice, a woman, having properly drawn up and contracted her own *bindu* (vital essence), [unites with] a man during his *rajas* (semen) by means of the *vajrolī* mudrā;

One should protect her; she too, that woman, is to be known as a Yoginī endowed with excellent yoga. However, if the reading is "puṃso bindusamāyuktam" (endowed with the bindu of the man), then this is an adjective for the *rajas* (menstrual blood). || 99 ||
p. 116) || Root Text ||
Not even a trace of her menstrual flow perishes; of this there is no doubt.
Within her body, the *nāda* (vibratory sound) itself attains the state of the *bindu* (the drop). 100.
That *bindu* and that *rajas*, having become one and residing within one's own body through the practice of *vajrolī*, bestow all supernatural powers (*siddhis*). || 1 ||
Commentary:

He states the fruit of the Vajrolī performed by a woman: "Of her" (tasyāḥ). For that woman who is habituated to the practice of Vajrolī, the *rajas*—even the slightest, even a minute amount—does not go to destruction; it does not become lost, nor does its falling [downward] occur.

The meaning is that he attains [it]. Here, there is no doubt, no uncertainty. In the body of that noble lady, the *nāda* indeed becomes the *bindu*; the *nāda* arising from the *mūlādhāra* reaches the state of *bindu* above the heart.
The meaning is that it becomes one with the *bindu*. In the *Amṛtasiddhi*:
"The seed is said to be of the male, and the *rajas* arises from the female; through the external union of these two, the creation of men occurs. When there is internal union, then..."
He is celebrated as the Yogi. The Bindu is said to consist of the Moon, and the Rajas likewise consists of the Sun.
From the union of these two alone, the supreme state is born. The Bindu bestows heaven, bestows liberation, bestows dharma, and likewise bestows adharma. Within that [Bindu] dwell the deities.
All these exist in a subtle form. || 100 ||

Regarding the term *bindu*: that *bindu* of the man and that *rajas* (menstrual blood) of the woman—the practice of the *vajrolīmudrā* is "vajrolī-abhyāsa. Having become one through that very yoga, having merged together, they bestow all supernatural powers (*sarvasiddhi*) when residing within one's own body; they have been bestowed.
p. 117) || Root Text ||
One should protect [the breath] above the contraction; for that which is the *rajas* is indeed the Yoginī.
One knows the past and the future, and the power of moving through space (khecarī) certainly arises. || 2 ||
And one attains the perfection of the body through the practice of the yoga of Vajrolī. This meritorious yoga bestows liberation even while one is experiencing worldly enjoyments. || 3 ||
Now, the movement of Śakti: Kuṭilāṅgī (the curved-bodied), Kuṇḍalinī, Bhujaṅgī (the serpent-like), Śakti, Īśvarī, Kuṇḍalī, and Arundhatī—these are synonymous terms. || 4 ||
Commentary:

"She should protect" means: that woman who, by contracting [her body] and constricting the womb (*yoni*), draws [the *rajas*] upward to the upper place and protects the *rajas*; for this is well-known in the Yoga scriptures as "hi.
She is a *yoginī* who knows—that is, perceives—the past and future, the present and the yet-to-be.
"Dhruvam" means certain; "khecary" means she who moves in the sky (the atmosphere), thus she becomes a mover in the atmosphere. || 2 ||

"Dehasiddhim iti": From the yoga—the application or method—of the practice of *vajrolī*, they obtain the perfection of the body, which consists of beauty, grace, strength, and adamantine firmness. This yoga, the application of the practice of *vajrolī*, is merit-producing; it generates a specific kind of unseen spiritual force (*adṛṣṭa*).
What kind of yoga is it that is "enjoyed"? It is enjoyment (*bhoga*), which refers to the sense objects; even while those are being enjoyed, it grants liberation (*muktida*). || 3 ||

Desiring to explain the movement of the *śakti*, [the author] states, in seven verses beginning with "kuṭilāṅgī," the synonyms of Kuṇḍalinī as an introductory prelude, as well as her piercing of the door to liberation and so forth. *kuṭilāṅgī* (she whose body is curved) ... [and so on].
Kuṭilāṅgī (1), Kuṇḍalinī (2), Bhujaṅgī (3), Śakti (4), Īśvarī (5),
Kuṇḍalī (6), and Arundhatī (7)— these seven words are synonyms, expressing a single meaning. || 4 ||
p. 118) || Root Text ||
Just as one might forcibly open a door with a key, so too the yogi should pierce the door of liberation by means of Kuṇḍalinī. || 5 ||
By whichever path one must go to the stainless abode of Brahmā.
Having covered that opening with her mouth, the Supreme Goddess fell asleep.
Above the *kanda* lies the Kuṇḍalinī energy, sleeping for the sake of the liberation of yogins.
And for those who are deluded by bondage—he who knows that [reality] is a knower of Yoga.
Commentary:

"One should open" means: just as, in whatever manner, one might forcibly—that is, by means of physical strength—open or remove a door-panel using a key, which serves as the instrument for disengaging the bolt of the door; "forcibly" (haṭhāt) [is used here].
It is connected to both [sides] according to the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (*dehalīdīpanyāya*). In that manner, by means of *haṭha*— that is,

through the practice of *haṭha*— the yogi should pierce, specifically, the path of the *suṣumṇā*, which is the door to liberation (*mokṣadvāra*), the means for attaining liberation, by means of the power of *kuṇḍalinī*.
One should pierce [the path], for according to the Vedic scripture: "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality. || 5 ||

Regarding the word *yena*: *āmaya* refers to the suffering born of disease, which is an indicator for suffering in general; that from which one has emerged is *nirāmaya*, meaning free from all suffering. *Brahmasthāna* is the station that causes the manifestation of Brahman; it is the *brahmarandhra*.
According to the Vedic scripture, "The Supreme Self is situated within the center of that crest-lock";
having covered— that is, blocked— with his mouth, that is, with his face, the entrance to that path, the gateway through which one must go, namely the path of the *suṣumṇā*.
The Supreme Goddess Kuṇḍalinī is fast asleep, slumbering. || 6 ||
Regarding the phrase "above the *kanda*": the *Kuṇḍalinī* power is asleep above the *kanda*, in the upper portion of the *kanda*.
She is asleep for the liberation of yogis and asleep for the bondage of the deluded. By awakening her, yogis become liberated.

The meaning is that fools remain bound because of their ignorance of her. He who knows that Kuṇḍalinī is a knower of Yoga; for the reason that all systems of Yoga have their foundation in Kuṇḍalinī. || 7 ||
p. 119) || Root Text ||
Kuṇḍalinī is proclaimed to be curved in form like a serpent; he by whom that Śakti is set in motion is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, even a young widow practicing austerities may, by force,
attain that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The divine Iḍā is the Gaṅgā, and the Piṅgalā is the river Yamunā.
Between the Iḍā and Piṅgalā is Bālaraṇḍā, who is Kuṇḍalī.
|| Commentary ||

Regarding the term *kuṇḍalī*: the power (*śakti*) called *kuṇḍalī* has a coiled form, like a snake or a serpent; she whose nature is thus curved is proclaimed and described by yogis as being of a crooked shape.
That power *kuṇḍalī*, when moved upward from the *mūlādhāra* by a person—

He has been led [there] and is liberated from the bondage of ignorance; he has turned back [from worldly existence]. In this matter, there is no doubt, meaning there is no uncertainty. This is because of the Vedic scripture: "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality.
Regarding the phrase "of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā," it refers to the relationship between the container and the contained (the riverbed and the waters) of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

Through the meditation on those two as non-different from the Gaṅgā and Yamunā— or by meditating on the Gaṅgā and Yamunā as the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*— one should [meditate upon] the ascetic Kuṇḍalinī, who is called "the young widow" (*bālaraṇḍā*) because she abides in a state of fasting, within the path of the *suṣumnā* between those two.

One should seize her by force and with violence; that seizing of her between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is the supreme station of Viṣṇu, Hari, the all-pervading Self, or it is that which leads to the attainment of the supreme station. || 9 ||

He explains the referents of the terms Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and so forth: "Iḍā... etc. Iḍā is the channel for the left exhalation; it is the Gaṅgā—endowed with the sovereignty and other attributes of the Blessed One—and is denoted by the word "Gaṅgā.
Piṅgalā is the channel for the right exhalation; it is the Yamunā and is denoted by the word "Yamunā."
p. 120) || Root Text ||
Grasping the serpent by its tail, one should awaken it;
having abandoned sleep, that power rises up forcefully.
That hooded serpent remains stationary for half a watch (one hour and a half) from morning until evening;
having filled [the vessel] from the sun by means of the method of encircling, it must be constantly held and moved upward to a height of one *vitasti* (span) and with a width of four *aṅgulas*.
|| Commentary ||
The river: that Kuṇḍalinī which is situated in the middle between the Iḍā and Piṅgalā is the "child-widow" (bālaraṇḍā), denoted by the term "child-widow. || 110 ||
He speaks of the movement of the power (*śakticālana*): "In the tail," etc. Having seized that sleeping, slumbering serpent-like Kuṇḍalinī by the tail, one should awaken her;
that Kuṇḍalinī power, having abandoned sleep, stands up forcibly.
Such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). This secret, however, is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru. || 11 ||
"Established" means situated below, residing in the *mūlādhāra*,
that coiled serpent (*phaṇāvatī bhujaṅgī*), she who is Kuṇḍalinī; having filled from the sun— that is,
having performed the filling from the sun— by means of that method of encircling (*paridhāna-yukti*).

Having grasped, that is, having taken hold [of it]; in the evening at the time of sunset, and in the morning at the time of sunrise; constantly, day after day; for half a watch, that is, half of a *prahara* or *yāma*;
merely half a watch, that is, for the duration of just half a watch.
It should be moved around for only two muhūrtas; it is suitable to be rotated in every direction. The method for donning it should be learned from the instructor. || 12 ||
Desiring to explain the movement of the *śakti* by means of the pressing of the *kanda*, [the author] first states the location and nature of the *kanda*: "Above," and so forth.
p. 121) || Root Text ||
It is said that the characteristic of the wrapped cloth is that it be soft and white.
While seated in the vajra posture, one should firmly hold the feet with both hands.
And near the region of the ankle, one should press upon the *kanda* there.
The yogi, seated in the vajra posture, having set the kuṇḍalinī in motion, [should proceed].
Commentary:

From the root-place (*mūlasthāna*), measuring one *vitasti* (span) upwards—that is, at a distance of one *vitasti* above—the location is between the navel and the genitals. By this, the location of the *kanda* is stated. Thus it has been said in the *Gorakṣaśataka*: "Above the genitals and below the navel is the womb of the *kanda*."

Like the eggs of a bird; therein, seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) have arisen. Yājñavalkya says: Two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis is the center of the body, the middle of the physical form.

Thus it has been declared regarding human beings: the location of the *kanda* (the root-center) for humans is nine finger-breadths from the middle of the body; it is four finger-breadths in width and likewise in length;
its form is adorned like that of an egg, and it is covered with skin and other tissues.
Regarding the phrase "situated in the middle of the mouth" for quadrupeds, birds, and the twice-born:
two finger-breadths above the anus, one finger-breadth is the middle; from there, nine finger-breadths is the location of the *kanda* (bulbous root).
Taken together, this measures twelve finger-breadths, which is the extent of a span (*vitasti*).
It is born. A collection of four fingers is "four-fingered" (*caturaṅgula*), meaning a width of four finger-breadths.
Width is also indicative of length; thus, it is four finger-breadths long and soft.
That which has characteristics and a form like those of a soft, white, and bright cloth— meaning a garment that is wrapped or fashioned into the shape of a wrapping—
is thus described and declared; such is the nature of the *kanda*.
The word "yogibhiḥ" (by yogis) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 13 ||

"Satīti" means: when the *vajrāsana* has been assumed, with both hands—that is, with the two palms—one places them near the two *gulphas*, which are the regions of the ankles (*pādagraṃthi*). "Near those" means slightly above the two *gulphas*. According to Amara, *ghuṭika* and *gulpha* both mean the ankle. [One places] the two feet...

One should hold the two feet firmly and tightly; by the word "and" (ca), it is implied that with the feet thus held, one should press the *kanda* at that location, pressing it intensely. [With] both hands, [one should hold them] above the ankles.
The meaning is that, having grasped the feet, one should press the *kanda* in the region below the navel.
Regarding "in the *vajrāsana*": the yogi, situated in the *vajrāsana*, should move the *kuṇḍalinī* by means of the *śakticālanamudrā*.
p. 122) || Root Text ||
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the bhastrā [breathing exercise] and quickly awaken Kuṇḍalinī. || 15 ||
One should perform the contraction of the sun (the solar channel) and then cause Kuṇḍalinī to move.
Even for one who has entered the jaws of death, whence can there be fear of death? || 16 ||
By moving it fearlessly for a period of two muhūrtas, this [prāṇa] is drawn slightly upward and rises into the suṣumnā. || 17 ||
Therefore, her coiled [kuṇḍalinī] certainly leaves the mouth of that suṣumnā;
consequently, this prāṇa proceeds spontaneously into the suṣumnā. || 18 ||
Commentary:

The meaning is "having performed. Immediately after—that is, immediately after the movement of the power (śakti)—one should perform the *bhastrā* [kumbhaka], the breath-retention known as *bhastrā*. In this manner, one should quickly and swiftly awaken the Kuṇḍalinī power; that is, one should cause her to become awakened. [This is to be done] in the *vajrāsana* posture.
Although the vajrāsana was already prescribed previously for the practice of *śakticālana*, its mention again here is for the purpose of establishing a rule:
that the vajrāsana must be performed specifically on the bellows (*bhastrā*) immediately following *śakticālana*. || 15 ||

Regarding the word "bhānoḥ": one should perform the contraction of the sun (bhānu) situated in the region of the navel. By the very contraction of the navel, its contraction occurs. Then, from that contraction of the sun, one should move the Kuṇḍalinī power. [This is] the mouth of Death.
Even for that person who has reached the very mouth [of death], from where could there be fear of death or fear of Time? The meaning is: from nowhere at all. || 16 ||
"Two muhūrtas" means a pair of two muhūrtas,
consisting of four ghaṭikās; up to that limit, up to that duration, this power (śakti), having risen within the Suṣumnā, moves fearlessly and without hesitation.
When it is drawn slightly upward, it becomes drawn up. || 17 ||
"By that" means: by that upward drawing, Kuṇḍalī enters the mouth—that is, the opening—of that well-known Suṣumnā.
Root Text
Therefore, one should constantly move Arundhatī, who is sleeping comfortably;
by that very movement of her, the yogi is liberated from diseases. 19.
The yogi by whom power (śakti) is thus set in motion becomes a vessel for spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). What is the use of much speaking on this matter? He conquers time with ease. 20.
Success is seen from the maṇḍala for the yogi who practices kuṇḍalinī, provided he is constantly devoted to celibacy and eats food that is wholesome and moderate. || 21 ||
|| Commentary ||
He abandons—that is, leaves behind—the path that is firm and certain.

Therefore, due to this abandonment of the path, this vital breath (prāṇavāyu) goes by itself, of its own accord, into the Suṣumnā; even before reaching the opening of the Suṣumnā, [it enters] the Kuṇḍalinī.
The meaning is: "because it has emerged. || 18 ||

"Therefore" means: because the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the Suṣumnā through the activation of the Śakti, therefore one should daily—every day—properly activate that Śakti Arundhatī, who is "sukhasuptā," meaning sleeping comfortably; one should thoroughly move her. Of her...
By the very movement of the *śakti*, through that mere movement, the yogi is liberated from diseases such as cough, asthma, old age, and so forth; he becomes completely freed. || 19 ||

"By whom" (yena): that yogi by whom the power Kuṇḍalinī has been set in motion becomes a vessel, a receptacle, for the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as aṇimā and the rest. Regarding this matter, what is the use of much speaking or excessive praise? The meaning is: none at all. Time... [text fragment]
The meaning is that he conquers or overcomes death with ease, through play, and without even exertion.

Regarding the term *brahmacarya*: *brahmacarya* is the restraint of the generative organ together with the ears and other senses; for one who delights in that and is devoted to it, [this applies] constantly.
Root Text
Having set the Kuṇḍalinī in motion, one should especially practice the bellows-breathing (bhastrā).
For one who practices thus constantly, how can there be fear of Yama? || 22 ||
Regarding the purification of the impurities of the seventy-two thousand channels, what means of washing exists other than the practice of Kuṇḍalinī? (23)
But this central channel [is mastered] by yogins through firm practice.
|| Commentary ||

He who always eats what is beneficial, wholesome, and moderate—specifically avoiding one-fourth of his usual portion—for him there is the practice of Kuṇḍalinī, which is the practice of activating the Śakti; that itself is Yoga. One who possesses this is "he who has it" (yogin). For such a person, perfection follows after forty days consisting of [the practice of] Maṇḍala.
The perfection of *prāṇāyāma* is observed:

the vital breath (*prāṇa*), flowing through the right nostril, is made exceedingly long; appearing like the moon, its body filled with nectar, it first [reaches] the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*) and then, having severed...
That body, which has entered the channels of the openings between the eyebrows under the influence of the fire of time and space, certainly makes it anew again, like a severed tree trunk.
"Having moved Kuṇḍalī"—that is, having performed the movement of the Śakti by activating Kuṇḍalī;

"then immediately thereafter," one should perform the *bhastrā*, which is the *kumbhaka* known as *bhastrā*. This should be done daily, every day, by the self-controlled yogin who practices in the manner thus described.

From what source could there be fear for one who fears Yama? The meaning is: from no source whatsoever. The intended sense is that for a yogi, the relinquishing of the body is under his own control. || 22 ||
Seventy-two thousand— that is, seventy increased by two— thousands; when the purification of the impurities of those channels numbering seventy-two thousand must be performed.

Without the practice of Kuṇḍalī and the practice of activating the Śakti, from what source could there be a means of purification? From no source whatsoever. The intention is that only through the practice of activating the Śakti does the cleansing of the impurities of all the *nāḍīs* occur. || 23 ||
"This, however," etc. This middle channel, the *suṣumnā*, is the seat for yogins through firm practice; [the postures] such as *svastika* and so forth.
Root Text
Through the postures, breath control, and mudrās, she becomes straight. || 24 ||
But when, through practice, one holds the mind in meditative absorption while remaining sleepless, then the Rudrāṇī Mudrā bestows auspicious perfection. || 25 ||
Without Rājayoga, the earth [is no earth]; without Rājayoga, the night [is no night];
without Rājayoga, even a diverse mudrā does not shine. (26)
Commentary:
Through breath control (prāṇasaṃyama), breath regulation (prāṇāyāma), and the mudrās such as Mahāmudrā and others, she becomes straight and upright. || 24 ||
Regarding the word "abhyāse" (in practice): having fixed the mind through concentration (*samādhi*), which consists in the cessation of other mental fluctuations and one-pointedness,

and having made the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) steadfast in *dhāraṇā* (steadfastness), they are those for whom sleep has departed— that is, those who possess such effort toward the stability of the mind in practice.

The term *nidrā* (sleep) is an indicator of *ālasya* (laziness); thus, it means "for those who are not lazy. Whether it be the *rudrāṇī* or *śāṃbhavī* mudrā, or else another supreme [mudrā] such as *unmanī*, it bestows—that is, grants—the auspicious (*bhadra*) and propitious (*śubha*) perfection (*siddhi*), namely the perfection of yoga (*yogasiddhi*). By this...
Rājayoga is said to be that which assists Haṭhayoga. || 25 ||
He states, by means of a figurative metaphorical connection, the futility of postures and other practices in the absence of Rājayoga.
Regarding "rājayoga": it is as follows.

Rājayoga is the continuous stream of non-conceptual mental modification (*nirvikalpa-vṛtti*) directed toward the Self, preceded by the cessation of other modifications. Regarding the phrase "Rājayoga without Haṭha," this refers either to the practice of its means as indicated therein, or— without that [Haṭha] and apart from it— to what is denoted by the word "earth" (*pṛthvī*).

The quality of stability is indicated by the posture (*āsana*) through *rājayoga*; the reason—that without *rājayoga* the fruit of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*) cannot be accomplished—should be applied here as well as in what follows.
Without *rājayoga*, the retention (*kuṃbhaka*) does not shine, just as the night does not shine without the moon.

Generally, because of the absence of the movement of the royal [vital] breaths, the word "night" (niśā) indicates the *kumbhaka* (retention) characterized by the absence of the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). *Rājayoga*— even though it is manifold, diverse, and distinct— is [accomplished] without the various *mudrās*, such as the *mahāmudrā* and others.

Or it does not shine, it does not appear beautiful. In the alternative sense: without the *rājayoga*—the union with, or connection to, a king—the earth does not shine; for without a ruler, various calamities arise upon the land. [The word] *rājā*...
p.126) || Root Text ||
One should practice the entire procedure for the vital air (mārūta) with a concentrated mind; the wise person should not allow the activity of the mind to wander elsewhere. || 27 ||
Thus have the ten mudrās been proclaimed by Śambhu, the Primordial Lord; among them, each one bestows great siddhi upon those who practice self-restraint. (28)
He who imparts the traditional instruction on the mudrās is indeed the illustrious Guru, the Master; he is the Lord himself in visible form. || 29 ||
|| Commentary ||
The Moon: According to the sacred tradition (*śruti*), Soma is the king of us Brahmins;

without his union—that is, his connection—the night does not shine. Just as a royal seal (*mudrā*) on documents does not [bear authority] without the connection of a king—that is, without its association with the monarch.

A specific mark being produced; though variegated—on the side of the earth, because it produces gems and the like, it is distinct; on the side of the night, it is variegated by planets, constellations, and so forth; and on the side of a seal, it is variegated by lines—even so, [it is not...]
He shines. || 26 ||

Regarding the phrase "of Māruta": one should practice thoroughly— that is, practice correctly— the entire procedure of Māruta, namely Vāyu, which consists of the rules for *kumbhaka* (retention) and *mudrās*, joined with the mind— that is, conjoined with the mind— by a wise person, that is, by an intelligent man, elsewhere.
The mental activity—the functioning or operation of the mind—should not be directed toward any object other than the ordinance of the Wind-god; it must not be performed. || 27 ||

He presents the mudrās. Regarding the word "iti" (thus): by the Primordial Lord, the Sovereign of All, Śambhu—so called because from him (Śam-bhu) happiness (śam) arises—it is stated that, according to the manner described, ten mudrās, numbering ten, have been proclaimed or spoken.

Among those mudrās, even each single one—whichever mudrā it may be—is a bestower of great siddhis, such as *aṇimā* and the rest, for the self-controlled, the disciplined, and the yogins. [Verse 28] He praises the guru who instructs in the mudrās: "The instruction... he who...
The person [is the master] of the mudrās, such as the Mahāmudrā and others.
(p. 127) || Root Text ||
Becoming intent upon his words and concentrated in the practice of the mudrās, one attains the deception of time along with the qualities beginning with *aṇimā*. || 130 ||
Thus ends the third instruction, titled "The Method of Mudrās," in the *Haṭhapradīpikā* composed by the lord of yogis, Śrī Svātmarāma.
Commentary:
He gives— that is, he bestows— the traditional instruction (*sāṃpradāyika-upadeśa*) which has come down from the lineage of gurus (*guruparaṃparā*) of yogis. He alone, that very person,
is the *Śrīguru*, meaning the venerable teacher who is superior to all other gurus.
The master, the lord—he is indeed the Lord himself, manifest and perceptible;
the meaning is that he is non-different from the Lord. || 29 ||

"Of him" (tasya): [it means] of that guru who teaches the mudrās; "devoted to his word" (vākyaparaḥ) means intent upon his instructions concerning the practice of postures, breath-control (kumbhaka), and so forth, as well as those concerning proper diet, conduct, movement, and the like. "Devoted to that" (tatparaḥ) means intent upon that [instruction].
And being intent upon that, he is respectful; respect consists in performing the prescribed austerities,

and having combined with them, there is the practice of the mudrās, such as the Mahāmudrā and others— the repeated performance of which constitutes that practice of mudrās— and he is concentrated, that is, attentive, toward that practice of mudrās.

The person, together with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the supernatural powers (siddhis) beginning with atomization, attains—that is, reaches—the deception or evasion of Time, which is death. || 130 ||
Thus ends the third instruction, titled "The Description of Mudrās," in the *Jyotsnā*, a commentary on the *Śrī Haṭhapradīpikā* composed by Brahmānanda. || 3 ||
The Fourth Instruction.
Root Text.
Salutations to Śiva, the Guru, whose nature consists of the Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā; he who is eternally devoted to Him attains the stainless state. || 1 ||
Now I shall proclaim the supreme sequence of meditative absorption (samādhi), which destroys death, is an easy means [to liberation], and brings about the highest bliss of Brahman. || 2 ||
|| Commentary ||

Desiring to explain Rājayoga— the fruit resulting from the āsanas, kumbhakas, and mudrās taught in the first, second, and third chapters— Svātmārāma notes that since "blessings are beset by many obstacles" and a profusion of obstacles is likely to arise therein, he seeks to prevent them.
He performs an auspicious invocation consisting of salutation to the Guru who is non-different from Śiva, [beginning with] "Namaḥ."

To Śiva, who is of the nature of bliss, or who is non-different from the Lord; as it has been said: "Salutations to you, O Lord, O Blessed One, Śiva, in the form of the Guru. To the Guru, the instructor; or rather, to the Guru who is Śiva and the Lord, by virtue of being the inner controller of all and the teacher of everything. And thus:

The Pātañjala Sūtra: He is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time. Let there be salutation—let there be a state of complete prostration—to the Guru Śiva, whose nature consists of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā; [to him] whose resonance (anuraṇana) is like the sound of a bronze bell, which is Nāda.

The *bindu* is the sound (*dhvani*) that arises subsequent to the *anusvāra*. A *kalā* is a portion of *nāda*; he whose self (*ātman*)—that is, whose essential nature (*svarūpa*)—is composed of those [three] is "he whose self is *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*. The meaning is: "to Him who exists as the self of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*. In that regard, [one should worship] the Guru, Śiva, who eternally exists as the self of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*.

A person who is daily devoted and attentive—by this, it is stated in the preceding quarter-verse that he is intent upon the pursuit of *nāda*, and the non-duality of the Guru and Śiva is indicated. "Ointment" (*añjana*) refers to the limiting adjunct of *māyā*; [the state] devoid of that is meant.
The "goal" (*pada*) is Brahman, which is stainless and pure; it is so called because it is reached and attained by yogis. As he will state later:
"One who possesses the samādhi resulting from the contemplation of the *nāda*," and so forth. || 1 ||
He promises to explain the sequence of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) with the words "Now" (*atha*).

Now, immediately following the description of the postures, breath-retentions, and mudrās, at this juncture I shall explain—the connection being that I shall speak of it with excellence and analytical detail—the sequence of samādhi, which consists of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) and so forth. Of what nature is this sequence of samādhi? It is the supreme (uttama).
It is the most excellent among the ten million modes of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) taught by the illustrious Ādinātha for accomplishing [the goal].
Furthermore, it is "death-conquering" (*mṛtyughna*), meaning it destroys— that is, wards off— death or time,
and brings about the voluntary relinquishment of the body at one's own will.

Furthermore, by means of the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*), and the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), what is the supreme means for attaining the bliss of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti-sukha*)— that which produces the bliss of the Supreme Brahman once the karma of past momentum (*prārabdha-karma*) has been exhausted?
This brings about disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), which consists in the attainment of absolute Brahman-bliss through the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.

In that state, "cessation" (*nirodha*) occurs through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), when all fluctuations of the mind— including their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)— are ceased, and the states of tranquility, agitation, and delusion have come to an end.

Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) consists in abiding in the changeless true nature, as described in such scriptural passages as, "Even while living here, the wise man is liberated from joy and sorrow.
Supreme liberation (paramamukti), however, occurs at the end of the experiences already attained, when the qualities of the internal organ [are dissolved].
Through reversion (*pratiprasava*), when conditioned forms have ceased absolutely, there is an absolute abiding in one's own true nature, which is established by that reversion.
The latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence, cessation, and meditative absorption dissolve into the mind.

The mind [subsides] into egoism (*asmitā*), egoism into the Great One (*mahat*), and the Great One into the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*); this is the reversion of the qualities of the mind, the dissolution, the return to its own cause. Now, one might object: for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), there is the thought "I am a Brahmin."

If it is argued that because we observe worldly usage such as "I am a human," and because the arising of conditioned states through the mind and other factors would cause the loss of one's true nature— just as milk loses its nature when mixed with sour gruel— that is not so;
for in the state of *saṃprajñāta-samādhi*, there is the certainty of the reality of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the Self as experienced therein.

Because an unreal transformation does not entail change, whereas the transformation of milk into curds by means of sourness is real. Furthermore, due to the disparity between the example and the case at hand,
the Puruṣa’s empirical usage such as "I am a Brahmin" is conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
The form of the crystal is merely adventitious, conditioned by its proximity to a hibiscus flower, and is not real;

just as the crystal remains in its own true nature when the hibiscus flower is removed, so too, upon the cessation of all modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the Puruṣa’s abiding in its own nature is indeed immutable. || 2 ||
p. 130) || Root Text ||
The samādhi of royal yoga, the state of Unmanī and Manonmanī; immortality, dissolution, the ultimate reality, the void and non-void—the supreme state. || 3 ||
"Mindless," "non-dual," "supportless," "untainted," "liberation while living," "the innate," and "the fourth state"—these are synonyms for the same reality. || 4 ||
Just as salt in water attains a state of equilibrium through union.
Likewise, the unification of the self and the mind is designated as *samādhi*.
When the vital breath is completely attenuated and the mind dissolves away,
that state of equal flavor is designated as samādhi.
And that equality is the unity of the two: the individual self and the supreme self.
When all mental constructions have utterly perished, that is designated as samādhi.
Commentary:
He speaks specifically of the synonyms for *samādhi* with the two verses beginning with "rājayoga" and so forth;
this is clear. (3–4) He describes *samādhi* with three [verses], beginning with "salila."
Just as rock salt— salt produced in the region of Sindhu—
attains equality with water, that is, achieves identity with water through contact or union,
in the same way, the self and the mind (the two together: *ātma-manasī*) likewise [attain identity].

The unity of those two—the self and the mind—is their state of having a single form. When the mind, held within the self, takes on the form of the self, it attains identity with the self; such a unity of the self and the mind is called *samādhi*, meaning it is expressed by the term *samādhi*. || 5 || 6 || 7 ||
p. 131) || Root Text ||
Who truly knows the greatness of Rājayoga?
Knowledge, liberation, stability, and perfection are obtained through the words of the Guru.
The renunciation of sense objects is difficult to attain; the vision of reality is difficult to attain; and the innate state is difficult to attain without the compassion of a true guru. (9)
Through various postures, diverse vessels, and also through specific yogic techniques,
when the Great Power (Mahāśakti) is awakened, the vital breath (prāṇa) dissolves into the void.
Commentary:
Now follows the praise of the royal yoga (rājayoga). Regarding "of the royal yoga":
Who indeed knows, in truth—that is, in its actual reality—the greatness and power of Rājayoga, which was just described? The meaning is that no one knows it.
Although it is impossible to describe it in its entirety, he speaks of the power of Rājayoga by way of a single aspect: knowledge.

Liberation (*mukti*) occurs upon the direct experience of one's own true nature; disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*) is that state, while liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is the abiding in an unchanging essential nature.
These perfections (*siddhi*), such as *aṇimā* and the rest, are obtained through the words of the Guru—that is, by the Guru’s speech—[attained] via *rājayoga*.
The remainder. || 8 ||

Regarding the term *durlabha* ("difficult to attain"): objects (*viṣaya*)—whether pertaining to this world, such as wives and so forth, or pertaining to the hereafter, such as nectar and so forth—are so called because they specifically cause the knower (*pramātṛ*) to swell with attachment and bind him.
The renunciation of these, which is the absence of the desire for enjoyment, is difficult to attain.

The vision of reality is the direct experience of the Self; it is difficult to attain. The innate state is the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*). It is [attained] through the grace (*karuṇā*)—meaning compassion (*dayā*)—of a true Guru, whose gaze is steady even without an object of sight, according to the definition to be stated hereafter. This applies in every case.

The word *duḥ* is connected [to the following], meaning "difficult to obtain" (*durlabhā*) or "impossible to attain" (*aśakyā*). According to the lexicon (*kośa*), *duḥ* is used in the senses of "suffering" (*kaṣṭa*) and "prohibition" (*niṣedha*). The underlying sense is that, however, through the grace of the Guru, everything becomes easily attainable (*sulabha*). || 9 ||
"By various [means]" means:

By means of various and manifold postures (*āsana*), such as the seats of Matsyendra and others, and by various kinds of breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*). The word "vicitraiḥ" (various) is connected to both [terms] according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*). It means "of many different types."
Root Text (Mūla) (p. 132)
For the yogi whose power of consciousness has arisen and who has abandoned all karma without exception, the innate state (sahajāvasthā) arises spontaneously of its own accord. || 11 ||
When the vital breath flows through the Suṣumṇā and the mind enters the void,
then the knower of yoga eradicates all karmas from their very root.
Commentary:

When the great power Kuṇḍalinī has been awakened— that is, when she is free from sleep— by means of the great mudrās such as Mahāmudrā, which are the most excellent auxiliaries for the attainment of Haṭha through the instruments [of yoga], the vital breath (prāṇa), which is air, [enters] into the void.
It dissolves; it reaches dissolution. The absence of activity of the vital breath (prāṇa) is dissolution. || 10 ||
"Arising" (utpanna): for that yogi in whom the awakening of power (*śaktibodha*)—the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī—has arisen or been born;
by whom all actions (*karmāṇi*), without exception and in their entirety, have been abandoned or relinquished;
