when physical activity has been ceased through the practice of posture (*āsana*), [and] within the vital breaths and senses...
Activity remains.

When mental activity has been relinquished through withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and cognitive absorption (samprajñāta-samādhi), activity remains in the intellect (buddhi). For this person (puruṣa) is indeed unattached.
According to scripture, the Puruṣa is unchanging and pure, whereas the intellect (buddhi) consists of the quality of sattva and is subject to transformation. || 11 ||

When the activity of the intellect has been relinquished either through supreme detachment or solely by means of long-term practice of *saṃprajñāta* [samādhi], there occurs a state of abiding in one's own immutable nature;
that itself is the innate state (*sahajāvasthā*), the state of the Fourth (*turyāvasthā*), and liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which requires no further effort.

"It is born" means it manifests; for the Śruti says, "That by which you abandon, abandon that," and thus one should become free from attachment through wisdom. Regarding the term *suṣumnā*: when the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the wind, flows through the *suṣumnā*—that is, when it flows through the central channel (*madhyamā nāḍī*)—it occurs.
p. 133) || Root Text ||
Salutations to you, O Immortal One; even that Time has been conquered by you—the one into whose mouth this entire world, both moving and unmoving, has fallen. 13.
When the mind has attained equanimity and the vital breath moves into the central channel, then Amaroli, Vajroli, and Sahajoli arise. || 14 ||
How can knowledge arise in the mind here, as long as the vital breath continues to live and the mind does not die?
Commentary:

When the mind— the internal organ— enters into the void Brahman, which is devoid of the limitations of space, time, and substance, at that time the knower of Yoga, who understands the cessation of the modifications of the mind,
eradicates all karmas, including those already set in motion (prārabdha), making them rootless.
From the word *nirmūla*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule "that which makes it so" (*tat karoti*).
He pays homage to the yogi who has conquered time, because through the practice of *samādhi*, even *prārabdha* karma is overcome. Regarding the word "amarāya": one who does not die is "amara";
salutations to you, that yogi, the immortal and long-lived one. Even for him, time—which is otherwise difficult to ward off—[is conquered].

"Death has been conquered and overcome by you, O Yogin"—this statement is the reason for your salutation. Who is he? He into whose mouth this visible world—the cycle of existence consisting of the moving and the unmoving, the animate and the inanimate—has fallen. Even he...
The meaning is that he is even the devourer of the world. || 13 ||

Since the previously mentioned [powers], such as *amaryolī* and so forth, are accomplished only upon the attainment of *samādhi*, he states—immediately following the definition of *samādhi*—that their accomplishment occurs when *samādhi* is attained: "In the mind...

In the *citta*, that is, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), "equanimity" (*samatva*) consists in the continuous flow of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) in the form of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*).

When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has entered or reached the middle *suṣumnā*, as it proceeds therein, this is the cause for the equanimity of the mind. At that time, the previously mentioned *amarolī*, *vajrolī*, and *sahajolī* arise; they do not arise for one who has not mastered the *prāṇa*.
The sense is that they do not succeed for one whose mind is unconquered. || 14 ||
He says that without the practice of Haṭha, neither knowledge nor liberation is accomplished.
"Knowledge" [is that which exists] as long as the vital breath [persists]. (p.
134) Root Text.
The man who brings both of these—the vital breath and the mind—to dissolution attains liberation; no other does so in any way whatsoever. || 15 ||
|| Commentary ||

It lives. By the use of the word "api" (also), it is meant that the sense organs live and do not die; as long as the mind does not die, it indeed lives. The flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels is the life of the breath, while the grasping of their respective objects is the life of the sense organs.

The production of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) in the form of various objects is intended here as the "life" of the mind, while their respective dissolution is its "death. Now, [one might ask: is it not the case that their destruction by their very nature occurs within the mind? [The answer is: Knowledge is the direct experience of the Self within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

How could it arise? It cannot, because even the agent [is subject to] the fluctuations of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the senses, and the mind, which act as obstacles to knowledge; this is the sense. That yogi who would bring about the dissolution—the destruction—of these two, namely the vital breath and the mind, [attains liberation].
One goes to—that is, attains—liberation, which is characterized by abiding in one's ultimate essential nature.

The dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is its state of non-activity within the *brahmarandhra*, resulting from absorption into the form of the object of meditation. Another [form of] dissolution of the mind occurs through the absence of other objects.

The meaning is that one whose vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not subdued and whose mind (*manas*) is not subdued does not attain liberation even by some hundred means. As it is said in the *Yogabīja*: "The mind cannot be brought under control by various kinds of deliberations; therefore, its conquest generally comes through the conquest of the vital breath."

"Indeed, thus": through various paths, the supreme state of isolation (*kaivalya*), which consists primarily of pleasure and pain, is attained by means of the perfected path (*siddhamārga*) and not otherwise; so it was spoken by Śiva.
The perfected path is the path of yoga (*yogamārga*). By this [it is shown that] without yoga, neither knowledge nor liberation exists.
It is established that it is accomplished; this is well-known in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth. For instance: "Now, Yoga is the means for the vision of That";
the vision of That is the vision of the Self. Having known the Divine through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self (adhyātma-yoga)...

"The steadfast one abandons both joy and sorrow. "One knows through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation. When the five [senses] come to rest along with the mind, and the intellect no longer stirs—that they call the supreme goal; that they consider to be yoga.
"One becomes vigilant at that time through steady concentration on the senses.
When one, joined here with the nature of Brahman as being like a mirror, perceives the reality of the Self;
having known the Lord—who is unborn, eternal, and purified of all principles—one is liberated.
With all fetters [cast off], one should join the self with the thought, "Om! To the Great Brahman, you!

Having thus established oneself three times, standing erect with the body balanced, and having withdrawn the senses and the heart into the mind by means of the invocation of Brahman, one should cross over.

"One who speaks thus [is a sinner], for all streams are fraught with danger"— such are the scriptural passages beginning with "Om, meditate thus on the Self. Manu, in the section concerning the duties of ascetics (*yatidharma*), states:
One should contemplate the past and the future through the yoga of the Supreme Self; having swiftly abandoned the two bodies, one becomes liberated from bondage. (From the Yājñavalkyasmṛti:
Among the acts of sacrifice, conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and Vedic study, this indeed is the supreme...
Dharma is that through which one perceives the Self. The great seer Mātaṅga said:

"Having abandoned all [rituals] such as the Agniṣṭoma, the best of the twice-born, being peaceful and devoted to the practice of yoga, attains the Supreme Brahman. [This applies] to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas."

It is the purifier for women and Śūdras; for the sake of pacifying other actions, there is nothing other than Yoga for liberation. This has been stated by way of contrast in the *Dakṣasmṛti*: "That Brahman is indeed self-realizable, like the pleasure of a young maiden; one who is not a yogi does not know it at all."

For instance, there are such traditional sayings as "just as one born blind [sees] a jar," and so forth; and Vyāsa, in the *Yogamārga* section of the *Mahābhārata*, states: "Even one who is low in caste, or even a woman, if they desire dharma—even those two may go to the supreme [state] by this path."
Whether he be a knower of all phenomena or even an unskilled man;
whether he be a most excellent righteous person or even the worst of evildoers; whether he be a tiger among men or one who bears impotence—a man must endure great suffering while serving him.
"Even one who merely desires to know transcends the ocean of old age and death, and goes beyond the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*).
Thus it is said in the *Bhagavadgītā*: "The yogi, with a restrained mind, thus constantly yoking the self, attains the peace that culminates in *nirvāṇa*."
"One attains that state which resides within me," and so forth, as stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa*. "From yoga arises knowledge; yoga is one-pointedness of mind upon Me.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "Liberation comes through self-knowledge, and that [knowledge] does not exist without yoga. He...

And yoga is perfected only through practice over a long period of time. From the Kūrma Purāṇa, the words of Śiva: "Henceforth I shall explain yoga, which is exceedingly difficult to attain, by means of which they behold the Self as the Lord, like the radiant sun; the fire of yoga consumes [all impurities]."

The entire cage of evil quickly perishes; clear knowledge arises, and from knowledge one attains nirvāṇa. As stated in the *Garuḍapurāṇa*: "A wise person should strive in such a way that supreme liberation may be attained; for that [liberation] is obtained through yoga, and not otherwise."

And by no other means; for those scorched by the heat of worldly existence, yoga is indeed the supreme medicine. He whose intellect is intent upon the higher and the lower and is free from despondency, and who has burnt away the entire accumulation of afflictions with the fire of yoga, attains the supreme, eternal Nirvana.

He certainly attains it, there is no doubt. But he who has attained the perfection of yoga through the vision of the Self is complete; no further task remains for him, as everything has been accomplished by him alone. Delighting always in the Self, he is full and has reached ultimate bliss.

Therefore, even for that [state] which consists of supreme bliss, there is detachment. Yogis whose selves are purified by austerity and whose senses are restrained—those great-souled ones—cross over the great ocean by means of yoga alone. As stated in the *Viṣṇudharma*: "That which is the highest good for all beings..."

"It is beneficial even for women, and even for insects and moths; tell us that which is our supreme good. Thus addressed by the gods and celestial sages in the past, Kapila previously declared that Yoga alone is their supreme good. [As stated] in the Vāsiṣṭha regarding Duḥsaha.
O Rāma, the cholera-like affliction caused by the force of the poison of saṃsāra is pacified by the purifying Gāruḍa mantra of Yoga. Now,
it may be argued that even through sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), there arises immediate valid cognition (aparokṣapramāṇa).
Why should effort be exerted in yoga, which involves such extreme hardship?
Nor should it be argued that there is no evidence for the directness (*aparokṣatva*) of the knowledge produced by the [Vedic] sentence.

The knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is immediate (*aparokṣa*), because its object is immediate, just like the direct perception of a jar through the eyes; this is because such an inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor [is there a problem] regarding the immediacy residing in the object...

It should not be said that the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because of its formlessness; for that [reason], in the form of either being the consciousness whose object is ignorance or having attained identity with it, is easily established. Just as, for example, in the case of a jar and so forth...
When the internal organ undergoes a modification through contact with the eye,
ignorance regarding the consciousness that is its substrate is removed, and thus that consciousness ceases to be an object of ignorance.

In that case, the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) of the pot consists in its having attained identity with the consciousness that is the object of ignorance; likewise, when the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) gives rise to an internal mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) in the form of pure consciousness, [the same applies] to that ignorance.

Since reality (tattva) is the object of ignorance precisely because it is [by nature] ceased, consciousness possesses immediacy; thus, there is no lack of proof for the reason (*hetu*). Nor is the reason inconclusive (*aprayojakatva*), because immediacy consists in being accessible through knowledge.

This is because [the distinction between direct and indirect perception] is determined by having an object that is either immediate (*pratyakṣa*) or mediate (*parokṣa*). It is not, however, "being produced by a sense organ" (*indriyajanyatva*), because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of pleasure and so forth, since the mind (*manas*) lacks the status of being a sense organ.
Alternatively, it is "appearing as non-different from manifested consciousness."
The immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) and manifestation (*abhivyaktatva*) of the object consist in the removal of the veil of concealment (*āvaraṇa*).
In cases of indirect mental modification (*parokṣavṛtti*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the veil has not been removed.
However, for one who possesses a defect (*doṣa*) that causes the error of mistaking a rope for a snake, [the cognition] "this is not a snake, but a rope" [arises].

Since the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by a sentence does not remove the veil [of ignorance], its object in that case remains merely indirect (*parokṣa*). However, the knowledge generated by Vedāntic sentences is indeed immediate (*aparokṣa*), because it removes the veil; this is the case for that [knowledge] resulting from reflection (*manana*) and so forth.
It has arisen previously;

for it is only that [knowledge] which is qualified by the general absence of defects such as the impossibility of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that can remove ignorance. Furthermore, "Him, who is described in the Upaniṣads... (*taṃ tvaupaniṣadam*).

If it is argued that the statement "I ask about the Person" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 14.6.7.27)— which establishes that [Brahman] is accessible through the Upaniṣads alone— is consistent with its being accessible through yoga,
and therefore immediate realization arises from sentences such as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) alone, we say no.
Because inference is not the determining factor; and because, with respect to perception,
the aforementioned generality of the sense organ (*akṣa-sāmānya*) is the cause by virtue of being a sense organ (*indriyatva*),

it is precisely the state of being produced by that which is the determining factor for [the definition of] perception, whereas for the status of being a perception common to both the eternal and the non-eternal, however—

In that view, however, there would be no causal agency whatsoever; rather, for a specific instance of perception, the sense organ (*indriya*) would be the cause, and for a specific instance of that [perception], a specific sound would be the cause—thus there would be two distinct cause-and-effect relationships. Furthermore, the mind (*manas*) is not non-sensory.

Since there is no subverting evidence against its being a sense organ, the statement "the mind is the lord of the senses" merely expresses a certain degree of excellence within the senses themselves— just as one might say, with respect to humans, "he is the king of men"— and does not imply that it is a non-sense-organ or that such a status is its true nature.

It is simply a specific limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the sixfold parts. For this very reason, it is evident that the organs of action, such as the anus and so forth, and the organs of cognition, such as the mind and the eyes,
are "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) when they are sensory (*aindriyaka*), and "imperceptible" (*atīndriya*) when they are beyond the senses.

By stating that knowledge which lacks a sense organ as its instrument is not perceptual even within the treasury of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the fact that the mind is the indicator of the status of being a sense organ is established. The statement from the *Gītā*, "The senses are eleven, including the mind," is the authority for the mind's status as a sense organ. Furthermore:

The knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) is verbal (śābda), because it is produced by words, just like the knowledge produced by sentences such as "One should sacrifice" (yajeta). This argument constitutes a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa) against the proof of its being immediate (aparokṣa), as it establishes its status as verbal. Nor is this [reason] inconclusive (aprayojaka).
Because sound is the producer of verbal cognition itself, there is a supporting argument based on parsimony (*lāghava*);
however, in your view, since you accept that perception arises even from sound, [the argument lacks parsimony].

There is complexity in postulating two distinct relations of cause and effect. Moreover, [the knowledge] has already arisen prior to reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*); for in your view, even that which is non-perceptual (*aparokṣa*) does not remove ignorance. Therefore, with respect to the removal of ignorance, it must function solely as a subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*).
The claim that [the Self] is the cause [of knowledge] involves complexity; for me, however,

when the Self is perceived by the internal organ— which has been purified of all impurities such as doubt through the ripening of the practice of *samādhi*— ignorance ceases upon that very perception alone.
There is some room for reverence: This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
yet it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect. The wise man should restrain speech and mind.

Beginning with these words and ending with "he is released from the mouth of death," which signifies the cessation of ignorance, this very meaning is accepted through the instruction on Death found in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad; thus, there is no dispute whatsoever on this point. This being so, if knowledge has already arisen prior to reflection (*manana*) and the other stages...
The view that [the means of knowledge] are indeed indirect, and thus do not carry the weight of being directly connected [to the result], is respected;
yet even that [view] holds that once the purification of the mind through hearing and so forth is accomplished, the vision of the Self is possible immediately thereafter. Following that—

Indeed, the postulation of [the necessity for] recollection of sentences and so forth would result in great conceptual complexity. Now, we do not assert that knowledge produced by words is immediate through mere reasoning alone;
rather, we do so on the basis of scripture as well. For instance: "I ask you about that person known from the Upaniṣads."
Furthermore, the status of being "known through the Upaniṣads" (*aupaniṣadatva*) does not consist merely in being the object of a cognition produced by the Upaniṣads;
for if it were so, the term would inappropriately apply even to things accessible through perception and other means. As it has been said:

Just as when there are eight potsherds within a *dvādaśakapāla* (twelve-potsherd) offering, the designation "eight-potsherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth is applied based on what has been prepared with twelve potsherds— just as one might refer to someone with two sons as "one who has one son"— so too it is here, and not otherwise.

Regarding the term "vyavahāra" (conventional usage): the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is precisely that [Brahman] is cognizable through the Upaniṣads alone. If it is argued that this is untenable given that [Brahman] is also cognizable by the mind, we say no; for the suffix does not exclude everything other than the Upaniṣads as a cause [of its cognition]. This is the view of the proponent of the direct perception of the Word (*śabdāparokṣavādin*).
For you also accept that the mind and other faculties serve as instruments (*karaṇa*) in the investigation of the self.

However, since there is a traditional injunction (*smaraṇa*) stating, "One should hear [the meaning] from the words of the Purāṇas and so forth, which are themselves based on the Vedic statements," and since that very purpose is also approved by me, this objection amounts to nothing.

Furthermore, the assumption that the intention [of the speaker] lies in the exclusion of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara) is only appropriate to state once it has already been established that verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition regarding objects not perceptible to oneself. However, as for the intention to exclude other words...

Since this is in accordance with the Śruti and other authorities, it is indeed proper to postulate [this]. This being the case, scriptural passages such as "It is to be seen by the mind alone" and "This is to be attained by the mind alone" are also established in their primary sense.

[Such things] would be possible. As for what has been stated by some—that scriptural passages concerning the dependence of the mind alone upon the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the functioning of perception are not contradictory—that is utterly incapable of withstanding scrutiny; for when there is a requirement for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the scripture must provide it].

How could those [mental states], having come into existence, be sublated by the grasping [of another]? For, through the scriptural passage beginning with "Desire, resolve, doubt... which is definitive in its restriction, it is made known that all mental modifications have the mind alone as their material cause (*upādāna*).

How could they be described as having the purport of being the material cause in the absence of such a desire? [This addresses] the doubt that since the *praṇava* was previously stated in the second chapter to be the indicator of Brahman, it too must be a cause for direct realization (*aparokṣa*).
138) It can be explained that statements such as "it should be perceived by the mind alone" are indeed intended to be definitive (sāvadhāraṇa).

Enough with this web of excessive talk. In reality, however, the knowledge of objects situated at a great distance during the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of yogins is well-established in all the scriptures and is not indirect (*parokṣa*), because at that time the causal conditions for indirect perception are absent. Nor is it memory.

This is because they have not previously experienced anything superior; nor is it of the nature of a witness (*sākṣin*), like the cognition of pleasure and so forth, for that would entail an undesirable conclusion (*apasiddhānta*);
nor is it without a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), since there is a necessary rule regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*) for all types of valid knowledge (*pramā*). Nor...

Since that [knowledge] is produced by the eyes and other [senses] despite their lack of contact [with the object], it must be declared to be merely mental valid cognition (*mānasikī pramaiva*); thus, the status of the mind as both a sense organ (*indriyatva*) and a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) is utterly beyond denial.
This also applies to those who postulate a synthesis (*samuccaya*) of Yoga and Śruti.
The multitude of previously mentioned objections remains exactly as it was.

Therefore, it is established that the Self is accessible solely to the mind, aided by the impressions produced by yoga. Nor is it like the direct perception of a distant beloved woman by one who is meditating upon her.
There would be the undesirable consequence that the direct realization of the self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*), being produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), is not valid knowledge;
for its object is uncontradicted and it is not produced by any defect.
However, as for the direct realization of a beloved woman (*kāminīsākṣātkāra*)...
Invalidity does not arise from the sublation of the object nor from being produced by a defect,

because it is produced by *bhāvanā*. Nor does the fact that the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of *bhāvanā* serves as a means of cognition entail the introduction of another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for such is its nature.
Because it functions in conjunction with the mind (*manas*), even the Naiyāyikas and others— who are experts in defining the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—
have included yogic perception within "extraordinary perception" (*alaukika-pratyakṣa*). Through the extraordinary contact (*alaukika-sannikarṣa*) produced by yoga, the yogis...
They perceive even their own self, as well as objects that are obstructed, distant, or subtle, exactly as they are.
And so it is stated in the Pātañjala Sūtra: "In that state, wisdom is truth-bearing;
it has a different object than the wisdom derived from scripture or inference, because its object is the specific [nature of things]."

Regarding the wisdom (prajñā) within meditative concentration (samādhi), its objects are made distinct from those of the wisdom consisting of what has been heard— namely, hearing and verbal comprehension—
and from the wisdom consisting of inference— namely, logical reasoning and inferential knowledge.
Because it has a specific object as its referent. That which has a specific, non-conceptual object as its domain is "such" (*tathā*);
the state of being such is "suchness" (*tathātva*).
Therefore, for inference, [the object] is only by way of the delimitor of the word's non-referentiality.

The meaning is that, because there is a rule that a cognition is produced only by way of presenting the delimiting property of the pervader (*vyāpakatvāvacchedaka*), when that [pervader] is grasped, it refers only to the fit substrate (*yogyaviśeṣya*). On this point, there is the commentary composed by Bādarāyaṇa:
"The scriptural knowledge (*āgamavijñāna*) that has been heard has that [universal] as its object; for [the universal] is not [grasped] by means of scripture..."

It may be asked: why is it not possible to state a specific distinction, since a word has no convention established for a specific [object]? Starting from this point, [the answer is: the specific distinction is indeed to be grasped by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), whether it pertains to the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) or to the Person (*puruṣa*). As stated in the *Yogabīja*: "One who is established in knowledge..."

O beloved, even one who is dispassionate, knows the Dharma, and has conquered the senses does not attain liberation without Yoga, even if he be a god; for it is stated in the Śruti: "Furthermore, that very body (liṅga) [escapes] along with his karma, wherein his mind is infused," and "The cause of this is attachment to the qualities."
And because of the traditional teaching (smṛti), "In births from wombs that are good or bad," at the time of the body's end,
the individual soul (jīva) enters precisely that womb in which passion and other such tendencies have been awakened; thus,
for one devoid of yoga, there will certainly be another birth at the moment of death.

Because that which has arisen as a state of agitation cannot be warded off by one who is not a yogi. As it is said in the *Yogabīja*: "At the time of the body's end, whatever one contemplates in the mind, that very thing becomes the living soul; such is the cause of birth."

(139) Human beings do not know what birth will occur at the end of the body; therefore, knowledge, dispassion, and even recitation [of mantras] are merely labor. When an ant has attached itself to the body...

One is liberated through knowledge; how could one who is bitten by scorpions be happy at the end of the body? But for yogis, even at the time of death, liberation occurs indeed through the power of yoga and the contemplation of the Self, so that there would be no further birth. This was stated by the Blessed One regarding the time of departure: [at the time of death...]

This is established by such passages as "With a steady mind, endowed with devotion and the power of yoga," and so forth, as well as by the Śruti text, "There are one hundred and one channels of the heart," and so on. Furthermore, if the sentence "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) were to generate immediate, direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), then [the inquiry into it]— [The text continues: ...would be rendered useless. Therefore, the sentence "That thou art" generates indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). Subsequently, through the practice of meditation (*nididhyāsana*) upon that very object, direct knowledge arises. Thus, the inquiry into Brahman is indeed purposeful. Hence, the Vedānta is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The opponent objects: Even if the Vedānta is a valid means of knowledge, it cannot be an independent means of knowledge (*svatantra-pramāṇa*). Why? Because it depends upon another means of knowledge. That is to say, the Vedānta depends upon perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge for the cognition of the existence of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the relationship between words and their meanings (*śabdārthasaṃbandha*). Therefore, like inference (*anumāna*), the Vedānta is not an independent means of knowledge. To this we reply: This objection is not sound. For the cognition of the existence of the subject and the relationship between words and their meanings can be obtained from the Vedānta itself. Moreover, the Vedānta does not depend upon perception and other means of knowledge for the cognition of the relationship between words and their meanings. Why? Because the relationship between words and their meanings is established through the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). And that usage is understood through the Vedānta alone. Therefore, the Vedānta is indeed an independent means of knowledge. Furthermore, the Vedānta is an independent means of knowledge because it is a verbal testimony (*śabda*) whose object is something not previously known (*apūrvārtha*). It is not dependent on other means of knowledge, since its object is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is not accessible to perception or other means of knowledge. Therefore, the Vedānta is an independent means of knowledge. Thus, the inquiry into Brahman must necessarily be undertaken. This is the meaning of the first aphorism. *Note: The text provided appears to be an excerpt from the *Vedānta-paribhāṣā* or a similar commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*. The translation reflects the technical philosophical discourse typical of these works.*
It cannot be said that [this teaching] is useless, because the knowledge produced by the investigation of the scriptures is a means to direct realization through the gateway of yoga.
Regarding this, there is a great dialogue between Gaurī and Īśvara in the *Yogabīja*; therefore, a portion of it is written here.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, ocean of the nectar of compassion, tell me: what kind of destination awaits those who are indeed wise when they die?"
Īśvara said:
At the end of the body, the knower obtains the fruit of his merit and his sin;
having experienced whatever that may be, the knower is born again, and subsequently attains [liberation] through merit.
Through association with a Siddha, and then by the grace of that Siddha, one becomes a yogi;
it is not otherwise. Thereupon, saṃsāra is destroyed; it is not otherwise—this is the word of Śiva.
The Goddess said:
For the wise always declare that liberation comes from knowledge alone;
how then could yoga, through the perfection of yoga, not be the giver of liberation?
The Lord said:

For liberation comes through knowledge alone; their word is not otherwise. Everyone says that victory is achieved by means of a sword, but what then? How can one attain victory without battle and valor? Likewise, knowledge devoid of yoga does not lead to liberation.

It might be argued: "But since it is heard that Janaka and others attained unimpeded knowledge and liberation even without yoga, how can it be said that unimpeded knowledge and liberation result from yoga alone? To this it is replied: [This applies] to them...

It is heard in the Purāṇas and other texts that the attainment of knowledge results from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by yoga practiced in previous births. For instance: "Just as the brahmin Jaigīṣavya, and likewise Asita and others; the kṣatriyas such as Janaka and others; and the vaiśyas such as Tulādhāra and others [attained it]."
Having attained supreme perfection through their own previously practiced yoga—
such as the seven *śūdra*s including Dharmavyādha and Pailavaka, and the female ascetics Maitreyī,
Sulabhā, Śārṅgī, and Śāṇḍilī— these and many others [have done so].
"Even those born in low wombs have attained the supreme state of being established in knowledge through their own yoga practiced in previous lives. Furthermore,
according to the degree of merit resulting from the practice of yoga performed in former births, some attain the state of Brahman.

Some have attained the status of sons of Brahmā, some the status of celestial sages (devarṣi), some the status of brahminical sages (brahmarṣi), some the status of silent seers (muni), and others the status of devotees (bhakta).
Among them, there are those who have realized the Self even without formal instruction. For instance:

It is heard in the Purāṇas and other texts that Hiraṇyagarbha, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, Sanatkumāra, Vāmadeva, Śuka, and others were "perfected by birth" (*janmasiddha*). As for the statement found in the Purāṇas and elsewhere that only a Brāhmaṇa is qualified for liberation (*mokṣādhikārī*), that refers to those who are not yet yogis. Thus it has been said:
In the *Garuḍapurāṇa*: "For those men who have no practice of yoga from a previous birth, [the following is prescribed] for the attainment of yoga...

Having understood the true division of the Suṣumṇā and having brought the vital air into the center, one should remain always in the excellent place and restrain it within the Brahma-randhra.
The sun and the moon sustain time, which consists of night and day; Suṣumnā is the enjoyer of that time—this is declared as a secret. || 17 ||
Commentary:
The sequence for Śūdras, Vaiśyas, and the others is as follows: due to her female nature, she attains the state of a Śūdra;
from there, she would attain the state of a Vaiśya; then she becomes a Kṣatriya, and thereafter a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of compassion;
then he is remembered as an Anūcāna (one learned in the Vedas), then a Yajvā (performer of sacrifices), and after that, one who has renounced action (Karmanyāsī). Then...
"The yogin attains the state of a knower and shall obtain liberation in due course"—

the meaning is that by becoming a yogin through the sequence beginning with Śūdras and Vaiśyas, one obtains liberation. And thus, because the scriptures declare that all have the qualification for yoga, through the knowledge of reality produced by yoga, everyone [attains the goal].

Thus it is established that they are liberated. However, even for a fallen yogin, there is no sequence [of rebirth] such as being born as a Śūdra and so forth; rather, "the one fallen from yoga is born in the house of the pure and the prosperous," or else, "among the very yogins," and so on.
Enough with this [objection] based on the words of the Blessed One. || 15 ||

It has been stated that liberation is not accomplished without the dissolution of both the vital breath (prāṇa) and the mind (manas). In that regard, since the dissolution of the mind is also accomplished through the dissolution of the vital breath, he now describes the method for that dissolution.

"Having known this": always, that is, at all times, having stayed—that is, having established one's residence—in a good place, meaning in a beautiful location, a well-governed kingdom, a righteous country, and so forth, as previously described; [one should practice] the "excellent piercing" (*sadbheda*) of the *suṣumnā*, which is the central channel.

Having understood the method of piercing and having learned it from the mouth of the Guru, one should cause the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to move through the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*), and then restrain it completely within the *brahmaraṃdhra*, the space at the crown of the head. Of the vital breath...
When the cessation and dissolution [of the breath] occurs at the *brahmarandhra*, and once the dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has taken place, the mind also dissolves.
As it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "When the movement of the vital breaths comes to an end through practice, the mind attains tranquility, and liberation (*nirvāṇa*) remains."

When there is the dissolution of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the mind (manas), through the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) assisted by samādhi in the form of a specific contemplation, the direct realization of the Self occurs as something uncontradicted; at that time, the person becomes liberated even while living. || 16 ||
He states that the conquest of time occurs during the dissolution of the vital breaths: "The sun and the moon... and so forth.
The Sun and the Moon are the two Sūryās. (p. 141) || Root Text ||
There are seventy-two thousand channel-entrances within the cage; Suṣumnā is the Śāmbhavī power, while the rest are indeed useless.
|| Commentary ||

*Caṃdramasau*: the suffix *ānaṅ* is applied according to the rule *devatādvaṃdve ca*. *Rātriśca divā ca rātriṃdivam*: this is an irregular formation (*nipātita*) according to the rule beginning with *acatura-*. That whose nature (*ātmā*) or essence (*svarūpam*) is night and day is "having night and day as its nature" (*rātriṃdivātmaka*); [he meditated upon] that time which has night and day as its nature.

They maintain and ordain the *samaya*. Suṣumnā is Sarasvatī; she is the consumer, the devourer, and the destroyer of the *samaya* consisting of day and night, which is produced by Time—the Sun and the Moon. This secret mystery has been declared.

It has been stated: this is the meaning. The sun flows for two and a half ghaṭikās, and the moon flows for two and a half ghaṭikās. When the sun flows, it is called day; when the moon flows, it is called night.
Within five ghaṭikās, there occurs a period consisting of night and day.
Within one worldly day and night (laukikāhorātra), there occurs the temporal convention of yogins consisting of twelve days and nights. By such a measure of time—

There is a measure of life for living beings. When the vital air (vāyu) becomes dissolved in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by way of the Suṣumṇā channel, then, due to the absence of time consisting of night and day, it is said that "the Suṣumṇā is the devourer of time."
As long as the vital air (vāyu) remains dissolved in the aperture of Brahma (brahmaraṃdhra), for that long the life-span of the yogi increases.
A yogi who has practiced samādhi for a long time, having known the time of death beforehand,
leads the vital air into the aperture of Brahma and wards off death according to his own will.
And he effects the abandonment of the body. || 17 ||
"Seventy-two" means: in the cage—that is, in the body bound together by the bones of the cage—there are seventy-two plus two [bones]. (p.

Since the vital air (vāyu) is well-acquainted with the Kuṇḍalinī, it awakens her and enters the Suṣumṇā without obstruction along with the fire. || 19 ||
When the vital breath flows through the Suṣumṇā, the state of Manonmanī is indeed accomplished; otherwise, other practices lead only to exhaustion for yogins. (20)
Commentary:
There are seventy-two thousand channels, veins, or gateways for the entry of the vital breath; among them, the Suṣumnā is the central channel, known as Śāmbhavī.

"Śambhu" is the Lord (Īśvara) because from him "śam"—meaning bliss—arises for his devotees; "Śāmbhavī" is that which belongs to him. It is called Śāmbhavī because it brings about the attainment of Śambhu through meditation, or because it generates the manifestation of Śambhu.
Alternatively, *śambhu* is the Self (*ātman*) who exists as bliss (*śam*), being of the nature of happiness;
this [power] is *śāmbhavī* because it is the locus for the manifestation of that consciousness and because, through meditation, it is the cause for the direct realization of the Self.
The remaining channels, such as Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and so forth, are indeed useless (*nirarthakāḥ*), meaning they are devoid of purpose (*nirgato 'rthaḥ*) because they lack the aforementioned utility.

Regarding the word "wind" (*vāyu*): since the wind has been mastered and practiced, therefore by means of that [wind], the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*)— [Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.]
Having awakened the power (śakti) together with the coiled one (kuṇḍalinī), one should enter the Sarasvatī within the Suṣumnā without obstruction—that is, without impediment;
the meaning is that practice must be performed for the sake of the vital air (vāyu) entering the Suṣumnā. || 19 ||

Regarding the term *suṣumnā*: when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows through the *suṣumnā*, the state of *unmanī*—the state beyond mind—is indeed accomplished. Otherwise, if the vital breath does not flow through the *suṣumnā*, then other practices—the practices of others than the *suṣumnā*—are for yogins who practice yoga.
The meaning is that they result only in exertion and only in fatigue. || 20 ||

By that which the breath is bound, by that very thing the mind is bound; and by that which the mind is bound, by that the breath is bound. 21.
The two causes of the mind are latent impressions (vāsanā) and the vital breath (samīraṇa). When one of these two is destroyed, both of them perish. || 22 ||
Commentary:

Regarding the term *pavana*: by whichever yogi the *pavana*—the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*)—is bound, that is, rendered restrained, by that very same yogi the mind (*manas*) is bound. By whomsoever the mind is bound, by him the *pavana* is bound. When either one of the two—the mind or the *pavana*—is bound, both are bound.
The meaning is that it comes to be. || 21 ||

"But there are two causes for the mind. Regarding the activity of the mind, there are two causes, two reasons; what are they? He says: latent impression (*vāsanā*), which is a formative tendency (*saṃskāra*) known as mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and the impeller, the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*).

When one of these two—the latent impression (*vāsanā*) and the vital breath (*samīraṇa*)—is destroyed or exhausted, both of them perish. This is the intended meaning: when the latent impression is exhausted, the vital breath and the mind (*citta*) become exhausted; when the vital breath is exhausted, the mind and the latent impression become exhausted; and when the mind [is exhausted]...
When the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the vital breath (*samīraṇa*) are exhausted, both [the body and the mind] become exhausted. As it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
"O Rāma, there are two seeds of the mind: the vibration of the vital breath and the latent impressions.
When one of these two is destroyed, both are quickly destroyed. In that same work, it is stated by way of contrast:

As long as the mind has not dissolved, there is no destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). As long as the latent impressions have not been destroyed, the mind does not become stilled. As long as discernment (*vijñāna*) does not arise, there is no cessation of mental doubt. As long as there is no tranquility of the mind, there is no realization of reality.

As long as there is no destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how can there be the attainment of reality (*tattva*)? As long as there is no attainment of reality, there is no destruction of latent impressions. Knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions—having become mutually dependent causes for one another—are difficult to accomplish.
Therefore, as long as these three are not practiced equally and repeatedly, the attainment of reality does not occur, even for those who have taken refuge [in them]. (22)

Where the mind dissolves, there the vital air dissolves; where the vital air dissolves, there the mind dissolves. || 23 ||
For both the mind and the vital breath are merged like milk and water, performing identical functions.
Wherever there is the activity of the mind, there is the activity of the vital air (marut); wherever there is the mind, there is the activity of the vital air.
In that regard, from the destruction of one follows the destruction of the other; from the activity of one follows the activity of the other.
When the two paths are unimpaired, there is the functioning of the group of senses; when they are destroyed, there is the attainment of the state of liberation.
(Commentary)
Regarding the word "mana" (mind): the syntactical connection is that in whichever substratum the mind dissolves, in that very same substratum the vital air (pavana) also dissolves. || 23 ||

Regarding the phrase "like milk and water": like milk and water (*kṣīranīra*), those two—the mind and the vital breath (*mānasamārutau*)—are thoroughly blended (*saṃmilitau*). Both the mind and the vital breath (*cittaprāṇau*) possess identical functions; that is, their activity (*kriyā*) is equal and the same.
They are such that their activity proceeds in the same manner. He states this very equality of action with the word "yataḥ" (wherefrom).

The suffix *tasi* here functions as all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). In which wheel the wind (*marut*) moves, there—in that very wheel—there is the activity of the mind (*manaḥpravṛtti*), [the activity] of the mind.

Activity occurs. The meaning is that in whichever wheel the mind operates, in that very wheel there is the operation of *marut*—that is, the operation of the vital air (*vāyu*). As it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "The life-force (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*cetas*) are eternally inseparable for living beings."
"Like sesame oil mixed with the fragrance of flowers, they both, through their destruction, accomplish the supreme task known as liberation. (24)
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): therein, that is, between those two—the mind (*mānasa*) and the vital air (*māruta*)—due to the destruction of one, either the mind or the vital air.

The fickleness of both the *rasa* and the mind is inherent by nature; when the *rasa* is bound and the mind is bound, what on this earth cannot be accomplished? (26)
O Pārvatī, when swooned, mercury removes diseases; when dead, it restores life itself; and when bound, it bestows the power of moving through the sky, as does the vital air (vāyu).
Commentary:
When there is the destruction or dissolution of another— that is, of another wind or of the mind—
due to the activity or operation of one [wind or mind],
there occurs the activity of the other wind or mind.

Activity is operation. When the mind and the vital breath are neither destroyed nor dissolved, the activity of the group of senses—that is, the functioning of the collection of sense organs—occurs toward their respective objects. When those two are destroyed and dissolved, there is the state of liberation.

The accomplishment, that is, the realization, of the state called liberation occurs; the meaning is that this happens because, upon the dissolution of those two, the person (puruṣa) abides in its own essential nature. Even there, the destruction of the vital breath (pavana) is to be achieved through the practice of the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) and so forth, whereas the destruction of the mind (manas) is [achieved] through the Guru.
Through grace, it is indeed easily accomplished in the mere twinkling of an eye. This is the subsequent verse to the root verse in the *Yogabīja*. || 25 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the *rasa*": mercury (*rasa*), which is *pārada*, possesses instability (*cañcalatva*) by its very nature (*bhāvataḥ*), just as the mind (*manas*) or the mental faculty (*mānasa*) does. If the mercury (*rasa*) is bound, then the mind (*citta*) becomes bound. Therefore, upon the surface of the earth (*bhūtala*).
What is not accomplished? Everything is accomplished; this is the meaning. || 26 ||
He says that very thing: "Mūrchita" (fainted/stiffened). By means of the application of a specific medicinal herb, the mercury whose restlessness has departed is called *mūrchita*;
or, the breath (*vāyu*) which has ceased its exhalation at the end of the *kumbhaka* [retention] is called *mūrchita*.
"O Pārvatī"—this is the Lord’s speech for the easy understanding of Pārvatī; [it refers to] the mercury that has become *mūrchita*.
The *pārada* (mercury) is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the pervasive wind (*vyāna*); it removes—that is, destroys—diseases and ailments.

When the mercury has been reduced to ashes and merged into the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), and the wind itself has become "dead" by its own power—that is, through its own inherent capacity—it brings back to life, meaning it effects a long-lasting existence.

The mercury, rendered into the form of a pill through a specific ritual process, and the vital air (vāyu), held by means of a specific meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) at the center of the eyebrows and other locations, become "bound" (baddha); this means they bestow, maintain, or effect the state of a sky-walker (khecaratā), that is, movement through the sky.

When the mind is steady, the vital air becomes steady; from that, the bindu becomes steady.
From the steadiness of the bindu, the steadiness of the piṇḍa always arises.

The mind is the lord of the senses, but the vital breath (māruta) is the lord of the mind; the dissolution of the vital breath is its lord, and that dissolution is dependent upon sound (nāda). || 29 ||
Let this very state be what is called liberation, or let it not be so according to other schools of thought; nevertheless, some kind of bliss arises when the mind and the vital breath dissolve. (30)
Commentary:

This has been stated in the *Gorakṣakaśataka*: "That which is situated between the two eyebrows, resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, consists of the element of air (vāyu) and is accompanied by the letter Pa; the presiding deity there is Īśvara.
Having dissolved the vital breath (prāṇa) there for five ghaṭikās, together with the mind..."

If one should hold [the breath], it enables movement through the sky for the self-restrained; this is known as "dhāraṇā by means of the wind" and results in stability of mind. When there is stability of mind, the vital wind (prāṇa) becomes stable.
Then, from the stability of the wind, the drop (bindu), which is the semen (vīrya), becomes stable. From the [stability] of the drop...
From constant steadiness at all times, essence and strength arise; from the steadiness of the physical mass, the steadiness of the body is produced. || 28 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the senses": the mind (*manas*), which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is the lord (*nātha*)—that is, the activator—of the senses, such as hearing and the rest. The lord of the mind is the vital air (*māruta*), namely *prāṇa*. The dissolution of the vital air (*prāṇa*), which is the dissolution of the mind (*manovilaya*), is its lord.
That dissolution is the dissolution of the mind; it means that the mind, having resorted to the sound (nāda), becomes dissolved in the sound. || 29 ||
"This is that" means: this very dissolution of the mind (*cittalaya*) is what is called liberation (*mokṣa*), denoted by the term "liberation.

Whether it be accepted in another system (*matāntare*) or not—since the dissolution of the mind exists even in deep sleep (*suṣupti*)—when there is the dissolution of both the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there arises something indescribable (*anirvācya*).
p. 147) || Root Text ||

Victorious is the absorption (laya) of yogis, in which inhalation and exhalation have ceased, the perception of sense objects has been destroyed, and one is motionless and free from all modification. || 31 ||
With all volitions severed and all activities entirely ceased, a certain dissolution arises that is self-realizable and beyond the reach of words. || 32 ||
Commentary:
Bliss arises and becomes perfectly established;
the sense is that when ineffable bliss manifests, the happiness of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) truly comes to be.

"Pranaṣṭa" means: that in which inhalation (*śvāsa*) and exhalation (*niśvāsa*)—the pair of inhalation and exhalation—are lost or dissolved. Inhalation is the entry of external air into the interior; [exhalation is] of that which is situated within.

The outward emission of breath is the exhalation (*niśvāsa*). It is "completely destroyed" (*pradhvasta*), meaning utterly ruined or lost. In this state, there is no grasping or perception of sense objects such as sound and the like; movement, which is bodily activity, has ceased; and modification, which is the activity of the internal organs, has departed.

Such absorption (laya) of the mental modifications (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) of yogis— consisting of a modification in the form of the object of meditation— is victorious, meaning it exists with supreme excellence. || 31 ||

"Ucchinna" means: that in which all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*), which are transformations of the mind, have been cut off and destroyed; that from which no remainder has emerged; that in which all activities (*ceṣṭita*) are entirely and completely absent; and that which can be realized and known by oneself alone.
A certain extraordinary state of absorption (laya), which is self-realized, beyond the range of words, and unique in its nature, arises for yogis. || 32 ||
p. 148) || Root Text ||
Wherever there is vision, there is the dissolution of the elements and the senses;
that is the power of living beings when both have gone to dissolution in the Unperceivable.
They say, "laya, laya"—what is the defining characteristic of *laya*?
Absorption (laya) is the forgetting of sense objects due to the non-arising of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 34 ||
The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are like common courtesans; the single Mudrā of Śambhu alone is like a guarded lady of noble family.
|| Commentary ||

"Wherein the vision": wherein, in which object—that is, in Brahman—the vision, which is a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti), there alone does dissolution occur. The elements (bhūtāni) such as earth and so forth, the senses (indriyāṇi) such as hearing and so forth, and the eternal (sanātanāni)—that is, the perpetual—[all dissolve there].
In that [state], according to the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the entire collection of effects exists within ignorance (*avidyā*).

The power of living beings—that is, sentient creatures—which is knowledge (*vidyā*), these two dissolve into the unmanifest Brahman; the word "of the yogins" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 33 ||

Regarding the word *laya*: many say "it is *laya*"; they speak thus. Having raised the question, "What is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of *laya*, and what is its essential nature (*svarūpa*)?", he explains the essential nature of *laya*.
"Apunar" [means] "not again."

Because there is no further arising of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and because there is no locus for the persistence of further impressions, there is a forgetting of objects—that is, a forgetting of objects such as sound and so forth, or of the object in the form of the meditative focus;
this "laying down" (*laya*) is the meaning of the term *laya*. This is the sense. || 34 ||

She experiences [them]. The four Vedas, the six Śāstras, and the eighteen Purāṇas are like common courtesans or prostitutes, because they are accessible to many men. Only the single Śāmbhavī Mudrā is like a woman of good family or a noble wife, for she is well-guarded.
Because it is accessible only to a distinguished person. || 35 ||
p. 149) || Root Text ||
The inner focus with the gaze directed outward, free from blinking or opening—the Śāmbhavī Mudrā is this, hidden within the Vedas and the scriptures. || 36 ||
When the yogi abides with his mind and breath dissolved within the internal mark (antarlakṣya),
looking outward below with a steady gaze and yet seeing nothing— even while not seeing— this indeed is the Śāmbhavī Mudrā; it is truly attained through the grace of the Guru.
That supreme Śāmbhava reality, which is characterized by being neither empty nor non-empty, vibrates forth.
Commentary:

Desiring to explain the *mudrā* that serves as the means for the dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the mind (*citta*), he speaks therein of the *śāmbhavī-mudrā*: "The internal object" (*antarlakṣyam*). This means:
within—that is, among the wheels (*cakras*) beginning with the *ādhāra* and ending with the *brahmarandhra*—in whichever wheel one prefers.

The object of perception is the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*). "Vision" refers to the connection with the eyes in the region outside the body. What kind of vision? It is "devoid of winking and opening," where *nimeṣa* is the closing of the eyelids and *unmeṣa* is the opening of the eyelids.

Free from those two, devoid of them, the gaze becomes one that is free from the closing and opening of the eyes during the mind's absorption in the form of the object of meditation. This is said to be the Śāmbhavī Mudrā;
it belongs to Śambhu, thus it is Śāmbhavī; it is dear to Śiva, or rather, it generates devotion toward Śiva.

It exists. Of what nature is it? It is hidden—concealed and protected—in the Vedic scriptures, namely the Vedas such as the Ṛgveda and others, and in the philosophical treatises such as Sāṃkhya, Pātañjala, and so forth. || 36 ||

Having performed the Śāmbhavī Mudrā, he demonstrates it, saying: "The internal object of focus. This refers to that which is to be focused upon internally—in the unstruck lotus (*anāhata-padmam*) and so forth—such as the form of the Lord with attributes (*saguṇeśvara-mūrti*), or the reality signified by statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).
"I am Brahman," [realizing] the non-difference between the individual soul and the Lord.
(p. 150) || Root Text ||
And [the distinction] between Śrīśāmbhavī and Khecarī arises from the difference in their states and abodes.
In the void, there arises the bliss of the dissolution of the mind, which is of the nature of the happiness of consciousness. || 38 ||
Having joined the gaze upon the star Tārā, one should slightly raise the eyebrows.
Commentary:

That yogi exists in such a state, in whom the mind and breath— the mental faculty and the vital air— have become dissolved, specifically merged into that Brahman which constitutes the meaning of the Great Saying;
he gazes with a vision whose pupil is motionless and steady.

Even while seeing—that is, even while establishing a connection with the eyes—in the external region outside the body, he remains without seeing, not perceiving external objects; "khalu" is used as a rhetorical particle. This is the aforementioned Śāmbhavī Mudrā, so named after Śambhu.

It is called *mudrā* because it seals (*mudrayati*) the afflictions; if it has been obtained or attained through the grace and benevolent favor of the Guru, the instructor, then that which manifests within the *śāmbhavī-mudrā* is the *śāmbhava*, which is impossible to describe as "this" or "that."

The "foot" (*pada*) is that which is reached or attained by yogins; it is the nature of the self (*ātman*), distinct from both the void and the non-void. It is distinct from the void because of the existence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of the object of meditation, and [it is distinct from the non-void] because of that [modification] as well.

Due to the absence of mental activity (*bhāna*), the reality that is distinct from the non-empty—the actual, ontological entity—shines forth and is perceived. Thus it has been said: "The practitioner of restraint, seeing with joy and undistracted mind the internal mark, free from the opening and closing of the eyes—this is the *mudrā*."

This Śāmbhavī [mudrā] is secret; it has been concealed by Giriśa, the knower of Tantras, within the Tantras for those seekers of truth. For self-restrained practitioners, it brings about the dissolution of the mind and bestows liberation, yet it is difficult to attain.
With the gaze directed upward and the gaze directed downward, there is indeed the upward piercing with the head turned downward.
By means of the ritual procedure for the Rādhāyantra, one shall become liberated while living on this earth. || 2 || 37 ||
Regarding the phrase "of the venerable Śāmbhavī":
this refers to the venerable Śāmbhavī, that is, the Śāmbhavī-mudrā and the Khecarī-mudrā.

Due to the distinction between their states (*avasthā*) and abodes (*dhāman*)—where "state" means the manner of being established and "abode" means the location—the [qualities] belong to the Śāmbhavī.

With the gaze directed outward, the state is external; with the gaze fixed between the eyebrows, the state is in *khecarī*. In *śāmbhavī*, the locus is the contemplation of the heart; in *khecarī*, the locus is precisely the space between the eyebrows.

In that Self— which is devoid of duality between those two, devoid of the limitations of space, time, and substance, and devoid of internal distinctions as well as distinctions from similar and dissimilar things; which consists of the bliss of consciousness and whose very nature is the joy of consciousness— there shall arise the bliss of the dissolution of the mind.

The meaning is that there is a difference between the Śrīśāmbhavī and Khecarī [mudrās] regarding the aspects of their state (avasthā), abode (dhāma), form (rūpa), and means of practice (sādhana), but not regarding the aspect of the fruit, which consists of the bliss of the dissolution of the mind (cittalayānanda). || 38 ||
He describes the Unmanī-mudrā: "In the Tārā," etc. In the *tāre* [of the eyes], the two pupils are the two lights; in the *tāra* [of the nose], they are at the tip of the nose.
Root Text
Yoking the mind to the former yoga, he becomes one who transcends the mind (unmanī) in an instant.
Some are bewildered by the web of scriptures, some by the complexities of the Vedas, and some by logic;
they do not know the Savior at all.

With eyes half-closed, mind steady, and gaze fixed upon the tip of the nose, he who, through a state of motionlessness, brings even the moon and sun to dissolution, beholds the entire form of light— [The remainder of the verse: ...which is the supreme Brahman, free from all attributes, beyond the reach of speech and mind, and which is the very essence of the Self.]
|| Commentary ||
Having joined and united the light that shines at a distance of one *yojana*, and having slightly raised or directed the eyebrows upward,
[one practices] that yoga or method in which the previously mentioned internal focus with external vision is employed.

The yogi, by joining—that is, making steady—that very mind or internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), becomes in a moment or a short while a maker of the *unmanī* state, one who brings about the condition of *unmanī*. || 39 ||
He says that there is no other means of crossing [to liberation] than the state of *unmanī*: "Some... and so forth.

Some, who are experts in scriptures, tantras, and so forth— those scriptures, tantras, and the like are called *āgamas* because meanings (*arthāḥ*) ascend (*ārohanti*) to the intellect (*buddhim*) from them—
they become entangled in their "nets," that is, in the means of bondage which are like nets, and in the fruits described therein, and thus they fall into delusion.

They attain [these results]. The sense is that those who are attached to them become bound. Some Vaidikas are deluded by the profusion of fruits resulting from the "multitudes of the Nigamas"—that is, the multitudes of the Nigamas and what is taught in the Nigamas. Others, such as the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth, are deluded by logic (*tarka*).

They are deluded by their own imagined specific arguments; they do not know the *tāraka*—the means of crossing over—because it "saves" (*tārayati*). The meaning is that they do not know that very *unmanī* which has been described as the means of crossing over. || 40 ||
"Ardhonmīlita" means: that by which the eyes are half-opened is "ardhonmīlite locane. (p.
Root Text
The entire seed, brilliantly shining, attains that supreme reality, that state; what more need be said here regarding that ultimate object which is to be expressed? 41.
One should not worship the Liṅga by day, nor should one worship it at night;
one should always worship the Liṅga by transcending the distinction between day and night.
|| Commentary ||
"With half-opened eyes" means with eyes partially opened;
"with a steady mind" means one whose mind is motionless;
he places [the gaze] at the tip of the nose, that is, on the front part of the nose, or at a distance of twelve finger-breadths from the nose.
Because his gaze was directed there, he had his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose.

Thus Vasiṣṭha has said: "When the consciousness and the two eyes have become stilled at the tip of the nose, twelve finger-breadths away in the stainless sky, the movement of the breath is obstructed."

The state of being motionless (*niṣpanda*) is *niṣpandabhāva*; it is the immobility of the organs of action, the senses, and the mind. By means of that, even the moon and the sun—the moon and the sun—attain dissolution;
bringing about or causing them to reach dissolution, which is the state of being dissolved (*līnatā*), [he dissolves] the organs of action, the senses, and the mind.
The meaning is that, by means of immobility, he even arrests the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

This was stated previously: "Wherein the mind dissolves," and so forth. A yogi endowed with these aforementioned qualifications possesses a form that is "of the nature of light" (*jyotīrūpa*), meaning his form is like light, illuminating everything.

It is the seed of all without exception; through the production of space and the other elements, it is the cause of everything; it is "all-pervading" (akhila) and "full" (pūrṇa); it is "blazing intensely" (dedīpyamāna), meaning it shines with exceeding brilliance; thus it is self-luminous, the supreme witness of the effects, the senses, and the mind.

"Reality" (*tattva*) means that which is non-superimposed and real. "That very thing" (*tad idam*) is the "state" (*pada*); it is so called because it cannot be described in words, yet it is "reached" (*padyate*) or realized by yogis. It is the supreme, most excellent reality, the very nature of the Self (*ātman*). In the state of *unmanī*, one remains established in one's own true nature and attains it.
The meaning is that he becomes a yogi. What more is there to be said here? The meaning is: what further need is there to say that he attains another reality? || 41 ||
He states the absence of a fixed temporal rule for the contemplation of *unmanī*: "Not by day. By day, during the movement of the sun, [one contemplates] the *liṅga*.
Root Text
Now, concerning Khecarī: the vital breath (māruta), residing in the left and right channels, moves in the middle.
The khecarī mudrā remains in that place; of this there is no doubt. || 43 ||
One should swallow the void and the vital air between the iḍā and piṅgalā;
there the khecarī mudrā abides—this is the truth again and again. (44)
|| Commentary ||

The Self is the cause of all, according to such scriptural passages as, "From this Self, space was produced," and so forth. One should not worship [the Self] in the conventional sense, nor should one cultivate [it as an object]; for meditation itself is the worship of the Self.
As it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "The Self is indeed the offering of meditation; meditation is its [means of] worship."

Without that great worship, this self is certainly not attained by other means. Furthermore, one should neither perform worship nor practice meditation at night or during the movement of the moon, because of the lack of stability of the mind when the moon and sun are in motion; for it has been said, "When the wind is moving, the mind is moving."

Having restrained the sun and moon through the cessation of day and night— here the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of the elision of the suffix *lyap* (meaning "by means of" or "after")— one should always, at all times, worship and meditate upon the Liṅga, which is the Self, once the restraint of the sun and moon has been effected within the Suṣumnā.
This is due to the steadiness of the mind within the vital breath (*prāṇa*). As it has been said: "When the wind has entered into the *suṣumnā*, steadiness of the mind arises. (42)

He speaks of Khecarī: "On the left," etc. Where the wind—the vital air—residing in the left and right channels moves in the middle, that is, flows in that central region; in that place, in that region, is Khecarī.

The *mudrā* remains steady and becomes stable. The use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is according to the rule "in the senses of 'making manifest' and 'being a judge'. "There is no doubt" means that there is no uncertainty regarding the stated meaning. || 43 ||

Regarding the phrase "of Iḍā and Piṅgalā": between Iḍā and Piṅgalā, that is, the left and right channels, the void (śūnya) or space (kha), as the agent, swallows the wind (anila), which is the vital breath (prāṇa). The "swallowing" (grāsa) is simply the stabilization of the breath within the void. In that [state], within that void, is Khecarī.
The mudrā remains; it should be joined with "repeatedly, truly" [to form the mantra]. || 44 ||
p. 154) || Root Text ||
Furthermore, that which is situated within the wheel of space (vyomacakra), in the supportless interval between the sun and the moon, is the mudrā named Khecarī. || 45 ||
The stream that has arisen here from the *soma* is directly the beloved of Śiva; it fills the incomparable, divine *suṣumnā* at its western opening.
When [the breath] is filled from the front, Khecarī becomes certain; once Khecarī Mudrā has been practiced, Unmanī arises. || 47 ||
|| Commentary ||

Regarding the phrase "of the sun and moon": between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, which are the sun and moon, in that supportless interval or space; furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) serves to complete the meter;
in the wheel or collection of the voids (*vyoma*), that is, of all the cavities, in the center of the earth.
Because of its endowment [with these]. As it has been said: "That which is endowed with the five streams is the mudrā named Khecarī. (45)

"From Soma": *Soma* refers to the moon; from that [moon], in which *khecarī*, the stream—the stream of nectar (*amṛta*)—has arisen or emerged, that *khecarī* is directly the beloved of Śiva, meaning she is dear to Śiva. This connects with the preceding [verse]. She is incomparable, stainless, and peerless.
One should fill the divine Suṣumnā, the best of all channels, at its western opening; the word "with the tongue" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 46 ||

"And also from the front" means that it should also be filled from the front—that is, by the *prāṇa* into the *suṣumnā*; this is the remainder of the sense. "If, then, the *khecarī*—the mudrā named *khecarī*—should become certain and free from doubt," [it follows] that if, however, it is not filled from the front by the *prāṇa*.

If [the breath] were filled from the rear by the tongue alone, then it would produce a state of delusion; the sense is that Khecarī would not be perfected. When the Khecarī-mudrā is practiced, Unmanī arises through the mind's absorption into the form of the object of meditation, which is the fourth state (turya).
The meaning is that it comes into being. || 47 ||
p. 155) || Root Text ||
Between the eyebrows is the abode of Śiva; there the mind is dissolved. That state should be known as the fourth (turya); there time does not exist. || 48 ||
One should practice khecarī until one becomes absorbed in the sleep of yoga.
For one who has attained the yoga-sleep, there is never any [limited] time.
Having made the mind free from support, one should not think of anything at all;
remaining like a jar within the space both outside and inside, one certainly abides as the eternal void.
Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "between the eyebrows": between the two eyebrows, in the space between them, is the station of Śiva—the station of the Lord (Īśvara), which is to say, the abiding place of the Self whose nature is bliss (Śiva). There, in that [station], the mind is dissolved.
That state of the mind, which consists of absorption (laya) and flows as a continuous stream of mental modifications (vṛtti) in the form of Śiva, is the fourth state (turya);
it should be known as the fourth, distinct from waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. In that state, time and death do not exist. Or rather:

The meaning is that because of the cessation of the source of the sun and moon, time—which causes the exhaustion of life—does not exist; as it has been said: "Bhoh and Kri are the Suṣumnā of Time. (48)

"One should practice" means: one should practice the khecarī mudrā until one is "asleep in yoga. Yoga is the cessation of all mental fluctuations; that itself is sleep, hence "yoga-sleep. One who has this [sleep] arisen is "asleep in yoga"—one by whom such yoga-sleep has been attained. He...
For him who has attained the yoga-sleep, there is never at any time death or end. || 49 ||

"Without support" (nirālambam): the meaning is that one who, having made the mind supportless—devoid of any object of focus—should not think of anything at all; when the khecarī mudrā has arisen, one should abandon even the mental state (vṛtti) whose form is Brahman through supreme dispassion (paravairāgya). He...
The yogi remains fixed like a jar in space—both externally and internally, being outside in what is external and inside in what is internal.
Root Text
Just as the external wind subsides, so too does it within; there is no doubt that the vital air, together with the mind, attains steadiness in its own place. 51.
For one practicing in this manner day and night on the path of the vital air, the wind is digested through practice,
and the mind dissolves right there.
One should flood the body with nectars from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
Commentary:

This is certain: just as a jar in space is filled with space both inside and out, so too the yogi, through the abandonment of all focal points in Khecarī, remains filled with Brahman; this is the meaning. || 50 ||

Regarding the word "external" (*bāhya*): just as the external wind, which exists outside the body, becomes dissolved during the practice of moving through space (*khacaryā*) because it no longer functions externally, so too the internal wind, which resides within the body, becomes dissolved because it no longer functions externally. Of this there is no doubt.

The meaning is that there is no doubt regarding this matter. "Sthānam" (the place) refers to that in which one stands or becomes established; it is the place of one’s own vital breath (*prāṇa*), the foundation of stability, namely the *brahmarandhra*. Therein, together with the mind (*manas*) or consciousness (*citta*), [one remains].
The vital breath (prāṇa) attains steadiness, that is, it reaches a state of motionlessness. || 51 ||
In the manner thus described, that is to say, on the path of the wind— the path of the vital breath (prāṇa), namely in the *suṣumnā*—
for the yogi who practices day and night,
performing repeated cultivation, the wind— the vital breath— is worn away (*jīryate*) at which point, in which substratum (*ādhāra*).
"It is destroyed" means "it dissolves. In that very locus of the dissolution of the wind, the mind, being accumulated, dissolves; that is to say, it decays. || 52 ||
Regarding the phrase "with nectars": with the nectars (*amṛta*) emerging from the apertures, [he sprinkles] the soles of the feet and the head;
the term *pādatalamastaka* is a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
Root Text
The one of great body and great strength and prowess certainly attains success. Thus ends the Khecarī [mudrā].
Having placed the mind within the Śakti, and the Śakti within the midst of the mind, one should perceive the mind with the mind and hold fast to the supreme state.
Place the self within the void, and place the void within the self; having made everything composed of the void, one should not think of anything at all.
Commentary:

The term *prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām* takes the singular form [as a collective compound]. "From the soles of the feet to the crown of the head" means pervading the body from the soles of the feet up to the head; one should cause it to flood, that is, one should make it flooded. He is one whose body (*kāya*) is great, that is, excellent.
A yogi who possesses such a great body and great strength and prowess certainly attains perfection; through immersion in the nectar, he indeed becomes perfected. || 53 ||

"Śakti" refers to Kuṇḍalinī. Having placed the mind in her midst—meaning having fixed the mind upon her and made the mind take her form—one should place the Śakti within the center of the mind. Through the absorption resulting from meditation on the Śakti, one [attains] the Śakti.

Having unified [the mind] within the mind—meaning, by that [unification], having awakened Kuṇḍalinī; for Gorakṣa has stated: "By means of the mind and together with the vital air (marut), through the union with the awakened fire.
Having observed the mind with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—that is, having observed the intellect (buddhi) by means of the mind through such observation.
The meaning is "having made firm. The meaning of "one should hold the supreme state" is that one should take the most excellent essential nature as the object of concentration (*dhāraṇā*). || 54 ||

"Within the void (khamadhye)": Brahman is full like the void; within that void, make yourself—your own true nature—to be [Brahman]. The meaning is: contemplate "I am Brahman. And within the self—within your own true nature—make the void to be the full Brahman; and likewise, [contemplate] "I am Brahman."
