The meaning is: "one should meditate. Having made everything consist of space and having contemplated it as consisting of Brahman, one should not think of anything at all; the meaning is that one should even abandon the meditation "I am Brahman."
p. 158) || Root Text ||
Empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky; full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean. (56)
One should not engage in external thoughts, nor likewise internal reflections;
having abandoned all thought, one should not think of anything at all.
The entire world is merely a construction of volition; the mind is merely a construction of volition. (Commentary)
Thus, he describes the state of one who is thus composed, abiding in his own true nature: "Empty within" (*antaḥśūnya*). This means empty within, that is, within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
it is devoid of a second because of the absence of any mental activity other than Brahman.

It is empty both internally and externally, even beyond the external; because a second thing is not perceived, it is like a jar or pot in the sky—that is, in the space of the atmosphere—which is empty within and without. In the same way, within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) or the space of the heart, [the mind] is filled with the air of the modification (vṛtti) that takes the form of Brahman.
Because of the existence of reality (*sadbhāva*), because it is the abode of Brahman (*brahmavāsatvāt*);
or because it is full externally due to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), or full externally due to the space of the heart (*hṛdavakāśa*);
or because, by its very being (*sattayā*), there is no function apart from Brahman, and thus it is full of Brahman; [it is] in the ocean (*arṇave*).
Just as a jar or pot in the ocean becomes filled with water on all sides, so too the yogi established in samādhi becomes filled with Brahman; this is the meaning. || 56 ||

Regarding the phrase "external thought" (*bāhyacintā*): the words "by the yogi who is concentrated" (*samāhitena yoginā*) are to be supplied as an ellipsis. External thought—that is, thought directed toward external objects—must not be performed; likewise, just as with the performance of external thought, internal reflection upon internal [objects] must be avoided by means of the mind.

The construction [of the sentence] is by changing the gender: "one should not engage in the contemplation of imagined things such as wish-fulfilling cakes, mansions, or gardens. Having abandoned all contemplation—meaning both external and internal contemplation—one should not think of anything at all.

One should contemplate through supreme dispassion and even abandon the mental modification (vṛtti) that takes the form of the self; the sense is that upon its abandonment, there occurs liberation while living (jīvanmukti), which consists in abiding in one's true nature. || 57 ||
He cites the words of Vasiṣṭha as authority for the fact that peace arises when one abandons thoughts of both the external and the internal: "saṃkalpa...
Root Text
O Rāma, abandon the mind that consists of mere conceptualization; resorting to the state free from conceptualization, attain the certainty of peace. 58.
Just as camphor [is dissolved] in fire, and as rock salt [is dissolved] in water,
so too the mind, when being integrated, dissolves into the Reality.
All that is to be known is the perceived object, and the knowledge thereof is called the mind.
|| Commentary ||

*Saṃkalpa* is a mental activity; that alone is *saṃkalpamātra*. The entire visible world is merely its fabrication (*kalana*) and construction (*racanā*). The meaning is that the external phenomenal world is imagined by the mind alone. It is the play (*vilāsa*) of the mind, of the internal organ (*mānasa*).

The conceptualization of various objects and forms—the play consisting of imagining things such as sweetmeats, palaces, and gardens—is merely the fabrication of volition (*saṃkalpa*). The meaning is that even the mental world (*mānasa-prapañca*) is nothing but a construction of volition alone. In mere volition...
Abandon that notion of reality which regards the external and internal phenomenal world as true.
To the question, "What then should be done?", he says: "Nirvikalpa" (free from conceptual construction). Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a specific mental fabrication regarding the Self.

O Rāma, that which consists of the conceptualization of distinctions— such as agency, enjoyership, happiness, similarity, dissimilarity, internal differences, and the limitations of space, time, and substance— is transcended by that which is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa). Taking refuge in that Self and making it the object of concentration (dhāraṇā) and so forth, [one attains it].

"Attain with certainty and without doubt the supreme peace; from that, you shall also obtain happiness"—this is the intended meaning. This was stated by the Blessed One by way of contrast: "There is no peace for one who does not meditate; for one who lacks peace, how can there be happiness? (58)
"Like camphor," etc. Just as, for example, camphor being joined—that is, being applied—to fire dissolves; it dissolves specifically, it becomes absorbed;
it takes on the form of the fire. Just as [it dissolves] when joined to water—that is, to liquid—...

Just as rock salt dissolves, abandoning its form as salt and becoming the form of water, in that same way, the mind being joined with and directed toward the Self, the Reality, dissolves and becomes the form of the Self. || 59 ||
He says in three verses that when the dissolution of the mind has occurred, even duality dissolves: "That which is to be known," etc.
All, entirely. (p. 160) || Root Text ||
Knowledge and the object of knowledge have equally perished; there is no other second path.
All this that exists, whether moving or unmoving, is the visible manifestation of the mind. Indeed, through the state of the mind's transcendence (unmanībhāva), duality is no longer perceived.
Through the relinquishing of the objects of knowledge, the mind dissolves; when the dissolution of the mind has occurred, absolute liberation remains.
Commentary:

That which is to be known, that which is worthy of knowledge, that which is perceived, that which is already known, and knowledge itself—all this is called the mind (*manas*). Because everything is merely a mental construction, it is designated by the word "mind. This includes both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
The mind dissolves equally along with the mental faculty; if it is thus destroyed, then there is no second.
"A second" means precisely a second; there is no path that is an object of the mind.
The realized meaning is that duality does not exist. || 30 ||
"Mind-visible" (manodṛśya) means this: whatever is being perceived—whatever is moving (cara), that is, mobile; and whatever is non-moving (acara), that is, stationary;
and that which exists together with both the moving and the non-moving, namely the world (jagat)—all of that is mind-visible, [perceived] by the mind.

The visible world is merely a mental construction; this is the meaning. Since it is perceived when mental construction exists and not perceived when it is absent, the entire universe is nothing but an illusion (*bhrama*), for an illusion consists solely of what is perceived. Nor does this entail the consequence of [falling into] the Buddhist position.
Because Brahman, the substratum of delusion, is admitted to be real;

due to the mind’s transformation into the state beyond mind (*unmanībhāva*) and its dissolution, duality—distinction—is neither perceived nor cognized, because the mental volition that causes the delusion of duality no longer exists. Indeed, when that cause is absent, [the result] is imperishable.

Regarding the term "jñeyam" (the knowable): by the renunciation—that is, the complete abandonment—of that which is to be known, the object of knowledge, namely all things moving and unmoving, whatever is visible, consisting of name and form; through that total relinquishment, [the mind] becomes dissolved into the form of the Self, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss. Of the mind...
When dissolution has occurred, isolation (*kaivalya*) remains—the state of the solitary Self; the meaning is that the non-dual nature of the Self alone remains. || 62 ||
p. 161) || Root Text ||
Thus, these various means are endowed with one's own correct personal experience.
The paths of meditative concentration have been described by the great-souled former teachers. || 63 ||
Salutations to you, Suṣumnā, Kuṇḍalinī, Sudhā, and the one born of the Moon; salutations to Manonmanī, the Great Power (Mahāśakti), whose essence is consciousness (Cit).
It is also accepted even by the deluded who are incapable of awakening to reality.

"Thus" means: by those great souls (*mahātman*)— those whose inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the self purified by the practice of great meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in the manner previously described, namely "the internal object of focus while the gaze is directed outward"— and by those former teachers (*pūrvācārya*), who were both ancient and masters.

Matsyendra and others have described those paths—the means for attaining *samādhi*, which is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. Of what nature are these paths to *samādhi*? They are characterized by various means; that is, they possess diverse methods and practices as their instruments of realization.
Likewise, they are endowed with—that is, joined to—that self-experience which is perfectly correct, being free from doubt and error. (63)
Having accomplished his purpose through Suṣumnā and the others, he bows to them: "To Suṣumnā," and so forth.
To her who is Suṣumnā, the central channel; to Kuṇḍalinī and Ādhāraśakti; to her whose birth is from the nectar (sudhā)—the ambrosia (pīyūṣa)—located between the eyebrows and the moon;
to Manonmanī, the state of the Fourth (turyāvasthā); she whose self (ātman) and essential nature (svarūpa) is consciousness (cit-caitanya).

Likewise, to her— namely, the supreme power known as *cicchakti* (the power of consciousness), which is of the nature of the *puruṣa* and which, being great, bestows consciousness upon the inert organs of action and the mind— to her, [the word] "to you" (*tubhyam*) is connected with each [of the preceding terms]. *Namaḥ* (salutation).
May there be the state of complete subsiding. || 64 ||
Having described various methods for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), [the author] declares the primary method that corresponds to the continuous practice of the inner sound (*nāda*) (p.
Root Text
The worship of Nāda, as proclaimed by Gorakṣanātha, is now being described.
The methods of the thirty-five million *layas* taught by the illustrious Ādinātha are victorious.
We consider the practice of following the resonance (nāda) alone to be the most primary among all methods of dissolution (laya).
Seated in the liberated posture (muktāsana), the yogi should assume the Śāmbhavī mudrā.
With one-pointed mind, one should listen to the internal sound within the right ear.
Commentary:

Regarding the word *nīte*: "Incapable" (*aśakya*) means that for those who are unlearned (*avyutpanna*), the awakening to reality—that is, the knowledge of reality—is impossible; they are thus "the deluded ones.
By the use of the word "even" (*api*), it is understood: "How much more so for those who are learned?"—according to Gorakṣanātha.

By the word "proktam" (spoken), its worthiness of adoption is understood because it was spoken by the Great One (Mahādeva). The "cultivation" (upāsanā) of the sound (nāda)—that is, the unstruck resonance (anāhata-dhvani)—is said to consist of continuous contemplation (anusaṃdhāna); this is what is being described. || 65 ||

Regarding the phrase "by the illustrious Ādinātha": the methods of dissolution (layaprakāra)—meaning the various means for the dissolution of the mind—numbering ten million and accompanied by a fourth part (pāda), were spoken and proclaimed by Śiva, the illustrious Ādinātha; they "triumph," meaning they exist in a state of excellence.
We, however, consider the continuous following of the sound (*nādānusaṃdhāna*)— the mere contemplation of the sound alone—
to be the most principal, that is, pre-eminently the chief, among all methods of absorption (*laya*), among the various means for attaining absorption,
and indeed among the most excellent means for absorption.
The sense is that, because it is the most excellent and because it is favored by Gorakṣa, the contemplation of the *nāda* alone must necessarily be practiced. || 66 ||
He describes the contemplation of the sound (nāda) within the Śāmbhavī-mudrā: "In the Muktāsana," and so forth.

Seated in the Muktāsana or Siddhāsana, the yogi, having assumed the Śāmbhavī Mudrā— described as "the internal object of focus while the gaze is directed outward," and so forth— becoming single-minded with a one-pointed consciousness, [should look] to the right.
One should hear the sound that is already present within the ear, in the *suṣumnā* channel.
(p. 163) || Root Text ||
One should perform the closing of the two ear-pits, the pair of eyes, the nose, and the mouth.
In the pure channel of Suṣumṇā, the stainless sound is clearly heard.
In all yogas, there are four stages: the beginning, the pot-like stage, as well as the stage of familiarity, and completion. (69)
Now, the stage of commencement: when the knot of Brahma is pierced, there arises bliss born of the void.
Commentary:

As it has been said in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*: "In the beginning, there is that primordial sound (*nāda*), which produces the purification of all sounds through a resonance like the humming of a swarm of intoxicated bees, resembling the sound from a flute shimmering when filled with air by a flutist."

"Following that, there is a sound like the ringing of a bell, then a deep resonance as steady as the roar of the ocean, and finally a thundering like the sound of clouds; this supreme [sound] exists here within the cavity of the *brahmanāḍī*.
(67) Thus he describes the contemplation of the *nāda* by means of the *parāṅmukhī* mudrā. [It occurs] in the cavity of the ear.

The pair, or couple, of eyes—that is, the two eyes—and the nostrils, which are designated by the word "prāṇa," as well as the mouth, which is the face; although, according to the rule for *dvandva* compounds involving parts of living beings, a singular form would have been expected, it does not occur here because the singularization of all *dvandva* compounds is optional. Of these...
The blocking [of the sense organs] should be performed with the fingers. The method of blocking is as follows:
having covered both ears with the two thumbs, the eyes with the two index fingers, and likewise the nostrils with the other two fingers, one should block the sense organs.

By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that one should cover the mouth with the other two [nostrils]. In the pure path of the Suṣumṇā— that channel of the Suṣumṇā which is free from impurity by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma)— the stainless sound is clearly and distinctly heard.
Now he describes the four stages of *nāda*: "And the beginning (*ārambha*)," and so forth.

The stages of commencement, the stage of the pot, the stage of mastery, and the stage of completion—these four stages occur in all yogas, that is, in all means for the cessation of mental fluctuations, such as the Śāmbhavī and others. And thus it is said: "ca caiva tathā pi caḥ."
They serve the purpose of filling out the meter. || 69 ||
In that regard, he states the stage of commencement: "Of the knot of Brahman," and so forth.
The piercing of the knot of Brahmā situated in the Anāhata-cakra.
(p. 164) || Root Text ||
A diverse resonance, the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), is heard within the body. (70)

Possessing a divine body, radiant, with a divine fragrance and free from disease, one whose heart is fulfilled yet remains empty of worldly attachment becomes a practitioner of yoga at the very outset. || 71 ||
Now, the state of the jar (ghaṭāvasthā): When the second [state] has been brought to the condition of a jar, the vital air becomes centered within;
then the yogi, possessing firm posture and knowledge, becomes equal to a god. 72.
|| Commentary ||

"When the piercing occurs through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma)"—here there is an ellipsis of the correlative "then" (tadā) following the relative "when" (yadā). It is called "bliss" (ānanda) because it causes bliss; it is "born in the void" (śūnyasaṃbhava), meaning it arises in the space of the heart (hṛdākāśa), having been produced within that space.

"Vicitra" means manifold; "kvaṇa" is the sound of ornaments, which is itself "kvaṇaka. The meaning is that it resembles the sound of ornaments. For Amara states: "The tinkling of ornaments is called *śiṃjita*; it is also called *nikvāṇa*, *nikvaṇa*, *kvāṇa*, *kvaṇa*, and *kvaṇana*."
The unstruck sound (anāhata-dhvani), the unstruck resonance (anāhata-nirhrāda), is heard within the body, in the middle of the body;
the meaning is that it becomes an object of hearing. || 70 ||
Regarding the phrase "divine body": when there is that initial emergence of sound (*nādārambha*) within the void of the heart-space (*hṛdākāśa*),
the yogis designate the heart-space, the pure space, and the space between the eyebrows by the terms "void" (*śūnya*), "supreme void" (*atiśūnya*), and "great void" (*mahāśūnya*).
One whose heart is completely filled with the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) is "saṃpūrṇahṛdayaḥ"; a yogi who possesses such a heart filled with bliss is "yogavān";
one whose body is divine—endowed with beauty, grace, and strength—is "divyadehaḥ"; and he is "tejasvī" (radiant).
The connection is as follows: he shall become powerful, possessed of divine fragrance—that is, one whose scent is supremely divine—and free from disease, being devoid of ailment. || 71 ||

He describes the state of the jar: "In the second [state]," etc. In the second state of the jar, the vital air (prāṇa), having formed a jar, unites the downward breath (apāna) and the *nāda* and *bindu* with itself; thus it becomes the "middle" (*madhyama*), situated in the middle wheel.
The middle wheel is located at the throat. (p. 165) || Root Text ||
Then, from the piercing of the Viṣṇugranthi, there arises the Vimarda, which indicates supreme bliss; likewise, in the state of Atiśūnya, there occurs the sound of a kettledrum.
On the third day, however, the sound of a mardala drum in the sky is to be known; then one enters the Great Void, which is the refuge of all accomplishments.
Commentary:

As it has been said right here regarding the Jālandhara-bandha: "This middle wheel (madhyacakra) is to be known as the binding of the sixteen supports. The word "when" (*yadā*) is to be supplied [to the verse].
Then, in this state, the yogi—the practitioner of yoga—whose seat (*āsana*) is firm...

One who possesses a firm posture and a steady seat is a man of knowledge; compared to the former state, his intellect becomes skillful, and due to his excellence in form and beauty, he becomes equal to a god—a deity-like being.
As it is said in the *Īśvarokta-rājayoga*: "Prāṇa and apāna, nāda and bindu..."
Because the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) come together and function as one, it is therefore called a "jar" (ghaṭa). || 72 ||

Regarding the phrase "by the knots of Viṣṇu": after that, following the piercing of the knot of Brahmā, by means of the *kumbhaka* breath-retentions which pierce the knot of Viṣṇu located in the throat, there arises the supreme bliss of Brahman that is about to manifest.

The indicator is the signifier. In an extremely empty space that resembles a tattered rag, there occurs at that time a crushing conflict of many sounds, a sound like the noise of a kettledrum, a kettledrum sound, and the resonance of a kettledrum. || 73 ||

He describes the stage of familiarity with two and a half verses: In the third stage, that of familiarity, "the sound of a mṛdaṅga drum in the sky" is to be understood specifically as a sound like that of a mṛdaṅga— a particular type of musical instrument— in the sky, which is the space between the eyebrows.

He becomes worthy of knowledge. Then, in that state, there is the "abode of all accomplishments," which is the locus of all accomplishments, namely the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth; for by practicing *saṃyama* upon that, one attains *aṇimā* and the other powers.
The "great void" is the space between the eyebrows; the word "goes" (*yāti*) implies that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) goes there.
(p. 166) || Root Text ||
Then, having conquered the bliss of the mind, there arises the innate bliss (sahajānanda).
He is free from defects, suffering, old age, disease, hunger, and sleep. || 75 ||

When the vital breath (anila), having reached the seat of Śarva, pierces the Rudra-knot, there arises at the moment of its completion a sound like that of a flute, resembling the resonance of a vibrating lute. || 76 ||
Then the mind becomes unified; that is designated as Rājayoga.
Commentary:
Regarding "cittānandam":

having conquered—that is, having overcome—the bliss born of the modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) directed toward the object of *nāda*, which is the bliss of mental joy (*cittānanda*), there arises innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), which is the natural bliss of the Self (*ātmasukha*). Its [arising].

"Origination" (saṃbhava) means manifestation; "defects" (doṣāḥ) are wind, bile, and phlegm; "suffering" (duḥkha) is the pain produced by them, such as that which is internal and so forth; "old age" (jarā) is the state of decrepitude; "disease" (vyādhi) is fever and the like; "hunger" (kṣudhā) is the desire to eat; and "sleep" (nidrā) is slumber—one who is free from and devoid of these is then a yogi.
Thus it is said. || 75 ||

In response to the expectation of "when then?", he says: "When Rudra... When the vital breath (*anila*), having pierced the Rudra-knot, reaches the Ājñā-cakra—the seat (*pīṭha*) of Śarva, that is, Īśvara, located at the station between the eyebrows—then [the state arises].

He speaks of the state of completion (*niṣpatti*): "In completion" means in the state of completion. When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has entered the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), the state of completion occurs. "Vaiṇava" means belonging to the bamboo (*veṇu*); it is a sound related to the flute (*vaṃśa*).
The resonance of that lute which is ringing and making sound would be its musical tone. || 76 ||
Then, in that state, the mind— the internal organ— becomes unified and focused on a single object;
because of the metaphorical treatment of the non-difference between the object and the subject, that is called Rājayoga.
That which has such a designation is called "Rājayoga.
(p. 167) || Root Text ||
He becomes the agent of creation and destruction, equal to the Lord of Yogins. || 77 ||
Whether liberation exists or not, here alone is unbroken happiness.
This happiness arising from absorption is attained through the royal yoga (rājayoga). || 78 ||
Those who do not know the Royal Yoga (rājayoga) and are merely practitioners of Hatha [yoga]—I consider these practitioners to be devoid of the fruit of their exertion. (79)
For the swift attainment of the state beyond the mind (unmanī), meditation on the eyebrows is my preferred method.
The state of Rājayoga is attained as an easy means for those of limited intellect; the dissolution born of Nāda arises, producing immediate conviction. (80)
Commentary:

The meaning is that one-pointedness of the mind itself is *rājayoga*. Regarding the phrase "creator and destroyer": that yogin who is intent on the contemplation of the *nāda* is a creator and destroyer; he performs both creation and dissolution, and is thus such a person. For this very reason, he is equal to the Lord (*īśvara*), that is, identical to God.
It would be so. || 77 ||
"Or let it be so," and "the royal yoga"—both have been explained previously. 78, 79.

"For the attainment of Unmanī" means for the sake of quickly—that is, swiftly—attaining or reaching the state of Unmanī. Meditation on the eyebrows (bhrū-dhyāna), that is, meditation between the eyebrows, is approved by me, who delight in my own Self; it is Rājayoga, the king of yogas.

That very state— the state of Rājayoga known as the fourth state (turya)— is to be attained; the means for attaining it is the previously mentioned meditation on the space between the eyebrows, which is an easy method (sukhopāya) and easily accomplished even for those of small minds and limited intellect.

The intention is: "How much more so for others? That which is born from *nāda*—the dissolution (*laya*) born from *nāda*, which is the dissolution of the mind—is called "joining conviction" (*pratyayasaṃdhāyī*) because it immediately and swiftly joins one with conviction; it becomes, that is, it manifests as something that produces realization.
p. 168) || Root Text ||

Only the illustrious Guru-Nātha knows that singular bliss, inaccessible to words, which increases in the hearts of the lords of yogis who partake in the samādhi of following the inner sound (nāda). 81.
Covering his ears with both hands, the sage should fix his mind upon whatever sound he hears, until he attains the state of stability. 82.
Regarding the phrase "in the continuous contemplation of the sound" (nādānusaṃdhāne):

Among those yogis who partake in the samādhi of contemplating the sound— that is, the continuous reflection upon the unstruck resonance (anāhata-dhvani) and the resulting one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgrya).

The lords are capable regarding those engaged in yoga; he who grows within their heart—*vardhamānaḥ*—is that one renowned in the Yoga-śāstra, who is inaccessible to words, beyond the reach of speech, and impossible to designate as "this. That one.

The glorious and venerable Guru alone—the one and non-dual Lord—is the primary bliss and delight; he alone knows and perceives it. By this, it is indicated that the bliss resulting from the contemplation of *nāda* is accessible only through the Guru. 81.
He describes samādhi through the sequence beginning with pratyāhāra, by means of following the resonance (nāda).

By the words "the ears," and so forth: the sage, whose nature is mental composure, by the phrase "with his two hands," indicates the thumbs of the hands. Having covered the two ears—the sense organs of hearing—with those two;
that is to say, having placed the thumbs of the hands into the openings of the ears. Yaṃ...

One hears—that is, one listens to—the unstruck sound (*anāhatanisvana*) which is resonance (*dhvani*); therein, in that resonance, one should stabilize the mind, making it steady where it was previously unsteady.
One should proceed until reaching the stable state (*sthirapada*), the state known as the Fourth (*turya*). As it has been said:
The perception of this [sound] is said to be the manifestation of the consciousness of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*);
thus, through the contemplation of sound (*nādānusaṃdhāna*), the stability of the vital air (*vāyu*) and even powers such as *aṇimā* arise.
And it is stated in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*: "By him for whom the innate breath (*sahaja-vāyu*) has been conquered here..."

A great roar arose; for him who was the source of the emergence of great qualities, immeasurable merit and the powers such as *aṇimā* came to be. Blocking the opening of the enemy of the son of the King of the Gods with two fingers of his own hand, he [stilled] that sound spreading within like the deep roar of the ocean.
"A mortal hears suddenly"—the king of the gods is Indra;
his son is Arjuna; his enemy is Karṇa. The rest is clear in its reference to that vulnerability. 82.
p. 169) || Root Text ||
This sound, when practiced, veils the external noise.
Having conquered all distraction from the side, the yogi shall become happy. || 83 ||
It is heard that at the first stage of practice, a great variety of sounds is heard;
then, as the practice increases, an increasingly subtle sound is heard.
At first, there arise sounds produced from the ocean, clouds, kettledrums, and jharjharas; in the middle, those arising from mṛdaṅgas and conchs, as well as from bells and kāhalas. (85)
Commentary:

"Being practiced" means that this sound called the unstruck (*anāhata*), when being practiced— that is, when being continuously attended to— shrouds the external resonance, the sound arising from outside,
which is the object of the ears. The yogi who practices the sound, within half a month or a fortnight, [perceives] everything...
Having conquered and overcome all distraction and mental agitation, one becomes happy and established in one's own bliss. || 85 ||

"It is heard" means that during the first practice— that is, the initial practice— a great sound of many kinds, resembling the ocean, clouds, drums, and so forth, namely the unstruck sound (*anāhata-svana*),
is heard or perceived. Thereafter, in the subsequent practice— namely, the practice of continuous contemplation upon that sound—
When [the sound] is increasing, the subtle-subtle (sūkṣma-sūkṣma) is heard—that is, it becomes an object of hearing—as something merely subtle. || 84 ||

He describes various kinds of sounds with two verses, beginning with "At first" (*ādau*). At the outset, at the time when the vital air (*vāyu*) reaches the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), there arise the ocean (*jaladhi*), the sea (*samudra*), the cloud (*jīmūta*), the thundercloud (*megha*), and the *bherī*—a specific type of musical instrument. According to Amara, "the *bherī* is feminine and the *dundubhi* is masculine. Also, the *jharjhara*...

A specific type of musical instrument. According to Amara, the various kinds of instruments include the *ḍamaru*, *maḍḍu*, *ḍiṇḍima*, *jharjhara*, *mardala*, *paṇava*, and others. Those whose origin (*saṃbhava*) is like that of the ocean and other sources [of sound] are such; [this refers to] the wind within the *brahmarandhra*.

Following *sthairya*, there are those arising from the *mardala*—a specific type of drum—and the *śaṅkha*—the conch; thus they are called *mardala-śaṅkhotthāḥ*. There are also those born from the *ghaṇṭā* (bell) and the *kāhala* (trumpet), two specific types of musical instruments; thus they are called *ghaṇṭā-kāhalajāḥ*. || 85 ||
p. 170) || Root Text ||
But at the end, sounds like those of small bells, flutes, lutes, and bees are heard;
thus, various kinds of sounds are perceived arising from within the body. (86)
Even when great sounds such as those of clouds or kettledrums are being heard,
one should there contemplate only the sound that is subtler than the subtle.
Either having abandoned the gross for the subtle, or having abandoned the subtle for the gross.
Even while enjoying [the object], one should not allow the distracted mind to wander elsewhere. || 88 ||
Commentary:

"At the end, however" means: at the end, following the great stability of the *prāṇa* in the *brahmarandhra*, there arise the aforementioned sounds of the *kiṅkiṇī* (small bell), the *vaṃśa* (flute), the *vīṇā* (lute), and the *bhramara* (bee).
Various and manifold kinds [of beings] are heard to have gone to and reached the interior of the body. || 86 ||
Regarding the word "mahati": it refers to that which has clouds, kettledrums, and so forth as its beginning—namely, the sounds of clouds and kettledrums, which here denote the resulting resonance.
Even when a great, vast sound or clamor is being heard, or while it is being listened to, therein...

Among those sounds, one should first perceive and contemplate that which is subtler than the subtle, exceedingly subtle; the sense is that because the subtle sound persists for a long time, one whose mind is attached to it will become steady-minded for a long duration.

Regarding the word "ghana": having abandoned the dense, great sound such as that of clouds, kettledrums, and so forth, he delights in the "dense" (ghanam) sound; that is, he sports by both grasping and abandoning either the dense or the subtle sound.

One should not cause the mind, when cast out by passion and exceedingly restless, to move toward another object; for the mind cast out—that is, attached to another object—is not concentrated, whereas that which delights in the [inner] sounds (nāda) becomes concentrated—this is the intended meaning. || 88 ||
p. 171) || Root Text ||
Wherever the mind first settles upon a sound, becoming perfectly steady right there, it dissolves along with that sound. (89)
Just as a bee drinking nectar does not look for fragrance, so too...
Likewise, the mind attached to the internal sound (nāda) no longer desires sense objects. || 90 ||
This sound, sharp as a goad, is capable of restraining the lordly elephant of the mind as it wanders through the garden of the sense-objects. || 91 ||
Commentary:

Regarding this: *vā* means "or"; that is, wherever in any sound—whether in some gross or subtle sound—the mind first attaches itself, having become fixed there, one should become well-stabilized, becoming perfectly steady in that very sound, and by means of that...
The meaning is that it dissolves together with, or simultaneously with, the *nāda*; it becomes absorbed.

Here, by the first statement, *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal) is described; by the second, *dhāraṇā* (concentration); and by the third, through the gateway of *dhyāna* (meditation), *samādhi* (absorption) is stated. || 89 ||

Regarding the verse beginning with *makarandam*: just as a bee (*bhṛṅga*) drinking (*piban*) or sucking (*dhayan*) the nectar (*makaranda*)— the essence of flowers— does not require (*nāpekṣate*) nor desire (*icchati*) fragrance, so too the mind (*citta*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), when attached to sound (*nādāsakta*), [does not require] sense objects.

Objects such as garlands, sandalwood paste, women, and so forth, are called *viṣayas* because they bind the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) through their own attachment; he does not desire them, nor does he long for them. The word "hi" indicates certainty.
As for "the mind": objects such as sound and the rest are themselves the garden or grove (*udyāna-vana*), and it is there that [the mind] moves.
His mind itself is a rutting lordly elephant wandering in the garden of sense-objects because it is difficult to restrain;
its very roar is the sound of the unstruck cymbal (*anāhata-dhvani*), which serves as a sharp goad capable of turning it back through disciplined practice. By these [means]...
By means of verses: The withdrawal of the senses, such as the eyes and so forth, from their respective objects in due order—that is proclaimed as *pratyāhāra*.
The withdrawal of the sense organs from their objects is *pratyāhāra*.
Thus has withdrawal (pratyāhāra), as defined above, been described. || 91 ||
p. 172) || Root Text ||
But when the mind, having abandoned its restlessness, is bound by the binding of the *nāda*, it attains extreme steadiness, like a bird whose wings have been clipped. (92)
Having abandoned all thoughts, one who desires the sovereignty of yoga should, with an attentive mind, focus exclusively upon the Sound (Nāda). || 93 ||
Sound acts as a snare for the deer of the inner essence in the act of slaying it.
And he acts as a hunter even toward the killing of the deer within his own inner self. || 94 ||
Regarding the phrase "but bound": *nāda* itself is the bond (*bandha*). It is called a bond because one is bound by it; it is the means of binding.

By that [means], through its own power—that is, by bringing [the senses] under its own control—it is "bound," meaning it has attained a state as if it were bound. The sense is that it is attached to the concentration on *nāda* and so forth.

For this very reason, the mind by which fickleness— consisting of the moment-to-moment grasping and abandoning of sense objects— is completely abandoned, attains extreme steadiness and reaches a state of perfect concentration (*dhāraṇā*). Regarding this, he states an illustration:

Just as a bird (*khaga*) that flies in the sky has its two wings clipped, so too, by means of this breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one brings the vital air under control, and by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the senses;
thereafter, one should establish the stability of the mind upon a virtuous object (*śubhāśraye*). Upon a virtuous object.
The fixing of the mind is called *dhāraṇā*; thus has the definition of *dhāraṇā* been stated. || 92 ||

"Having abandoned all thought" means having relinquished and cast aside the thinking and contemplation regarding all external and internal objects; with a mind that is attentive and one-pointed, [one attains] the sovereignty of the yogas, which is the state of being a sovereign (samrāṭ).

The word *yoga* ends in the suffix *ac* according to the rule beginning with *arśas*. It means, in effect, "the state of being a royal yogi" (*rājayogitva*). By a man who desires—that is, who longs for this—only *nāda*, the sound of the *anāhata* [cakra], is to be pursued and contemplated; it is a continuous flow of mental modifications in the form of *nāda*.
The meaning is that it must be practiced.

By this, O King, that meditation—which is a continuous flow of one-pointed cognition of that [object] and free from desire for anything else—is accomplished through the first six limbs. In that regard:
"Meditation (dhyāna) is the one-pointed continuity of cognition"—thus has the definition of meditation already stated been declared. || 93 ||
"Sound is the inner [snare]" means: sound is the inner mind itself;

it acts as a snare (*vāgurā*)—that is, it behaves like a net—for the binding, or the removal of the restlessness, of the *sāraṅga* deer. Just as a snare, by means of its binding, [removes] the restlessness of the *sāraṅga* deer...
p. 173) || Root Text ||
For the internal horse of the self-controlled practitioner, the practice of sound acts as a tethering post;
therefore, it must indeed be constantly maintained by the yogin. 95.
Bound and rendered motionless through the digestion of mercury (nāda) and sulfur (gandhaka), the mind attains the state of mercury and wanders in the sky known as the "unsupported. || 96 ||

The meaning is that *nāda* removes [distraction] in the same way; it removes the restlessness of the internal organ by its own power. The "internal organ" is the mind itself, which is like a *sāraṅga* deer;
its "binding" consists precisely in the production and removal of various mental modifications—that is, the binding of the mind.

"Vyādhāyate" means he acts like a hunter. Just as a hunter kills a deer caught in a snare, so too does sound kill the mind that is attached to it; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "of the internal": it refers to the internal mind of the *yamī*, the practitioner of yoga.

"Due to the restlessness of the horse," means that the neighing acts like a crossbar at the door of the stable; the word "neighing" is to be understood as the subject. Just as a stable crossbar prevents a horse from going elsewhere, so too does the sound [prevent] the internal [mind]—this is the meaning.

For this reason, the yogi must constantly—every single day—fix his attention upon the worship, that is, the meditative practice, of Nāda. The particle *hi* is an indeclinable used here to express certainty. 95.

"Bound" (baddha) means as follows: *nāda* itself is the *gaṃdhaka*, a specific secondary element (*upadhātu*); by means of that, there is "digestion" (*jāraṇa*), which is the process of making [the mercury] digestible.

Through the connection with *nāda-gaṃdhaka*, the removal of volatility occurs; therefore, it is "bound," being solely intent upon *nāda*. In another sense, it has attained the form of a pill (*guṭikākṛti*).

Therefore, it is that by which fickleness— which consists of transformations into the forms of various objects— has been liberated and abandoned; in another sense, it is the mind from which greed has been released, for the mind itself is like mercury (pārada), being inherently restless.
That which has "Brahman without support" as its name is called "Nirālambākhya"; that very [reality] is the root. (p. 174) || Root Text ||
From hearing the sound, the internal serpent quickly forgets everything;
with one-pointed focus, it no longer runs anywhere. || 97 ||
Fire set ablaze in wood is extinguished along with the wood;
the mind set in motion by the *nāda* dissolves along with the *nāda*. (98)
For the deer of the internal organ that is transfixed by the sound of the bell and other instruments, even striking it down is easy, provided one is skilled in aiming the arrow. || 99 ||
Commentary:

Because it is delimited by space (*kha*), "wandering in that" means a continuous flow of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) in the form of that [space]. In this context, it results in traveling through the sky; just as mercury, when bound, causes one to travel through the sky, so too does the mind when bound.
The meaning is that one makes the flow of the mental modification in the form of Brahman uninterrupted. || 96 ||

"Nādeti" means: from hearing—that is, listening to—the *nāda*, which is the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*), the internal mind itself quickly and swiftly [becomes still]. Because of its fickleness and because it is fond of sound, the mind is likened to a serpent (*bhujaṅgama*). Thus, the mind assumes the form of a serpent.

Having forgotten the entire universe and rendered it an object of oblivion, being one-pointed and possessing a continuous flow of mental modification in the form of *nāda*, he does not run toward nor even make a movement toward any other object whatsoever. By the subsequent verses concerning meditation, [the text describes] that very state of his.
"That which is the grasping of the true nature [of the object] free from conceptual construction, produced by the mind through meditation—
that is designated as *samādhi*," according to the definition stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*; that very state is what appears as the object alone (*arthamātranirbhāsa*).
And by the definition stated in the Pātañjala Sūtra, "samādhi is as if devoid of its own nature," the samādhi characterized as *saṃprajñāta* has been described. || 97 ||

Regarding the word "wood": just as fire set ablaze or ignited in a piece of wood—namely, a log—is extinguished along with the wood, casting off its form as a flame and remaining in the form of that [wood] alone; even so, [the sound] set in motion within the *nāda*...

The mind dissolves along with the sound (nāda). Through the destruction of the Rajasic and Tamasic modifications, it becomes a residue of Sattva alone, remaining as a mere latent impression (saṃskāra).
Regarding this, there is a mantra from the Maitrāyaṇīyas: "Just as a fire without fuel..."
It subsides in its own source; likewise, through the cessation of its fluctuations, the mind subsides in its own source. || 98 ||

"Beginning with the bell" (ghaṇṭādi) means those things for which the bell is the first—namely, the conch, the mṛdaṅga drum, the jharjhara drum, the dundubhi drum, the clouds, and so forth; these are "those beginning with the bell. Of them...
p. 175) || Root Text ||
The resonance that is perceived of the unstruck sound (anāhata-śabda), within which the mind—which is itself within the object of knowledge—is dissolved;
that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu. || 100 ||
As long as sound proceeds, there is the conceptualization of space; that which is beyond sound is the Supreme Brahman, celebrated as the Paramātman. || 1 ||
Commentary:
Your sound is not attached to them; for that very reason, you are "stabdha," meaning motionless.

In the case of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it is the weapon for striking the deer—the antelope—that is the internal organ itself, serving to obstruct various mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*). In the case of the actual deer, however:
Striking or killing is like [the action] of an arrow; for the wind moving swiftly,
in the alternative of its restraint in the Brahma-aperture via the path of the Suṣumnā, it is like the aiming of an arrow—
that is, the fixing of a shaft upon a bow— and he is skilled therein.
If it is wholesome, it is easy; it can be performed with ease. || 99 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the unstruck": that sound, the resonance or resonance-sound (*nirhāda*) of the unstruck sound (*anāhata-śabda*), which is perceived—that is, heard—within that sound, there exists the light (*jyotis*) to be known, which is self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśa-caitanya*); it is situated within that which is to be known.

The internal organ, the mind, which has assumed the form of the object of knowledge, dissolves into that very object of knowledge through supreme dispassion; it becomes devoid of all mental modifications, remaining as a mere residue of latent impressions (saṃskāra) within the pervasive Self of Viṣṇu.

Because it is devoid of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the supreme mental modification (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti), it is "without adjunct" (nirupādhika); it is called a "foot" (pada) because it is reached or attained by yogis as their true nature (svarūpa). || 100 ||
Regarding the word "tāvat": as long as the unstruck sound (anāhata-dhvani) proceeds and is heard, for that long there occurs the perfect conceptualization of space (ākāśa).
Because sound is a quality of space, and because of the distinction between a quality and its possessor, [there is a connection] of sound with the mind.
Upon dissolution, that which is silent and devoid of sound is the Supreme Brahman—

that which is denoted by the term "Supreme Brahman" and is celebrated as the "Paramātman" (the Supreme Self). It is He who, when all mental modifications have dissolved, remains established in His own essential nature.
The intended meaning is that it is expressed by the two terms "Supreme Brahman" (parabrahman) and "Supreme Self" (paramātman). || 1 ||
Root Text (mūla) (p. 176)
Whatever is heard in the form of sound is indeed Śakti;
that which is the end of reality, formless, is the Supreme Lord himself.
All methods of Haṭha and Laya Yoga are for the sake of attaining Rājayoga; a person who has ascended to Rājayoga is a deceiver of Time (death). || 3 ||
Reality is the seed, forceful effort is the field, and equanimity is the water; by these three [the tree of liberation grows].
The wish-fulfilling creeper of the Unmani state arises immediately. || 4 ||
Commentary:

"Whatever [is heard]" means that whatever is heard or perceived in the form of *nāda* (sound) or as the unstruck resonance (*anāhata-dhvani*), that is indeed Śakti. That in which there is the dissolution (*laya*) of all principles (*tattva*)—that is, the end of the principles—is thus;
it is formless (*nirākāra*), devoid of shape, and that alone is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

The meaning is that the Self is that which remains in its own essential nature when all mental modifications have ceased. Through these verses beginning with "Fire set in motion in wood," the asamprajñāta-samādhi—also known by the synonym rājayoga—is described. || 2 ||
"All" refers to the following: *haṭha* and *laya* constitute *haṭhalaya*; the means for these two are the *haṭhalayopāyas*.

The *haṭhopāyas* consist of postures (*āsana*), breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*), and gestures (*mudrā*). The *layopāyas* consist of the contemplation of sound (*nādānusaṃdhāna*), the *śāṃbhavīmudrā*, and so forth. [These are the means] for the mind of *rājayoga*.

The ellipsis is that these [methods] are taught for the sake of the accomplishment, that is, the perfection, of that which is characterized by the cessation of all mental fluctuations. A person who has ascended to *rājayoga*— meaning one who has properly ascended or attained it—
is a "deceiver of time," meaning such a person deceives or conquers *kāla*, i.e., death.
The word "syāt" (might be) is to be supplied as the remainder. || 3 ||

Regarding the term "tattva": *tattva* is the mind (*citta*), which is the seed because it transforms into the form of the sprout that is the state of *unmanī*. *Haṭha* is the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) characterized by the unification of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, [which acts] like a field.
In *prāṇāyāma*, there is indifference toward the arising of the wish-fulfilling creeper of the *unmanī* state.
177) [Root Text]
Through constant contemplation of the internal sound (nāda), the accumulations of sin are destroyed;
the mind and the vital breath certainly dissolve into the stainless state.
And he never hears the sound of conchs or kettledrums.
Through the state of Unmanī, the body certainly becomes like a piece of wood.
Freed from all states and devoid of all thought, that yogi remains as if dead;
he is liberated, of this there is no doubt. || 7 ||
Commentary:

Supreme detachment (*paravairāgya*) is its water, because it is the cause of its arising. A specific mental impression (*saṃskāraviśeṣa*) caused by supreme detachment is "non-cognitive" (*asaṃprajñāta*) samādhi, according to its definition. By these three [elements], that very state is the non-cognitive samādhi of *unmanī*.
Because it accomplishes all desired objects, the Kalpalatikā immediately—that is, very quickly—sets forth, becomes active, and comes into being. || 4 ||
"Always": always, at all times,
through the continuous pursuit of the *nāda* (the primordial sound) and the constant contemplation of the *nāda*, the accumulations of sin— the multitudes of sins—
are destroyed and perish, certainly and irrevocably, within the stainless and attributeless Consciousness (*caitanya*).
The mind-wind and the mental-vitality dissolve; they become completely dissolved. || 5 ||

The state of the yogi who has attained the stage of *unmanī* is described by eight verses, beginning with "the conch and the drum. "Conch" (*śaṅkha*) refers to a shell-born creature, and "drum" (*dundubhi*) refers to a specific type of musical instrument; [the verse speaks of] their sound or resonance at any time, on any occasion whatsoever.

At that time, one does not hear [any external sound]. "Conch and drum" is an elliptical expression for sound in general. By means of the state of *unmanī*, the body certainly becomes like a piece of wood; the meaning is that it becomes motionless. || 6 ||
That yoga which is specifically liberated from— the five states of emergence characterized by waking, dreaming, deep sleep, fainting, and death— and which is devoid of,
or separated from, all thoughts and memories.
The cessation of all mental fluctuations has occurred for this [yogi]; thus, [he is] a *muni*.
(p. 178) || Root Text ||
The yogi who is absorbed in samādhi is not devoured by time, nor is he afflicted by karma; he cannot be overcome by anyone at all. || 8 ||
Neither smell, nor taste, nor form, nor touch, nor sound.
The yogi, disciplined in meditative absorption, knows neither himself nor another.
The mind is neither asleep nor awake, being free from both mindfulness and forgetfulness.
Commentary:

The yogi who possesses the fourth state (turya) is liberated while still living; he is liberated even in this life because, upon the cessation of all mental fluctuations (vṛtti), the self abides in its own essential nature (svarūpa). This has been stated in the Pātañjala Sūtra: "Then the seer (draṣṭṛ) abides in his own nature."
The rest is clear. || 7 ||

"He is not devoured" means that the yogi, endowed with samādhi, is not devoured—that is, not eaten—nor slain by Time, which is death. He is not afflicted by action performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious; he is not distressed by the production of birth, death, and so forth.

And likewise, in the section on Samādhi, there is a Patañjali Sūtra: "From that, there is the cessation of afflictions and karma. This cannot be accomplished, nor can it be made to be accomplished, by any other person or by means such as mechanical devices and mantras. || 8 ||
They do not smell. The yogi endowed with meditative concentration does not perceive a fragrance—whether pleasant or unpleasant;
nor a taste, which is of six kinds, distinguished as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, astringent, and bitter;
nor a form, which is of seven kinds, distinguished as white, blue, yellow, red, green, brown, and variegated.
He does not perceive touch—whether cold, hot, or neither-hot-nor-cold;
nor sound—whether the resonance of a conch, a drum, the ocean, or clouds, whether external or internal;
nor does he perceive himself as the body, nor another as a separate person; this applies to all [objects].
According to Amara, the word *ātman* refers to the body, the vital breath (*dhṛti*), the individual soul (*jīva*), one's own nature (*svabhāva*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). (9)

Regarding the term *citta*: the *citta*, which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), of that yogin is not asleep, because of the absence of the obscuring *tamas* within the three-fold internal organ. (p. 179)
Root Text
He for whom there is neither setting nor rising is indeed liberated in this way. || 10 ||
The yogi who is disciplined in meditative absorption does not perceive cold or heat, nor likewise pain or pleasure; he perceives neither honor nor dishonor. 11.
Established in his true nature, he remains in the waking state as if asleep.
Deprived of both inhalation and exhalation, he is certainly liberated. || 12 ||

When *sattva* and *rajas* are overcome and *tamas*, which veils all the faculties, becomes manifest, then, due to the absence of the internal organ’s transformation into the form of objects, it is called "asleep.
It is not waking, because there is no apprehension of objects through the senses. This state involves both memory and forgetfulness.
It is devoid of memory and forgetfulness.
Due to the absence of any general mental modification (*vṛtti*) and the absence of any stimulus for awakening, it is devoid of memory;
due to the absence of any latent impression (*saṃskāra*) conducive to memory, it is devoid of forgetfulness. Nor does it...
It goes to destruction; it reaches [an end], because the mind remains as a mere residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

It does not arise; it does not manifest, because no mental modification (*vṛtti*) is produced. Thus, he is indeed liberated—liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)—and does not perceive [anything]. Endowed with *samādhi*, the yogi [perceives] both cold and heat.
"Cold and heat" is a collective dvandva compound. Neither cold nor heat is suffering; rather, it is [suffering] produced by another, such as being beaten and so forth. Neither is it happiness;
rather, it is a means to happiness, such as the anointing with fragrant sandalwood and so forth. And likewise in the sense of "artha": [it refers to the object].
"He does not perceive honor performed by others, nor disrespect, nor lack of regard"—this verbal phrase applies to each sentence. || 11 ||

"Healthy" (svastha) means one whose senses and internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) are serene; by this, states such as drowsiness and fainting are excluded. By the phrase "in the waking state," the dream and deep sleep states are ruled out. "Like one asleep" (suptavat) means equal to one who is sleeping.

The yogi who remains—meaning he stays—devoid of the activity of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), is [described as such]. The reflexive voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here according to the rule *samavapravibhyaḥ sthaḥ*. He is devoid of inhalation and exhalation;
inhalation (*niśvāsa*) is the drawing in of external air into the cavity of the chest, while [exhalation is] that of what resides within the cavity...
The exhalation of air is *ucchvāsa*; it is also connected here that he remains devoid of those two. This is certain. (p.
Root Text
Invulnerable to all weapons, impossible for any embodied being to overcome, and ungraspable by mantras or yantras, the yogi remains absorbed in meditative concentration.
Commentary:
He is undoubtedly liberated. The nature of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) has been described by Dattātreya:
"One who is perfected in the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) should then practice samādhi;
in just twelve days, he shall attain samādhi by restraining the vital breath."
The wise one shall certainly become liberated while living. || 12 ||

"Unslayable"—this refers to the yogi who is endowed with *samādhi*. The genitive case in "of all weapons" (*sarvaśastrāṇām*) expresses a general relationship; the meaning is "by all weapons. "Unslayable" means he is joined [with such power] that he cannot be killed. This also applies to the phrase "of all embodied beings" (*sarvadehinām*).

The sixth case (genitive) is used here to express mere relationship. "Incapable" (*aśakya*) means he cannot be overcome by force by any embodied beings; he is ungraspable by means of mantras and yantras, including those intended for subjugation, killing, expulsion, and other such results.

It is impossible to bring under control. Thus, many obstacles arise for the yogi who has attained yoga. Because the knowledge of those [obstacles] is required for their removal, they too are shown. Dattātreya says: "Laziness is the first obstacle; of the second..."

It is proclaimed: "The assembly of rogues previously mentioned is the third; the accomplishment of mantras is the fourth; and alchemy (dhātuvāda) shall be the [fifth]—so know those who understand Yoga.
Thus it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "For when obstacles arise, they are indeed perceived within oneself."
I shall fully declare those [paths] of the yogins; listen to me in brief.

A man who desires objects of longing—whether ritual acts for specific ends, as well as the fruits of desire, women, the results of giving, knowledge, illusion, base metals, wealth, or precious gems—[pursues these paths].

The state of divinity, the lordship over the immortals, the practice of elixirs for rejuvenation, Mount Meru, ascetic exertion, sacrifice, as well as entering water and fire, the fruits of ancestral rites (śrāddha) and the giving of power, likewise the observances, fasting, works of public utility (pūrta), and even the worship of gods and ancestors— [all these are attained through this].

"Afflicted by guests and ritual duties, one desires [worldly things]; thus an obstacle may arise—by effort, the yogin should turn it away. Making the mind unattached to Brahman, he is liberated from these afflictions. Thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa.
When his mind is not distracted by these obstacles, then he attains that supreme Brahman which is exceedingly difficult to reach. As stated in the *Yogabhāskara*:
"Relying on sattvic fortitude, the yogi, well-stabilized through sattva, [perceives] the attributeless [Brahman] with the mind."

"Meditating thus, one is liberated from obstacles. One who practices yoga in this manner, free from desire for the status of Indra and other gods, and having abandoned the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), becomes a sage liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). For fear of prolixity, I have not mentioned the many obstacles that exist.
For by means of meditation, the Yoginī is indeed to be restrained from Viṣṇu and Hara. || 13 ||
p. 181) || Root Text ||
As long as the moving breath does not enter the central channel, and as long as the bindu does not become firm due to the continuous flow of the vital wind;
Commentary:
Refuting the knowledge of non-yogins, he states that knowledge belongs only to yogins.

"Until"—meaning, as long as the vital air (prāṇavāyu), moving and traveling within the central channel (suṣumnā) along the middle path, does not enter; that is, until it enters thoroughly up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). [This refers to] one who has reached the aperture of Brahmā.
The meaning is that because of its steadiness, having reached the *brahmarandhra*, it does not remain stable;

[thus] the wind (*vāyu*) that does not move within the *suṣumnā* is called "unaccomplished" (*asiddha*). As it is said in the *Amṛtasiddhi*: "As long as the wind moving through the path is not indeed motionless..."
One should know that to be unaccomplished which moves through the middle [channel], following the wind (vāyu) under the influence of karma.
Because it breathes and gives life, it is called *prāṇa*; and since it is both that *prāṇa* and a wind (*vāta*), it is the *prāṇavāta*.
Through its continuous restraint—that is, by making it steady through *kuṃbhaka*—the seminal essence (*bindu-vīrya*) becomes firm.
The vital breath (*prāṇavāta*) does not become stable; it was stated in this very [work] previously that the stability of the *bindu* is [attained] through the stability of the mind.

When the mind is stable, the wind becomes stable, and from that, the *bindu* becomes stable. In the absence of that, however, there is failure for the yogin. This has been stated in the *Amṛtasiddhi*:

As long as this mercury, which is the very form of Brahman, remains situated within the body, that man is considered bound and unperfected, still subject to worldly existence. One should know such a man to be unperfected and lacking in celibacy, mired in old age and death.

Regarding the phrase "the basis of all afflictions": as long as the mind remains within meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), the meditative object-mind does not become similar to the innate (*sahaja*) state; because of the flow of mental activity directed toward an objective form that is merely adventitious, it neither arises nor exists as such due to the persistence of the vital breath (*prāṇavāta*).
The principle of the "lamp on the threshold" (dehalīdīpanyāya) applies here as well.

It is stated in the *Amṛtasiddhi* that when the breath is stabilized, the mind becomes stable: "When this breath is restrained within the central channel through the practice of the middle [path], then the bindu and the consciousness-mind die along with the breath."

Indeed, in the absence of that [state], non-attainment (*asiddhatva*) is stated in the *Amṛtasiddhi*: "As long as the mind wavers toward external and internal objects, one should know that mind to be unaccomplished (*asiddha*), being still possessed of the qualities of karma. Whatever verbal knowledge anyone may speak during that time—
How can this knowledge be characterized by hypocrisy and false prattle?
"Hypocrisy" refers to the speaking of knowledge with the thought, "May I become honored in the world by the pretense of possessing knowledge";
"false prattle" means false speech; that is to say, speech preceded by hypocrisy.

In the absence of victory over the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the bindu, and the mind, there is an absence of gnosis (*jñāna*), and consequently, saṃsāra is difficult to ward off. As it is said in the *Amṛtasiddhi*:
"When this wind moves, then the bindu is said to move; when the bindu moves..."

"The mind is as fickle as that very body upon which it rests. When the *bindu* (vital essence) wavers, when the mind wavers, and when the vital air (*vāyu*) wavers, the world is constantly born and dies; this word is the truth, the absolute truth.
It is also stated in the *Yogabīja*: "If the mind is utterly destroyed, then indeed [the Self] shines forth there."

Even the destruction of the vital breath (*marut*) is well-known; however, if it were not so, there would be neither scripture for it, nor self-realization, nor a teacher, nor liberation. By this, [it is shown that] through the conquest of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the drop (*bindu*), and the mind (*manas*), [liberation occurs] by means of knowledge.
p. 182) || Root Text ||
As long as reality does not arise in meditation as something innate, so long that which is called "knowledge" is merely hypocrisy and false prattle. || 14 ||

Thus ends the fourth instruction, titled "The Characteristics of Samādhi," in the *Haṭhapradīpikā* composed by the lord of yogins, Svātmārāma, the wish-fulfilling gem of the lineage of Śrī Sahajānanda.
The number of root verses is 393. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Commentary:

It has been indicated that liberation shall indeed belong to the yogin. As it is said in the *Amṛtasiddhi*: "The drop (*bindu*) reaches that very state which the wind (*vāyu*) reaches; for as the wind is accomplished, so is the accomplishment of the drop. When swooned (*mūrchita*), it removes disease; when increased (*vṛddha*), [it bestows immortality]."
One should lead [the mind] to the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratā*). When absorbed and motionless, it bestows all perfections and grants liberation.
Just as is the condition of the *bindu*, so too is the condition of the mind (*citta*).
Now, indeed, three types of yoga have been taught by me with the desire to bring about the welfare of men: knowledge (*jñāna*), action (*karman*)...

If it is asked: "Since devotion (*bhakti*) and [knowledge] are also means, and there is no other means anywhere—thus the three means to liberation have been taught by the Blessed One—how is it that *yoga* alone is stated to be the means to liberation? The answer is:
because they are included within the limbs of *yoga*. To explain: "The Self, indeed, my dear... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad).

The scriptures state, "It is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon," thereby prescribing hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*nididhyāsana*) as the means for the direct realization of the Self, which is the instrument for attaining the supreme human goal. Among these, regarding hearing and reflection:
The two [observances] included within the limb of self-study (*svādhyāya*) are [truthfulness and restraint of the senses].
Self-study consists in the study of the scriptures concerning liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*); and that should be understood as culminating in the ascertainment of the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).

Since the determination of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) occurs through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), these two are included within the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*). This was stated by Yājñavalkya in his exposition of the observances (*niyama*): "Hearing the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is declared to be the hearing of the Vedānta."
By the word "by the wise" (budhaiḥ), it is clearly stated that hearing [the scripture] is included within the observances (niyama).
As it is said: "The study of the Veda, or the Sūtras, or the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas; the recitation word by word, and constant practice—this is remembered as Japa."
It has been stated that *manana* (reflection), characterized by the continuous contemplation through reasonings and consisting of constant practice, is also included within the *niyamas*.
This [reflection] consists of a flow of homogeneous mental states preceded by the cessation of heterogeneous mental states.
Contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), as defined above, is included within meditation (*dhyāna*).
Furthermore, that [meditation], through the means of self-realization (*ātmasākṣātkāra*) by means of samādhi— which is its matured form—
becomes a cause for liberation when performed with the intention of dedicating it to the Lord (*īśvarārpaṇabuddhi*).

The inclusion of *karmayoga*—characterized by the performance of action without desire for fruit—within *kriyāyoga* occurs as follows: Patañjali has stated that "asceticism (*tapas*), self-study (*svādhyāya*), and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) constitute *kriyāyoga*," which is included among the observances (*niyamas*). Among these, asceticism...
